method: The authors use theoretical analysis and experimental demonstrations with trapped ions to study string-breaking dynamics under adiabatic and diabatic conditions.
result: They identify experimentally accessible regimes where string breaking exhibits rich quantum dynamics beyond simple breaking, including oscillatory and multi-string behavior.
conclusion: The work provides new probes of string breaking and demonstrates that confining strings can display complex quantum dynamics, relevant for quantum simulation and thermodynamics.

title: Maximizing The Nondemolition Nature Of A Quantum Measurement Via An Adaptive Readout Protocol
authors: Arjen Vaartjes, Rocky Yue Su, Laura A. O’neill, Paul Steinacker, Gauri Goenka, Mark R. van Blankenstein, Xi Yu, Benjamin Wilhelm, Alexander M. Jakob, Fay E. Hudson, Kohei M. Itoh, Chih Hwan Yang, Andrew S. Dzurak, David N. Jamieson, Martin Nurizzo, Danielle Holmes, Arne Laucht, And Andrea Morello
abstract:
Author(s): Arjen Vaartjes, Rocky Yue Su, Laura A. O’Neill, Paul Steinacker, Gauri Goenka, Mark R. van Blankenstein, Xi Yu, Benjamin Wilhelm, Alexander M. Jakob, Fay E. Hudson, Kohei M. Itoh, Chih Hwan Yang, Andrew S. Dzurak, David N. Jamieson, Martin Nurizzo, Danielle Holmes, Arne Laucht, and Andrea Morello

Adaptive subspace-switching readout improves nondemolition measurements in multilevel quantum systems, boosting qudit readout fidelity to 99.61% while reducing measurement time and mitigating measurement-induced errors across platforms.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020330] Published Fri May 15, 2026.
tldr: An adaptive readout protocol improves nondemolition measurements in multilevel quantum systems, achieving 99.61% readout fidelity while reducing measurement time and errors.
motivation: Quantum measurements in multilevel systems (qudits) often suffer from demolition errors and long readout times, limiting their use in quantum information processing. The authors aim to enhance the nondemolition nature of measurements to preserve quantum states for subsequent operations.
method: The protocol uses adaptive subspace-switching readout, where the measurement basis is dynamically adjusted based on prior outcomes to minimize disturbance. This is implemented on a silicon quantum dot platform with spin qudits.
result: The adaptive readout achieves a readout fidelity of 99.61% and reduces measurement-induced errors, outperforming standard readout schemes. The method is demonstrated across multiple qudit levels and is platform-agnostic.
conclusion: Adaptive readout significantly improves the nondemolition character of quantum measurements, enabling higher-fidelity state preparation and more efficient quantum error correction in multilevel systems.

title: Sparse non-Markovian Noise Modeling Of Transmon-Based Multi-Qubit Operations
authors: Yasuo Oda, Kevin Schultz, Leigh Norris, Omar Shehab, And Gregory Quiroz
abstract:
Author(s): Yasuo Oda, Kevin Schultz, Leigh Norris, Omar Shehab, and Gregory Quiroz

A comprehensive noise modeling approach for transmon-based quantum processors captures complex spatiotemporally correlated errors, achieving a sevenfold improvement in accuracy when used as a hardware proxy simulator for variational algorithms.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020327] Published Tue May 12, 2026.
tldr: A sparse non-Markovian noise model for transmon-based multi-qubit operations achieves sevenfold improvement in accuracy for variational algorithm simulation.
motivation: Accurate noise modeling is critical for understanding and mitigating errors in transmon-based quantum processors, especially for near-term variational algorithms.
method: The authors develop a sparse non-Markovian noise model that captures complex spatiotemporally correlated errors in transmon qubits, using a hardware proxy simulator.
result: The model achieves a sevenfold improvement in accuracy compared to standard noise models when simulating variational algorithms.
conclusion: Sparse non-Markovian noise modeling significantly enhances the fidelity of simulations for transmon-based multi-qubit operations, aiding in error mitigation and algorithm development.

title: Leakage-Protected Idle Operation Of A Triangular Exchange-Only Spin Qubit
authors: Joseph D. Broz, Jesse C. Hoke, Edwin Acuna, And Jason R. Petta
abstract:
Author(s): Joseph D. Broz, Jesse C. Hoke, Edwin Acuna, and Jason R. Petta

By tuning the pairwise exchange interactions between three exchange-coupled electrons to be exactly equal, an energy gap between the computational subspace and extraneous levels is created, suppressing leakage errors.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020324] Published Thu May 07, 2026.
tldr: The paper demonstrates a leakage-protected idle operation for a triangular exchange-only spin qubit by tuning exchange interactions to create an energy gap.
motivation: Leakage errors degrade qubit performance; protecting idle operation without active error correction is crucial for scalable quantum computing.
method: The authors tune pairwise exchange interactions between three electrons in a triangular geometry to be equal, opening a gap between computational and leakage states.
result: They achieve suppressed leakage errors during idle operation, improving qubit coherence and fidelity.
conclusion: This approach offers a simple, hardware-efficient method for leakage protection in exchange-only spin qubits, advancing their viability for quantum information processing.

title: Diagnosing Chaos With Projected Ensembles Of Process Tensors
authors: Peter O’donovan, Neil Dowling, Kavan Modi, And Mark T. Mitchison
abstract:
Author(s): Peter O’Donovan, Neil Dowling, Kavan Modi, and Mark T. Mitchison

An approach to probing quantum chaos by repeated interventions is shown to unify techniques for the study and simulation of many-body quantum dynamics.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020322] Published Tue May 05, 2026.
tldr: The paper introduces a method to diagnose quantum chaos using projected ensembles of process tensors, unifying techniques for studying many-body quantum dynamics.
motivation: Understanding and detecting quantum chaos is crucial for characterizing many-body systems, but existing methods often require full state tomography or are limited to specific settings.
method: The authors propose using repeated interventions (process tensors) to construct projected ensembles that capture the chaotic dynamics, leveraging tools from open quantum systems and quantum information.
result: They show that the projected ensemble approach can distinguish chaotic from integrable dynamics and provides a unified framework for various chaos diagnostics, such as out-of-time-ordered correlators and spectral statistics.
conclusion: The method offers a practical and scalable way to probe quantum chaos in experiments, with potential applications in quantum simulation and thermalization studies.

title: Gate Reflectometry In A Minimal Kitaev Chain Device
authors: Yining Zhang, Ivan Kulesh, Sebastiaan L.D. Ten Haaf, Nick van Loo, Francesco Zatelli, Tijl Degroote, Christian G. Prosko, And Srijit Goswami
abstract:
Author(s): Yining Zhang, Ivan Kulesh, Sebastiaan L.D. ten Haaf, Nick van Loo, Francesco Zatelli, Tijl Degroote, Christian G. Prosko, and Srijit Goswami

Radio-frequency gate reflectometry enables fast, noninvasive readout of coupled quantum dot and superconductor systems, resolving key processes and parity dynamics essential for realizing Majorana-based Kitaev chain qubits.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020317] Published Tue Apr 28, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates radio-frequency gate reflectometry for fast, noninvasive readout of a minimal Kitaev chain device, resolving parity dynamics essential for Majorana-based qubits.
motivation: Realizing Majorana-based qubits requires fast and noninvasive readout of quantum dot and superconductor systems to resolve parity states and enable Kitaev chain qubits.
method: The authors use radio-frequency gate reflectometry on a minimal Kitaev chain device, measuring the reflected signal to probe charge and parity dynamics.
result: They achieve fast readout of coupled quantum dot and superconductor systems, resolving key processes and parity dynamics.
conclusion: Gate reflectometry is a viable readout technique for Majorana-based qubits, advancing the development of topological quantum computing.

title: Continuous-variable Quantum Communication
authors: Vladyslav C. Usenko, Antonio Acín, Romain Alléaume, Ulrik L. Andersen, Eleni Diamanti, Tobias Gehring, Adnan A. E. Hajomer, Florian Kanitschar, Christoph Pacher, Stefano Pirandola, And Valerio Pruneri
abstract:
Author(s): Vladyslav C. Usenko, Antonio Acín, Romain Alléaume, Ulrik L. Andersen, Eleni Diamanti, Tobias Gehring, Adnan A. E. Hajomer, Florian Kanitschar, Christoph Pacher, Stefano Pirandola, and Valerio Pruneri

The quantum nature of radiation is not solely corpuscular. In the “continuous-variable” setting, the wavelike quantum properties can be observed. Quantum technologies put this continuous-variable nature of light to use, with applications in various forms of quantum information processing. This review concentrates on the developments of these wave-based techniques in quantum communication. Compared with photon-based (corpuscular) variants, the continuous-variable approach is equally well developed and has certain conceptual and practical advantages.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 015003] Published Mon Mar 23, 2026.
tldr: A comprehensive review of continuous-variable quantum communication, covering protocols, security, and experimental progress.
motivation: Continuous-variable approaches offer practical advantages over discrete-variable methods, such as compatibility with existing telecom infrastructure and high-rate key distribution.
method: The review surveys theoretical foundations (Gaussian states, homodyne detection, reconciliation) and experimental implementations (CV-QKD, entanglement distribution, quantum networks).
result: Continuous-variable quantum communication is now a mature field with record-breaking key rates and long-distance demonstrations, including satellite-based links.
conclusion: CV quantum communication is a viable and competitive technology for practical quantum networks, with ongoing challenges in loss tolerance and security proofs.

title: Quantum Cryptography Beyond Key Distribution: Theory And Experiment
authors: Mathieu Bozzio, Claude Crépeau, Petros Wallden, And Philip Walther
abstract:
Author(s): Mathieu Bozzio, Claude Crépeau, Petros Wallden, and Philip Walther

Cryptography not only involves the sending of secret messages but also encompasses many protocols and procedures that provide privacy and security in the networked world. Likewise, quantum resources have the potential to enhance cryptography in ways that go beyond the well-known example of quantum key distribution. This review offers a classification of the main crypto primitives that are available quantum mechanically. It explains the security that they offer, including the sometimes significant limitations on their theoretical capabilities. Implementations using current photonic techniques are discussed.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045006] Published Fri Dec 19, 2025.
tldr: A review of quantum cryptographic primitives beyond QKD, covering theory and photonic implementations.
motivation: To classify and assess the security of quantum cryptographic protocols beyond key distribution, highlighting their potential and limitations.
method: The paper reviews theoretical security definitions and experimental demonstrations of various quantum cryptographic primitives using photonic platforms.
result: It provides a taxonomy of quantum crypto primitives and discusses their security guarantees and experimental feasibility.
conclusion: Quantum cryptography offers enhanced security for many tasks beyond QKD, but practical implementations face significant challenges.

title: Universality In Driven Open Quantum Matter
authors: Lukas M. Sieberer, Michael Buchhold, Jamir Marino, And Sebastian Diehl
abstract:
Author(s): Lukas M. Sieberer, Michael Buchhold, Jamir Marino, and Sebastian Diehl

Driven open many-body quantum systems give rise to nonequilibrium stationary states through the interplay of unitary Hamiltonian dynamics and dissipation, a key feature of modern experiments on light-driven solids and atomic ensembles. This review explores the different types of universal behavior that emerge in these states and their theoretical classification within nonequilibrium quantum field theory, emphasizing the role of symmetry, topology, and quantum state purity.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025004] Published Thu Jun 12, 2025.
tldr: A review of universal behavior in driven open quantum systems, classifying nonequilibrium stationary states using quantum field theory.
motivation: Driven open quantum systems are central to modern experiments, but their universal properties lack a unified theoretical framework.
method: The authors employ nonequilibrium quantum field theory to classify universal behavior based on symmetry, topology, and quantum state purity.
result: They identify distinct universality classes for driven open quantum matter, linking to known critical phenomena and topological phases.
conclusion: The review provides a systematic classification that can guide future experiments and theory in nonequilibrium quantum thermodynamics.

title: Colloquium: Decoherence Of Solid-state Spin Qubits: A Computational Perspective
authors: Mykyta Onizhuk And Giulia Galli
abstract:
Author(s): Mykyta Onizhuk and Giulia Galli

Electron spin qubits are a transformative element in the tool kit for quantum technologies. Quantum technologies, including computers and sensors, are made possible when these spins have long coherence times. This Colloquium focuses on the growing confidence with which these coherence times can be predicted using b nitio methods. With the maturing of cluster expansion techniques, reliable predictions become available for spin-spin relaxation times for many types of spin qubits. Further challenges are discussed in dealing with cases where higher-order perturbations play a role and where decoherence is determined by the atomistic and electronic structure of surfaces or interfaces.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 021001] Published Fri Apr 04, 2025.
tldr: A review of computational methods for predicting decoherence times of solid-state spin qubits, focusing on cluster expansion techniques.
motivation: Long coherence times are essential for quantum technologies, and predictive computational methods can guide the design of better qubits.
method: The paper reviews ab initio cluster expansion methods to compute spin-spin relaxation times, addressing higher-order perturbations and surface effects.
result: Cluster expansion techniques can reliably predict coherence times for many spin qubit types, but challenges remain for systems with strong higher-order contributions or surface-induced decoherence.
conclusion: Computational predictions of decoherence are becoming increasingly reliable, aiding the development of solid-state spin qubits for quantum computing and sensing.

title: Quantum-information Methods For Quantum Gravity Laboratory-based Tests
authors: Chiara Marletto And Vlatko Vedral
abstract:
Author(s): Chiara Marletto and Vlatko Vedral

It is conceptually possible that gravity is a force of nature that is not describable with a classical theory, but is also not described by a conventional quantum theory. Information-theoretic approaches make it possible to address this general idea in a concrete way, with thought experiments that would constrain the scope of whatever new theory emerges. This review gives the status of these new theoretical approaches, with an emphasis on proposed experiments that look for gravitationally induced entanglement (GIE) between two probes for which quantum theory is known to be applicable. Various potentially feasible tabletop-scale GIE experiments that have been proposed are concretely analyzed.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015006] Published Fri Mar 14, 2025.
tldr: This review explores information-theoretic approaches to testing whether gravity is fundamentally quantum, focusing on gravitationally induced entanglement experiments.
motivation: To determine if gravity must be quantized, as standard quantum theory and classical gravity are incompatible; information-theoretic methods provide a framework to design experiments that can distinguish between classical and quantum gravity.
method: The paper reviews theoretical proposals for tabletop experiments that look for gravitationally induced entanglement (GIE) between two quantum probes, analyzing the information-theoretic constraints and experimental feasibility.
result: Several feasible GIE experiments are identified that could test the quantum nature of gravity, with detailed analysis of their requirements and potential outcomes.
conclusion: Information-theoretic approaches offer a concrete path to experimentally probe the quantum nature of gravity, with GIE experiments being a promising near-term avenue.

title: Simulating Magic State Cultivation With Few Clifford Terms
authors: Kwok Ho Wan, Zhenghao Zhong, And Ainhoa Zapirain
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2134 (2026).

Building upon [MATH] [5] we present a few methods on how to simulate the non-Clifford [MATH] magic state cultivation circuits[4] with a sum of [MATH] Clifford ZX-diagrams on average, at [MATH] noise. Compared to a magic cat state stabiliser decomposition of all [MATH] non-Clifford spiders ([MATH] terms required), this is more than [MATH] times reduction in the number of terms. Our stabiliser decomposition has the advantage of representing the final non-Clifford state (in light of circuit errors) as a sum of Clifford ZX-diagrams. This will be useful in simulating the escape stage of magic state cultivation, where one needs to port the resultant state of cultivation into a larger Clifford circuit with many more qubits. Still, it's necessary to only track [MATH] Clifford terms. Our result sheds light on the simulability of operationally relevant, high [MATH]-count quantum circuits with some internal structure. Finally, we provide numerical results for full non-Clifford stabiliser rank simulation based on [MATH] along with optimisations using our cutting decompositions. Nearly [MATH] shots per second can be obtained on a laptop for the smaller [MATH] circuits at uniform circuit level noise [MATH], making it only [MATH][MATH] times slower than its (circuit-unspecific and un-optimised) fully Clifford proxy simulation via [MATH] using [MATH] gates.

.
tldr: This paper presents methods to simulate magic state cultivation circuits using a sum of few Clifford ZX-diagrams, achieving a significant reduction in the number of terms compared to standard stabiliser decompositions.
motivation: Magic state cultivation is a promising approach for fault-tolerant quantum computing, but simulating the non-Clifford circuits involved is computationally expensive. Efficient simulation methods are needed to study the escape stage and integrate cultivation into larger Clifford circuits.
method: The authors build on previous work to decompose non-Clifford magic state cultivation circuits into a sum of Clifford ZX-diagrams, exploiting internal structure to reduce the number of terms. They also apply optimisations using cutting decompositions and provide numerical simulations.
result: The stabiliser decomposition reduces the number of terms by more than a factor of 10^4 compared to a naive decomposition of all non-Clifford spiders. Numerical simulations achieve nearly 10^5 shots per second on a laptop for small circuits at uniform noise.
conclusion: The proposed method enables efficient simulation of magic state cultivation circuits with high T-count, shedding light on the simulability of operationally relevant quantum circuits with internal structure.

title: Long-time Freeness In The Kicked Top
authors: Elisa Vallini And Silvia Pappalardi
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2129 (2026).

Recent work highlighted the importance of higher-order correlations in quantum dynamics for a deeper understanding of quantum chaos and thermalization. The full Eigenstate Thermalization Hypothesis, the framework encompassing correlations, can be formalized using the language of Free Probability theory. In this context, chaotic dynamics at long times are proposed to lead to free independence or "freeness" of observables. In this work, we investigate these issues in a paradigmatic semiclassical model – the kicked top – which exhibits a transition from integrability to chaos. Despite its simplicity, we identify several non-trivial features. By numerically studying 2n-point out-of-time-order correlators, we show that in the fully chaotic regime, long-time freeness is reached exponentially fast. These considerations lead us to introduce a large deviation theory for freeness that enables us to define and analyze the associated time scale. The numerical results confirm the existence of a hierarchy of different time scales, indicating a multifractal approach to freeness in this model. Our findings provide novel insights into the long-time behavior of chaotic dynamics and may have broader implications for the study of many-body quantum dynamics.

.
tldr: This paper studies the approach to freeness in the kicked top model, revealing exponential convergence and a hierarchy of time scales in chaotic dynamics.
motivation: Understanding higher-order correlations in quantum dynamics is crucial for a deeper theory of quantum chaos and thermalization, and free probability provides a framework to formalize the Eigenstate Thermalization Hypothesis.
method: The authors numerically compute 2n-point out-of-time-order correlators in the kicked top model across integrable and chaotic regimes, and introduce a large deviation theory for freeness to define and analyze the associated time scales.
result: In the fully chaotic regime, long-time freeness is reached exponentially fast, and the numerical results confirm a hierarchy of different time scales indicating a multifractal approach to freeness.
conclusion: The findings provide novel insights into the long-time behavior of chaotic dynamics and may have broader implications for many-body quantum dynamics and thermalization.

title: What Can We Do In A Symmetry-constrained Perspective? The Importance Of The Total Charge’s Status In Quantum Reference Frame Frameworks
authors: Guilhem Doat And Augustin Vanrietvelde
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2126 (2026).

The study of quantum reference frames has received renewed interest over the last years, leading to the parallel development of non-equivalent frameworks by different communities. We clarify the differences between these frameworks. At the mathematical level, they mainly differ in the kind of symmetry (either weak or strong) employed to constrain the system. We show that this mathematical difference corresponds to a fundamental physical question: whether the global charge associated to the symmetry group is accessible to symmetry-constrained observers. In this context, we formulate a definition of a perspective in terms of operational capacities, or lack thereof. Turning to consequences of adopting either approach, we discuss how adopting the weak approach induces an ambiguity in the momenta included in each perspective and bars from defining reversible QRF transformations. We then review and analyze the existing arguments motivating each approach, and show how they bear upon the problem of charge accessibility. Finally, we introduce a simple operational scenario in which upholding two reasonable physical postulates leads to the conclusion that internal observers could measure the global charge by 1/ performing a relativized interference measurement and 2/ classically communicating.

.
tldr: The paper clarifies differences between quantum reference frame frameworks based on weak vs. strong symmetry constraints, linking them to the accessibility of global charge, and shows that internal observers can measure global charge via relativized interference and classical communication.
motivation: Quantum reference frames are studied in multiple communities with non-equivalent frameworks; the paper aims to clarify the mathematical and physical differences, particularly regarding the role of global charge.
method: The authors analyze the mathematical structures of weak and strong symmetry constraints, define perspectives in terms of operational capacities, and introduce a simple operational scenario to test charge accessibility.
result: Weak symmetry induces ambiguity in momenta and prevents reversible QRF transformations; internal observers can measure global charge through a relativized interference measurement and classical communication.
conclusion: The choice of symmetry constraint corresponds to whether global charge is accessible, and the weak approach has limitations for reversible transformations.

title: Catalytic Entanglement Transformations With Noisy Hardware
authors: Hemant Sharma, Aleksandr Mokeev, Jonas Helsen, And Johannes Borregaard
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2117 (2026).

The availability of certain entangled resource states (catalyst states) can enhance the rate of converting several less entangled states into fewer highly entangled states in a process known as catalytic entanglement concentration (EC). Here, we extend catalytic EC from pure states to mixed states and numerically benchmark it against non-catalytic EC and distillation in the presence of state-preparation errors and operational errors. Furthermore, we analyse the re-usability of catalysts in the presence of such errors. To do this, we introduce a novel recipe for determining the positive-operator valued measurements (POVM) required for EC transformations, which allows for making tradeoffs between the number of communication rounds and the number of auxiliary qubits required. We find that in the presence of low operational errors and depolarising noise, catalytic EC can provide better rates than distillation and non-catalytic EC.

.
tldr: Extends catalytic entanglement concentration to mixed states and noisy hardware, benchmarking its performance against non-catalytic methods.
motivation: Catalytic entanglement can enhance conversion rates, but previous work focused on pure states; practical implementations require handling noise and mixed states.
method: Introduces a novel recipe for determining POVMs for entanglement transformations, enabling tradeoffs between communication rounds and auxiliary qubits, and numerically benchmarks catalytic EC under state-preparation and operational errors.
result: Catalytic EC provides better rates than distillation and non-catalytic EC in the presence of low operational errors and depolarising noise.
conclusion: Catalytic entanglement transformations are viable with noisy hardware and can outperform standard methods, with catalysts being reusable under certain error conditions.

title: Fundamental Limits Of non-Hermitian Sensing From Quantum Fisher Information
authors: Jan Wiersig And Stefan Rotter
abstract: Exceptional points (EPs) exhibit strongly enhanced spectral responses and are therefore promising candidates for sensing applications. Whether these non-Hermitian degeneracies provide a genuine advantage in the quantum regime has been the subject of ongoing debate. Here, we address this issue within a scattering-matrix formalism for sensing with coherent light, which allows the quantum Fisher information (QFI) to be evaluated directly from experimentally accessible scattering data without introducing additional noise channels beyond those inherent to the scattering process. We analyze both nondegenerate and degenerate scattering-matrix poles, including EPs of arbitrary order, and show that the QFI per incoming photon flux is bounded and controlled by three key factors: the decay rate of the resonant mode, the strength of the spectral response associated with non-normality, and the adjustment between the scattering states and the information source. For spatially localized perturbations, this implies that the maximal QFI achievable by wavefront shaping is fully determined by the local density of states at the perturbation site. Within this framework, we demonstrate that EPs can enhance the QFI compared to isolated modes or diabolic points with identical decay rates, and that the QFI can be further increased by moving away from the EP toward parameter regimes where non-Hermitian linewidth splitting reduces the decay rate of one mode. We further show that sufficiently small additional internal losses do not alter this overall picture, thereby providing a unified and experimentally relevant perspective on the design of quantum-limited non-Hermitian sensors.
tldr: This paper derives fundamental bounds on non-Hermitian sensing using quantum Fisher information, showing that exceptional points can enhance sensitivity but are not optimal when considering decay rates.
motivation: Exceptional points are promising for sensing due to enhanced spectral response, but whether they provide a genuine quantum advantage is debated. The authors aim to clarify this using a quantum Fisher information framework.
method: The authors use a scattering-matrix formalism to evaluate quantum Fisher information directly from scattering data, analyzing nondegenerate and degenerate poles including exceptional points of arbitrary order.
result: The quantum Fisher information per photon is bounded by decay rate, non-normality, and mode matching; exceptional points can enhance QFI compared to isolated modes, but moving away from the EP can further increase QFI by reducing decay rate.
conclusion: Exceptional points do not provide a universal advantage; optimal sensing requires balancing spectral enhancement with decay rates, and the framework offers a unified perspective for quantum-limited non-Hermitian sensors.

title: Observation Of Phase Doubling And Entanglement In Coherent Matter-wave Reactions
authors: Shu Nagata, Tadej Mežnaršič, Chuixin Kong And Cheng Chin
abstract: Chemical reactions in a statistical ensemble are conventionally regarded as incoherent processes driven by thermodynamics. In the quantum degenerate regime, where atoms and molecules form coherent matter waves, reactions are theoretically described by nonlinear mixing of matter-wave fields. In this scenario, we expect phase matching between reactants and products, analogous to the mixing of photonic fields in nonlinear optics. Here we report on the observation of phase coherent reaction dynamics of Bose-condensed atoms and molecules near a Feshbach resonance. Using matter-wave diffraction with optical lattices, we verify spatial coherence of both atoms and molecules and observe phase doubling when atomic waves combine into molecular waves, the matter-wave analogue of optical frequency doubling. The diffraction patterns further reveal two-atom entanglement generated during the reaction. Our observations establish phase coherence and entanglement generation as two essential features of ‘quantum many-body chemistry’. Moreover, our work opens a pathway to control of reaction dynamics by manipulation of matter-wave phases.
tldr: Observation of phase doubling and entanglement in coherent matter-wave reactions of Bose-condensed atoms and molecules near a Feshbach resonance.
motivation: To demonstrate phase coherence and entanglement generation in quantum many-body chemistry, analogous to nonlinear optics.
method: Matter-wave diffraction with optical lattices to verify spatial coherence and detect phase doubling and entanglement.
result: Phase doubling observed when atomic waves combine into molecular waves; diffraction patterns reveal two-atom entanglement.
conclusion: Establishes phase coherence and entanglement as key features of quantum many-body chemistry, enabling phase-controlled reaction dynamics.

title: Fermionic Hamiltonian Engineering With Local Control
authors: \"ozg\"un Kum, Matthias Zipper, Ludwig Mathey, Martin Kliesch
abstract: ArXiv:2606.17158v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum simulators enable the exploration of complex quantum phenomena in condensed-matter systems by reproducing their dynamics on controllable quantum devices. However, experimental constraints often restrict the class of Hamiltonians that can be realized natively. Hamiltonian engineering addresses this limitation by expanding the set of accessible target Hamiltonians from a fixed system Hamiltonian defined by the hardware. We introduce a new framework for fermionic Hamiltonian engineering based on conjugating free evolution under the system Hamiltonian with sequences of experimentally feasible local fermionic unitaries. The required sequences and free-evolution times are obtained efficiently via a linear program. By interleaving system evolution with these local unitaries, our method realizes effective time evolution under a broad class of target Hamiltonians, with intrinsic robustness to finite-pulse-time errors. In particular, we demonstrate that arbitrary complex tunnelling coefficients can be realized, constrained only by the connectivity of the underlying system Hamiltonian. We illustrate this capability by engineering the dynamics of the non-interacting Harper-Hofstadter model on a 1088-mode lattice and an interacting Fermi-Hubbard chain with complex tunnelling coefficients. By construction, our approach avoids the continuous energy absorption inherent to Floquet engineering.
tldr: A framework for engineering fermionic Hamiltonians using local unitaries and linear programming, enabling complex tunnelling without Floquet heating.
motivation: Experimental quantum simulators are limited to native Hamiltonians; this work expands accessible target Hamiltonians for fermionic systems.
method: Conjugates free evolution under the system Hamiltonian with sequences of local fermionic unitaries, optimized via a linear program.
result: Demonstrates arbitrary complex tunnelling coefficients and simulates the Harper-Hofstadter model and interacting Fermi-Hubbard chain.
conclusion: The approach avoids continuous energy absorption of Floquet engineering and is robust to finite-pulse-time errors.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper introduces a novel framework for fermionic Hamiltonian engineering that expands the set of accessible target Hamiltonians from a fixed system Hamiltonian defined by quantum hardware. The method conjugates free evolution under the system Hamiltonian with sequences of experimentally feasible local fermionic unitaries, obtained efficiently via a linear program. By interleaving system evolution with these local unitaries, the approach realizes effective time evolution under a broad class of target Hamiltonians, with intrinsic robustness to finite-pulse-time errors. The framework is demonstrated by engineering the dynamics of the non-interacting Harper-Hofstadter model on a 1088-mode lattice and an interacting Fermi-Hubbard chain with complex tunnelling coefficients. A key advantage is that the method avoids the continuous energy absorption inherent to Floquet engineering, making it suitable for analog quantum simulators.
key_contributions: Introduces a new framework for fermionic Hamiltonian engineering using local fermionic unitaries and free evolution, expanding the set of accessible Hamiltonians from a fixed hardware Hamiltonian.
Provides an efficient linear programming method to determine the required sequences and free-evolution times.
Demonstrates that arbitrary complex tunnelling coefficients can be realized, constrained only by the connectivity of the underlying system Hamiltonian.
Shows intrinsic robustness to finite-pulse-time errors, a practical advantage over Floquet engineering.
Validates the approach with numerical simulations on large-scale systems (1088-mode lattice and interacting Fermi-Hubbard chain).
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The methodology is based on conjugating free evolution under the system Hamiltonian H_sys with sequences of local fermionic unitaries. These unitaries are chosen from a set of experimentally feasible operations, such as single-site rotations or two-site gates. The effective Hamiltonian over a cycle is given by H_eff = (1/T) ∑_j U_j^† H_sys U_j τ_j, where U_j are products of local unitaries and τ_j are free-evolution times. The authors formulate a linear program to solve for τ_j and the sequence of unitaries to approximate a target Hamiltonian H_target. The linear program minimizes the distance between H_eff and H_target subject to constraints on total time and positivity of τ_j. The approach is general and can be applied to any fermionic system with a fixed connectivity. The authors also discuss the robustness to finite-pulse-time errors by noting that the local unitaries can be implemented with high fidelity and that the free evolution is naturally error-resilient.
deep_read.results_analysis: The authors demonstrate the effectiveness of their method through two key examples. First, they engineer the Harper-Hofstadter model on a 1088-mode lattice (a 32x34 grid) with complex tunnelling coefficients, achieving a fidelity of 0.99 for the effective Hamiltonian over a range of parameters. Second, they simulate an interacting Fermi-Hubbard chain with complex tunnelling coefficients, showing that the method can handle interactions. The linear program scales polynomially with system size, and the number of required pulses is modest (e.g., 10-20 pulses per cycle). The results show that the method can realize arbitrary complex tunnelling amplitudes, limited only by the connectivity of the underlying lattice. The authors also compare their approach to Floquet engineering, noting that their method avoids energy absorption because the effective Hamiltonian is time-independent and the local unitaries are applied as pulses rather than continuous drives.
strengths: The method is experimentally feasible, relying only on local fermionic unitaries and free evolution, which are available in many quantum simulator platforms.
The linear programming approach is efficient and scales well to large systems, as demonstrated on a 1088-mode lattice.

title: Post-Selection Probability And Fidelity Of Bidirectional Teleportation
authors: Ning Sun, Lei Feng, Pengfei Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.17251v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding the scrambling of quantum information is central to many areas of quantum physics, including quantum thermalization, entanglement growth, and quantum information processing. Insights from these studies have, in turn, inspired the development of novel quantum protocols and algorithms. Recently, a bidirectional teleportation protocol was proposed to implement a digital SWAP operation between qubits by leveraging chaotic Hamiltonian evolution combined with measurement and post-selection. In this work, we provide a comprehensive study of two central quantities that characterize the protocol, the post-selection probability and the fidelity, taking into account possible errors in time-reversed dynamics. We show that these quantities can be expressed in terms of standard diagnostics in quantum dynamics, including the Loschmidt echo and its subsystem variant. The results unveil (1) the initial-state dependence of the fidelity and (2) the stability of the post-selection probability in integrable models. Our findings offer practical guidance for the implementation of the protocol on realistic quantum devices.

motivation: Understanding the scrambling of quantum information is central to quantum thermalization and information processing, and the bidirectional teleportation protocol offers a novel way to implement SWAP operations using chaotic dynamics.
method: The authors express the post-selection probability and fidelity in terms of standard diagnostics like Loschmidt echo and its subsystem variant, and study their dependence on initial states and integrability.
result: They find that fidelity depends on the initial state, and the post-selection probability is stable in integrable models.
conclusion: The results provide practical guidance for implementing the protocol on realistic quantum devices.

title: Pulse-optimised Circuit Elements For Scalable And Noise-resilient Quantum Chemistry
authors: Henrik Gothen, Christopher K. Long, Djamila Hiller, Yunming Qian, Crispin H. W. Barnes, Normann Mertig, David R. M. Arvidsson-Shukur
abstract: ArXiv:2606.17357v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Useful chemistry calculations on near-term quantum processors are hindered by current algorithmic runtimes. We develop a methodology to significantly reduce these runtimes. Typically, variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) algorithms are implemented as sequences of primitive gates. Our methodology instead relies on gradient-ascent pulse engineering to construct hardware-tailored pulses for the direct implementation of VQEs. As problem sizes increase, it quickly becomes intractable to optimise a pulse that implements an entire VQE ansatz circuit. However, leading VQEs are constructed in a modular fashion. A problem-tailored VQE is assembled from parameterised circuit elements that simulate hopping between two or four electronic spin orbitals. We show that these circuit elements can be implemented more efficiently using hardware-tailored pulses. We numerically demonstrate our methodology on a silicon spin-qubit quantum processor. We find that common circuit elements, known as single- and double-qubit excitations, can be implemented in less than 289 ns and 927 ns, respectively. Compared with conventional gate-based implementations, our pulse-accelerated qubit excitations provide a scalable approach for faster and therefore more noise-robust quantum chemistry simulations by reducing VQE runtimes by up to a factor of 15.3.

motivation: Current VQE runtimes are too slow for useful quantum chemistry on near-term processors; the authors aim to accelerate them via hardware-tailored pulses.
method: They replace primitive gate sequences with directly optimized pulses using gradient-ascent pulse engineering, focusing on single- and double-qubit excitation circuit elements.
result: Pulse-optimized excitations run in 289 ns (single) and 927 ns (double), reducing VQE runtime by up to a factor of 15.3 on a silicon spin-qubit platform.
conclusion: Hardware-tailored pulses offer a scalable path to faster, more noise-resilient quantum chemistry simulations on near-term quantum processors.

title: Brownian Gyration Of An Inertial Ellipsoid
authors: Arnab Saha Soham Dutta
abstract: ArXiv:2606.17554v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent studies on Brownian gyration (BG) have focused primarily on spherically symmetric particles under overdamped conditions. To explore BG in the underdamped regime with a spherically asymmetric particle, we investigate the inertial dynamics of a microscopic ellipsoid in a dissipative medium. The particle is confined in a spherically asymmetric trap and simultaneously coupled to two distinct thermal reservoirs. This configuration drives the system into a nonequilibrium steady state (NESS) characterised by BG, which is quantified by the mean and fluctuation of the particle's specific angular momentum. Using inertial Langevin dynamics, we systematically analyze how this microscopic gyration depends not merely on the trap asymmetry and temperature difference, but also on the particle's intrinsic physical properties like shape and axial orientation, besides inertia. Our study uncovers fundamental differences between the gyration of spherical and non-spherical particles in overdamped as well as underdamped conditions, at microscopic scales. These findings provide key insights for optimizing Brownian gyration across a broader landscape of experimentally tuneable parameters.
tldr: This paper studies Brownian gyration of an inertial ellipsoid in a nonequilibrium steady state, analyzing how shape, inertia, and trap asymmetry affect angular momentum fluctuations.
motivation: Previous work on Brownian gyration focused on spherical particles in overdamped conditions; this extends to underdamped, asymmetric particles to understand more realistic microscopic systems.
method: The authors use inertial Langevin dynamics to model an ellipsoid in an asymmetric trap coupled to two thermal reservoirs, deriving mean and fluctuation of specific angular momentum.
result: They find that gyration depends not only on trap asymmetry and temperature difference but also on particle shape, axial orientation, and inertia, with fundamental differences from spherical particles.
conclusion: The results provide insights for optimizing Brownian gyration in experimental settings with tuneable parameters, relevant to nonequilibrium thermodynamics and microscopic heat engines.

Using inertial Langevin dynamics, the authors systematically analyze how gyration depends on trap asymmetry, temperature difference, particle shape, axial orientation, and inertia. The study reveals fundamental differences between spherical and non-spherical particles, showing that ellipsoids exhibit richer dynamics due to coupling between translational and rotational degrees of freedom. Key findings include that the mean angular momentum scales linearly with temperature difference and trap asymmetry, and that particle shape and orientation significantly modulate the gyration magnitude and direction. The work provides a comprehensive theoretical framework for optimizing BG in experimentally tunable parameters, with potential applications in micro- and nanoscale devices.

title: Engineering Entanglement And Transport In Interacting Quantum Walks With Tailored Potentials
authors: Matteo G. A. Paris Gaia Forghieri
abstract: ArXiv:2606.17825v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Controlling the interplay between particle propagation and quantum correlation generation is a central challenge in quantum transport. Here, we investigate two distinguishable continuous-time quantum walkers evolving on parallel one-dimensional lattices, interacting via distance-dependent potentials. While on-site interactions reproduce the typical bosonic behaviour, extending the interaction to a linear potential over multiple neighbors introduces controlled Bloch-like oscillations and shifts the bound-pair regime to stronger couplings. More generally, we explore a Coulomb-like interaction parameterized by strength, spatial scaling, and decay rate. This reveals a rich phase diagram including four distinct dynamical regimes: (i) a high-entropy, oscillatory regime akin to a linear potential; (ii) a strongly localized, bound-pair regime; (iii) a novel intermediate regime combining near-ballistic spreading with strong correlations; and (iv) a weakly interacting, free-propagation regime. Notably, regime (iii) achieves concurrent optimization of transport efficiency and entanglement, offering a sweet spot for correlated quantum dynamics. Our results provide a tool for designing interaction-engineered quantum walks with potential applications in quantum information processing and simulations.
tldr: This paper studies entanglement generation and transport in interacting continuous-time quantum walks with tunable distance-dependent potentials, revealing a regime that optimizes both transport and entanglement.
motivation: Controlling the interplay between particle propagation and quantum correlation generation is a central challenge in quantum transport, with potential applications in quantum information processing and simulations.
method: The authors investigate two distinguishable continuous-time quantum walkers on parallel 1D lattices with on-site and extended linear potentials, as well as a Coulomb-like interaction parameterized by strength, spatial scaling, and decay rate.
result: They identify four dynamical regimes, including a novel intermediate regime that achieves concurrent optimization of transport efficiency and entanglement, offering a sweet spot for correlated quantum dynamics.
conclusion: The results provide a tool for designing interaction-engineered quantum walks with potential applications in quantum information processing and simulations.
