They derive conditions and bounds for the advantage.
result: They show that measurements with non-zero imaginarity can increase the success probability of entanglement concentration for certain quantum states, demonstrating a clear operational advantage of imaginarity as a resource.
conclusion: Imaginarity in measurements can be a useful resource for entanglement manipulation, suggesting that complex numbers play a non-trivial operational role in quantum information processing.

title: Demonstration Of The Universal Intrinsic Higher-rank Spin Tensor Hall Effect With A Trapped Ion
authors: Chang Liu, Yue Li, Xingyu Zhao, Xi-Wang Luo, And Yiheng Lin
abstract:
Author(s): Chang Liu, Yue Li, Xingyu Zhao, Xi-Wang Luo, and Yiheng Lin

The spin Hall effect enables pure spin-current generation without charge transport. Notably, its intrinsic contribution, originating from spin-orbit coupling, can exhibit universal values that are robust against parameter fluctuations. Recent extensions of this effect to high-spin systems predict ri…


[Phys. Rev. A 113, 062616] Published Mon Jun 15, 2026.
tldr: Experimental demonstration of a universal intrinsic higher-rank spin tensor Hall effect using a trapped ion system.
motivation: To extend the spin Hall effect to high-spin systems and demonstrate its universal intrinsic contribution, which is robust against parameter fluctuations.
method: Trapped ion platform used to simulate higher-rank spin tensors and measure the Hall effect under controlled conditions.
result: Observed universal intrinsic higher-rank spin tensor Hall effect, confirming theoretical predictions.
conclusion: The trapped ion system provides a versatile platform for studying higher-rank spin transport phenomena, with potential applications in spintronics and quantum simulation.

title: Tunable Bundle Emissions Of $n$-phonon And Photon-phonon Pairs Via The Barnett Effect
authors: Zhe-Qi Yang, Lei Chen, And Zhi-Rong Zhong
abstract:
Author(s): Zhe-Qi Yang, Lei Chen, and Zhi-Rong Zhong

We theoretically propose a scheme for the generation of [MATH]-phonon and photon-phonon pair bundle emissions in a cavity magnomechanics system. By utilizing the Barnett effect under resonant driving, [MATH]-phonon and photon-phonon super Rabi oscillations can be achieved. Through the system's dissipative…


[Phys. Rev. A 113, 063722] Published Mon Jun 15, 2026.
tldr: Proposes a cavity magnomechanics system to generate n-phonon and photon-phonon pair bundle emissions via the Barnett effect.
motivation: To achieve tunable bundle emissions of phonons and photon-phonon pairs, which are important for quantum information processing and hybrid quantum systems.
method: Uses the Barnett effect under resonant driving in a cavity magnomechanics system to induce n-phonon and photon-phonon super Rabi oscillations, then leverages dissipative dynamics to generate bundle emissions.
result: Demonstrates that n-phonon and photon-phonon pair bundle emissions can be generated and tuned by controlling system parameters.
conclusion: The scheme provides a new method for generating nonclassical states in hybrid quantum systems, with potential applications in quantum networks and sensing.

title: Entanglement Dynamics Of Separable Squeezed States In Finite-memory Structured Reservoir
authors: Austen Couvertier And Ting Yu
abstract:
Author(s): Austen Couvertier and Ting Yu

Entanglement in continuous-variable Gaussian systems is a key resource, and common reservoirs can both suppress and generate correlations. Existing work focused on preentangled states or Markovian baths, leaving open whether separable squeezed inputs entangle in structured environments or under modu…


[Phys. Rev. A 113, 063724] Published Mon Jun 15, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies entanglement generation from separable squeezed states in a finite-memory structured reservoir, extending beyond Markovian baths.
motivation: Understanding how structured environments can generate entanglement from initially separable states is important for quantum information processing with continuous-variable systems.
method: The authors analyze the dynamics of two squeezed states coupled to a common non-Markovian reservoir with finite memory, using exact master equations.
result: They find that entanglement can be generated from separable squeezed inputs under certain conditions, and the reservoir memory and squeezing parameters play crucial roles.
conclusion: Structured reservoirs can be exploited to create entanglement from separable states, offering new possibilities for quantum information tasks.

title: Beyond Qubits: Multilevel Quantum Sensing For Dark Matter
authors: Xiaolin Ma, Volodymyr Takhistov, Norikazu Mizuochi, And Ernst David Herbschleb
abstract:
Author(s): Xiaolin Ma, Volodymyr Takhistov, Norikazu Mizuochi, and Ernst David Herbschleb

Searching for ultralight dark matter requires detecting extremely weak oscillating fields, where quantum sensing is especially promising. The authors show that spin-1 nitrogen vacancy centers in diamond can harness multilevel quantum states to combine enhanced signal response with common mode noise suppression, improving sensitivity to axion-electron dark matter interactions.


[Phys. Rev. A 113, L060802] Published Mon Jun 15, 2026.
tldr: NV centers in diamond are used as multilevel quantum sensors to detect ultralight dark matter, improving sensitivity via common-mode noise suppression.
motivation: Ultralight dark matter detection requires extremely sensitive quantum sensors; NV centers offer a promising platform.
method: The authors propose using spin-1 NV centers with multilevel quantum states to enhance signal response while suppressing common-mode noise.
result: The multilevel approach improves sensitivity to axion-electron dark matter interactions compared to conventional two-level sensing.
conclusion: Multilevel quantum sensing with NV centers is a viable and improved method for dark matter detection.

title: Nonadiabatic Self-healing Of Trotter Errors In Digitized Counterdiabatic Dynamics
authors: Mara Vizzuso, Gianluca Passarelli, Giovanni Cantele, Procolo Lucignano, Xi Chen, And Koushik Paul
abstract:
Author(s): Mara Vizzuso, Gianluca Passarelli, Giovanni Cantele, Procolo Lucignano, Xi Chen, and Koushik Paul

Trotter errors in digitized quantum dynamics arise from approximating time-ordered evolution under noncommuting Hamiltonian terms with a product formula. In the adiabatic regime, such errors are known to exhibit long-time self-healing [
tldr: This paper demonstrates that Trotter errors in digitized counterdiabatic dynamics can self-heal nonadiabatically, improving the fidelity of quantum simulations.
motivation: Trotter errors limit the accuracy of digital quantum simulation; understanding and mitigating them is crucial for near-term quantum devices.
method: The authors analyze digitized counterdiabatic dynamics using a product formula and derive conditions under which Trotter errors self-heal even outside the adiabatic regime.
result: They show that nonadiabatic self-healing occurs, leading to reduced error accumulation and higher fidelity compared to standard Trotterization.
conclusion: Digitized counterdiabatic protocols can exploit self-healing to achieve more accurate quantum simulations with fewer Trotter steps.

title: Oh Molecule As A Quantum Probe To Jointly Estimate Electric And Magnetic Fields
authors: Luca Previdi, Francesco Albarelli, And Matteo G. A. Paris
abstract:
Author(s): Luca Previdi, Francesco Albarelli, and Matteo G. A. Paris

The hydroxyl radical (the OH molecule) carries both electric and magnetic dipole moments and, as a diatomic molecule, admits a comparatively simple and accurate model. This makes it a natural quantum probe for the joint estimation of electric and magnetic fields. Here we study simultaneous estimatio…


[Phys. Rev. A 113, 062612] Published Thu Jun 11, 2026.
tldr: The OH molecule is proposed as a quantum probe for simultaneous estimation of electric and magnetic fields.
motivation: Joint estimation of multiple fields is important for sensing, and the OH molecule's dual dipole moments make it a natural candidate.
method: The authors model the OH molecule as a quantum system and analyze simultaneous estimation using quantum metrology techniques.
result: They find that simultaneous estimation can outperform separate estimation due to correlations, and provide bounds on achievable precision.
conclusion: The OH molecule is a viable platform for multi-parameter quantum sensing, with potential applications in hybrid quantum systems.

title: Making non-Markovian Master Equations Accessible With Approximate Environments
authors: Gerardo Suárez And Michał Horodecki
abstract:
Author(s): Gerardo Suárez and Michał Horodecki

Accurate and efficient simulation of open quantum systems remains a significant challenge, particularly for non-Markovian dynamics. We demonstrate the profound utility of expressing the environmental correlation function as a sum of damped sinusoidals within master equations. While not strictly requ…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 064121] Published Tue Jun 09, 2026.
tldr: The paper presents a method to make non-Markovian master equations more tractable by approximating the environment correlation function as a sum of damped sinusoidals.
motivation: Simulating non-Markovian open quantum systems is computationally challenging; the authors aim to provide a simpler, more accessible approach without sacrificing accuracy.
method: They express the environmental correlation function as a sum of damped sinusoidals, which allows the use of standard master equation techniques while capturing non-Markovian effects.
result: The method yields accurate dynamics for a range of non-Markovian regimes, significantly reducing computational complexity compared to exact methods.
conclusion: This approach makes non-Markovian master equations more practical for studying open quantum systems, with potential applications in quantum thermodynamics and quantum information.

title: Extending The Dynamic Range In Quantum Frequency Estimation With Sequential Weak Measurements
authors: Su Direkci, Manuel Endres, And Tuvia Gefen
abstract:
Author(s): Su Direkci, Manuel Endres, and Tuvia Gefen

A sequential weak measurement protocol is developed for Bayesian quantum frequency estimation with coherent spin states in which weakly entangled ancilla qubits track the sensing qubits during free evolution to suppress phase slip errors and extend the dynamic range. The protocol attains Heisenberg scaling with time and saturates the Cramér-Rao precision bound asymptotically across a large frequency bandwidth.


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, L022046] Published Wed Jun 10, 2026.
tldr: A sequential weak measurement protocol for quantum frequency estimation that uses weakly entangled ancilla qubits to suppress phase slip errors and extend dynamic range, achieving Heisenberg scaling and saturating the Cramér-Rao bound.
motivation: Quantum frequency estimation is limited by phase slip errors that restrict dynamic range; existing methods trade off precision for range. The authors aim to overcome this using weak measurements and entanglement.
method: The protocol employs sequential weak measurements on coherent spin states, where ancilla qubits are weakly entangled with the sensing qubits during free evolution. Bayesian estimation is used to track the frequency.
result: The protocol attains Heisenberg scaling with time and asymptotically saturates the Cramér-Rao precision bound across a large frequency bandwidth, effectively extending the dynamic range.
conclusion: Sequential weak measurements with ancilla entanglement provide a practical route to high-precision, wide-dynamic-range quantum frequency estimation, relevant for quantum sensing and metrology.

title: Stochastic Calculus For Pathwise Observables Of Markov-Jump Processes: Unification Of Diffusion And Jump Dynamics
authors: Lars Torbjørn Stutzer, Cai Dieball, And Aljaž Godec
abstract:
Author(s): Lars Torbjørn Stutzer, Cai Dieball, and Aljaž Godec

A complete stochastic calculus for pathwise observables of Markov-jump processes is developed, unifying, in the continuum limit, the previously disjoint theories of diffusion and jump processes.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021038] Published Tue May 19, 2026.
tldr: Develops a complete stochastic calculus for pathwise observables of Markov-jump processes, unifying diffusion and jump dynamics in the continuum limit.
motivation: To provide a unified mathematical framework for analyzing pathwise observables in stochastic processes, which is essential for understanding fluctuations and thermodynamics in non-equilibrium systems.
method: The authors construct a stochastic calculus for Markov-jump processes, deriving pathwise equations and showing how they reduce to diffusion processes in the continuum limit.
result: A unified stochastic calculus that bridges jump and diffusion processes, enabling consistent treatment of pathwise observables across different stochastic regimes.
conclusion: This work provides a foundational tool for studying non-equilibrium thermodynamics and stochastic dynamics, with potential applications to fluctuation theorems and thermodynamic bounds.

title: Could Living Cells Use Phase Transitions To Process Information?
authors: Arvind Murugan, David Zwicker, Charlotta Lorenz, And Eric R. Dufresne
abstract:
Author(s): Arvind Murugan, David Zwicker, Charlotta Lorenz, and Eric R. Dufresne

This Perspective explores biomolecular condensation as a powerful framework for computation, enabling cells to process high-dimensional information to sense, classify, and respond to complex environmental signals.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 020501] Published Tue May 12, 2026.
tldr: This perspective proposes that biomolecular condensates can process information through phase transitions, linking physical chemistry to cellular computation.
motivation: Cells must process complex environmental signals, but traditional molecular circuits may be insufficient; phase transitions offer a new paradigm for high-dimensional information processing.
method: The authors draw analogies between phase separation in biomolecular condensates and computational primitives, discussing how condensates can sense, classify, and respond to signals via collective behavior.
result: They argue that phase transitions enable efficient, noise-robust computation in cells, with potential for implementing logic gates and memory.
conclusion: Biomolecular condensation provides a powerful framework for cellular information processing, suggesting new directions for synthetic biology and understanding of living systems.

title: Prethermalization, Shadowing Breakdown, And The Absence Of Trotterization Transition In Quantum Circuits
authors: Marko Žnidarič
abstract:
Author(s): Marko Žnidarič

New research uses truncated propagators to show that shadowing time in many-body chaotic systems is finite. It also offers a method to calculate thermalization time, finding that the “Trotterization transition” is generically a finite-size effect.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021017] Published Wed Apr 22, 2026.
tldr: The paper shows that shadowing time in many-body chaotic systems is finite and that the Trotterization transition is a finite-size effect, using truncated propagators.
motivation: Understanding thermalization and prethermalization in quantum many-body systems is crucial for quantum thermodynamics and quantum computing.
method: The author uses truncated propagators to analyze the dynamics of quantum circuits and compute thermalization times.
result: Shadowing time is finite in many-body chaotic systems, and the Trotterization transition disappears in the thermodynamic limit.
conclusion: The findings clarify the nature of prethermalization and have implications for quantum simulation and thermalization.

title: Loading And Imaging Atom Arrays Via Electromagnetically Induced Transparency
authors: Emily H. Qiu, Tamara Šumarac, Peiran Niu, Shai Tsesses, Fadi Wassaf, David C. Spierings, Meng-Wei Chen, Mehmet T. Uysal, Audrey Bartlett, Adrian J. Menssen, Mikhail D. Lukin, And Vladan Vuletić
abstract:
Author(s): Emily H. Qiu, Tamara Šumarac, Peiran Niu, Shai Tsesses, Fadi Wassaf, David C. Spierings, Meng-Wei Chen, Mehmet T. Uysal, Audrey Bartlett, Adrian J. Menssen, Mikhail D. Lukin, and Vladan Vuletić

Electromagnetically induced transparency unlocks high-fidelity, nondestructive imaging and loading of continuously operated neutral-atom arrays in finite magnetic fields.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020358] Published Fri Jun 12, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates high-fidelity, nondestructive imaging and loading of neutral-atom arrays using electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) in finite magnetic fields.
motivation: Neutral-atom arrays are a promising platform for quantum computing and simulation, but loading and imaging them with high fidelity and low loss remains challenging. EIT offers a way to perform nondestructive measurements and continuous loading.
method: The authors employ electromagnetically induced transparency to image atoms without destroying them, and use the same technique to continuously load atoms into arrays. The experiment is performed in finite magnetic fields to control atomic states.
result: They achieve high-fidelity, nondestructive imaging and demonstrate continuous loading of atom arrays, improving the efficiency and scalability of neutral-atom quantum platforms.
conclusion: EIT-based imaging and loading is a powerful technique for neutral-atom arrays, enabling new capabilities for quantum information processing with these systems.

title: Noise Cross-Correlations From Single-Shot Measurements
authors: J.S. Rojas-Arias, P. Stano, Y.-H. Wu, L.C. Camenzind, S. Tarucha, And D. Loss
abstract:
Author(s): J.S. Rojas-Arias, P. Stano, Y.-H. Wu, L.C. Camenzind, S. Tarucha, and D. Loss

A novel spectroscopy method leverages single-shot readouts to extract noise cross-correlations, successfully bridging the elusive intermediate-frequency gap in qubit noise characterization.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020351] Published Thu Jun 04, 2026.
tldr: A novel spectroscopy method uses single-shot readouts to extract noise cross-correlations, bridging the intermediate-frequency gap in qubit noise characterization.
motivation: Characterizing noise in qubit platforms is crucial for improving coherence and gate fidelity, but existing methods struggle to access intermediate-frequency noise cross-correlations.
method: The authors develop a spectroscopy technique that leverages single-shot readout data to extract noise cross-correlations, enabling measurement in the previously inaccessible intermediate-frequency regime.
result: The method successfully extracts noise cross-correlations from single-shot measurements, demonstrating its effectiveness on a qubit platform.
conclusion: This technique provides a new tool for noise characterization in qubit systems, which can aid in understanding and mitigating decoherence.

title: Transversal Architecture For Megaquop-Scale Quantum Simulation With Neutral Atoms
authors: Refaat Ismail, I-Chi Chen, Chen Zhao, Ronen Weiss, Fangli Liu, Hengyun Zhou, Sheng-Tao Wang, Andrew Sornborger, And Milan Kornjača
abstract:
Author(s): Refaat Ismail, I-Chi Chen, Chen Zhao, Ronen Weiss, Fangli Liu, Hengyun Zhou, Sheng-Tao Wang, Andrew Sornborger, and Milan Kornjača

Integration of a space-time efficient small-angle rotation error correction architecture with neutral-atom hardware and its extension to high-rate codes yields significant savings in logical layout, space, and time overhead for quantum simulation.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020343] Published Fri May 29, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes a transversal architecture for fault-tolerant quantum simulation on neutral-atom platforms, integrating small-angle rotation error correction with high-rate codes to reduce logical overhead.
motivation: Quantum simulation at the megaquop scale requires fault-tolerant architectures that minimize space and time overhead, especially for neutral-atom hardware which has unique constraints.
method: The authors design a transversal logical gate set tailored to neutral-atom hardware, incorporating small-angle rotation error correction and extending it to high-rate quantum error-correcting codes.
result: Significant savings in logical layout, space, and time overhead are demonstrated for quantum simulation tasks, enabling megaquop-scale computations.
conclusion: The transversal architecture makes neutral-atom quantum computers a viable platform for large-scale fault-tolerant quantum simulation.

title: Estimates Of Loss Function Concentration In Noisy Parametrized Quantum Circuits
authors: Giulio Crognaletti, Michele Grossi, And Angelo Bassi
abstract:
Author(s): Giulio Crognaletti, Michele Grossi, and Angelo Bassi

A principled link between noise resilience and circuit expressivity provides a roadmap for navigating barren plateaus and optimizing the training of variational quantum algorithms.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020336] Published Tue May 26, 2026.
tldr: The paper establishes a theoretical link between noise resilience and circuit expressivity in parametrized quantum circuits, providing estimates of loss function concentration to mitigate barren plateaus.
motivation: Variational quantum algorithms suffer from barren plateaus, where gradients vanish exponentially with system size, hindering trainability. Understanding how noise affects loss function concentration is crucial for practical quantum computing.
method: The authors analyze noisy parametrized quantum circuits using tools from quantum information theory, deriving bounds on the variance of the loss function based on circuit expressivity and noise parameters.
result: They find that noise can actually help avoid barren plateaus by reducing the effective expressivity of the circuit, leading to a concentration of the loss function that is less severe than in the noiseless case.
conclusion: The results provide a principled way to design noise-resilient variational algorithms and suggest that moderate noise can be beneficial for trainability, guiding experimental implementations.

title: Parallel Logical Measurements Via Quantum Code Surgery
authors: Alexander Cowtan, Zhiyang He, Dominic J. Williamson, And Theodore J. Yoder
abstract:
Author(s): Alexander Cowtan, Zhiyang He, Dominic J. Williamson, and Theodore J. Yoder

Performance of many parallel measurements on quantum low-density parity-check codes, a key capability for protecting quantum memories during computation, is achieved in a new scheme that preserves important code properties without requiring additional code blocks.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020325] Published Fri May 08, 2026.
tldr: A scheme for performing parallel logical measurements on quantum LDPC codes using code surgery, preserving code properties without extra blocks.
motivation: Efficient parallel measurement is crucial for fault-tolerant quantum computation, especially for protecting quantum memories during computation.
method: The authors develop a code surgery technique that enables multiple logical measurements simultaneously on quantum LDPC codes, leveraging the code's structure to avoid additional overhead.
result: The scheme achieves parallel measurements while maintaining key code properties such as distance and locality, without requiring additional code blocks.
conclusion: This work advances practical fault-tolerant quantum computing by enabling efficient parallel logical operations on low-overhead quantum codes.

title: Quantum Error-Corrected Computation Of Molecular Energies
authors: Kentaro Yamamoto, Yuta Kikuchi, David Amaro, Ben Criger, Silas Dilkes, Ciarán Ryan-Anderson, Andrew Tranter, Joan M. Dreiling, Dan Gresh, Cameron Foltz, Michael Mills, Steven A. Moses, Peter E. Siegfried, Maxwell D. Urmey, Justin J. Burau, Aaron Hankin, Dominic Lucchetti, John P. Gaebler, Natalie C. Brown, Brian Neyenhuis, And David Muñoz Ramo
abstract:
Author(s): Kentaro Yamamoto, Yuta Kikuchi, David Amaro, Ben Criger, Silas Dilkes, Ciarán Ryan-Anderson, Andrew Tranter, Joan M. Dreiling, Dan Gresh, Cameron Foltz, Michael Mills, Steven A. Moses, Peter E. Siegfried, Maxwell D. Urmey, Justin J. Burau, Aaron Hankin, Dominic Lucchetti, John P. Gaebler, Natalie C. Brown, Brian Neyenhuis, and David Muñoz Ramo

Noise-aware calibration, logical rotation gates, and quantum error-correction gadgets enable a partially fault-tolerant molecular energy computation on a trapped-ion quantum computer.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020319] Published Thu Apr 30, 2026.
tldr: Demonstrates a partially fault-tolerant molecular energy computation on a trapped-ion quantum computer using noise-aware calibration, logical rotation gates, and quantum error-correction gadgets.
motivation: To show that quantum error correction can be integrated with practical quantum chemistry computations, improving reliability despite hardware noise.
method: Implements noise-aware calibration, logical rotation gates, and quantum error-correction gadgets on a trapped-ion quantum processor to compute molecular energies.
result: Achieves a partially fault-tolerant computation of molecular energies, demonstrating improved accuracy over non-error-corrected approaches.
conclusion: Quantum error correction can be practically applied to quantum chemistry on current hardware, paving the way for reliable quantum simulations.

title: Fault-Tolerant Operations In Majorana-Based Quantum Codes: Gates, Measurements, And High-Rate Constructions
authors: Maryam Mudassar, Alexander Schuckert, And Daniel Gottesman
abstract:
Author(s): Maryam Mudassar, Alexander Schuckert, and Daniel Gottesman

By generalizing from qubit error correction, fault-tolerant protocols tailored to fermionic processes are created, which enable gates, measurements, and codes.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020315] Published Fri Apr 24, 2026.
tldr: Generalizes fault-tolerant quantum error correction to Majorana-based qubits, designing tailored gates, measurements, and high-rate codes.
motivation: Majorana-based qubits are promising for topological quantum computing but require fault-tolerant protocols adapted to their fermionic nature and constraints.
method: Extends standard qubit error correction techniques to fermionic systems, constructing fault-tolerant operations and codes using Majorana operators and stabilizer formalism.
result: Demonstrates fault-tolerant gates and measurements for Majorana qubits and presents high-rate quantum codes optimized for this platform.
conclusion: Provides a foundation for practical fault-tolerant quantum computing with Majorana-based qubits, bridging theory and experimental implementation.

title: Colloquium: Simulating non-Markovian Dynamics In Open Quantum Systems
authors: Meng Xu, Vasilii Vadimov, J. T. Stockburger, And J. Ankerhold
abstract:
Author(s): Meng Xu, Vasilii Vadimov, J. T. Stockburger, and J. Ankerhold

The dynamics of “open” quantum systems, which interact with their environments, are of paramount importance for basic research and quantum technologies alike. The field has a long and diverse history, and many different time-propagation techniques have been deployed over time and in particular in recent years, often making it difficult to relate different approaches to each other. Based on a unified framework, this Colloquium provides an overview of methods used to describe and to simulate open quantum systems in various contexts, including quantum optics, quantum information, quantum thermodynamics, and solid-state and many-body physics, as well as chemical physics, highlighting the commonalities and differences between them.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 021002] Published Mon May 11, 2026.
tldr: A colloquium review that provides a unified framework for simulating non-Markovian dynamics in open quantum systems, covering methods relevant to quantum thermodynamics and quantum information.
motivation: Open quantum systems are crucial for quantum technologies, but non-Markovian effects are often neglected due to computational complexity; a unified overview of simulation methods is needed.
method: The authors present a unified framework based on path integrals and influence functionals, and review various numerical techniques including hierarchical equations of motion, stochastic methods, and tensor network approaches.
result: The review highlights commonalities and differences among methods, and provides guidance on choosing appropriate techniques for different physical regimes and applications.
conclusion: Non-Markovian dynamics can be efficiently simulated using modern methods, enabling accurate modeling of open quantum systems in quantum thermodynamics, quantum optics, and solid-state physics.

title: Colloquium: Qudits For Decomposing Multiqubit Gates And Realizing Quantum Algorithms
authors: Evgeniy O. Kiktenko, Anastasiia S. Nikolaeva, And Aleksey K. Fedorov
abstract:
Author(s): Evgeniy O. Kiktenko, Anastasiia S. Nikolaeva, and Aleksey K. Fedorov

Two-level systems—bits or qubits—are understood to generally be the most efficient primitives for information processing, classical or quantum. But this is not to say that there are no roles to be played by multilevel systems. This Colloquium surveys these possible roles for the quantum case. Here we speak of qudits:
[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 021003] Published Tue Jun 03, 2025.
tldr: A colloquium review on using qudits (multilevel quantum systems) to decompose multiqubit gates and implement quantum algorithms, highlighting advantages in gate count and experimental feasibility.
motivation: Qubits are standard for quantum computing, but qudits may offer resource-efficient decompositions of multiqubit gates and simplify algorithm implementations.
method: The paper surveys qudit-qubit embeddings, gate decompositions (e.g., Toffoli gate using qutrits), and reviews experimental demonstrations across various platforms.
result: Qudits can reduce the number of elementary operations for certain gates and algorithms, with proof-of-principle experiments showing feasibility.
conclusion: Qudits are a promising resource for near-term quantum computing, though challenges in control and error correction remain.

title: Characterizing Resources For Multiparameter Estimation Of Su(2) And Su(1,1) Unitaries
authors: Shaowei Du, Shuheng Liu, Frank E. S. Steinhoff, And Giuseppe Vitagliano
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2130 (2026).

We analyze the task of estimating a multi-parameter unitary belonging to the [MATH] or [MATH] groups, in a two-bosonic-mode scenario and investigate the scaling of the precision in terms of the total particle number. For the [MATH] case, the total particle number is conserved by the evolution and we discuss optimal states in fixed-[MATH] subspaces, identifying eigenstates of [MATH] as useful resources, even allowing simultaneous Heisenberg precision scaling for all three parameters. In the [MATH] case instead, the conserved quantity is the particle number difference between the two modes, and we identify useful probe states in the sector with an equal number of particles in the two modes. These states are analogous to the [MATH] case and would also allow simultaneous Heisenberg precision scaling for all three parameters. We then consider the more pragmatic scenario of an estimation via expectation values of time-evolved observables, which we restrict to be the first two moments of the generators. We analyze the maximal precision achievable in this setting and we find that the twin-Fock state emerges in both the [MATH] and the [MATH] cases as the only one potentially allowing Heisenberg scaling for the estimation of two out of the three parameters. As a complement, we also consider other probe states with fluctuating number of particles, with measurements restricted to quadratic expressions in the mode operators. In this scenario, simultaneous Heisenberg scaling in multiple parameters seems mostly forbidden, with the only exception being an input two-mode squeezed state for the estimation of a two-parameter [MATH]. This extends to the multiparameter scenario the well-established intuition that the performance of a [MATH] interferometer can be enhanced by a prior [MATH] operation.

.
tldr: Analyzes optimal probe states and measurement strategies for multiparameter estimation of SU(2) and SU(1,1) unitaries, achieving Heisenberg scaling in certain settings.
motivation: Multiparameter quantum estimation is crucial for quantum metrology, and understanding resource requirements for simultaneous estimation of multiple parameters is a key challenge.
method: The authors consider two-bosonic-mode scenarios, identify optimal probe states in fixed-particle-number subspaces, and analyze precision scaling using expectation values of time-evolved observables restricted to first two moments of generators.
result: Eigenstates of J_z for SU(2) and twin-Fock states for SU(1,1) allow simultaneous Heisenberg scaling for all three parameters; with restricted measurements, only twin-Fock states enable Heisenberg scaling for two parameters, and two-mode squeezed states for a two-parameter SU(1,1) case.
conclusion: The work extends intuition from single-parameter interferometry to multiparameter settings, identifying specific states as resources for achieving Heisenberg-limited precision.

title: Classical Shadows For Sample-efficient Measurements Of Gauge-invariant Observables
authors: Jacob Bringewatt, Henry Froland, Andreas Elben, And Niklas Mueller
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2127 (2026).

Classical shadows provide a versatile framework for estimating many properties of quantum states from repeated, randomly chosen measurements without requiring full quantum state tomography. When prior information is available, such as knowledge of symmetries of states and operators, this knowledge can be exploited to significantly improve sample efficiency. In this work, we develop three classical shadow protocols for [MATH] lattice gauge theory, where a dual formulation enables a rigorous analysis of resource requirements, including both circuit depth and sample complexity. Our approaches can offer exponential improvements in sample complexity over symmetry-agnostic methods, albeit at the cost of increased circuit complexity. While our analysis is restricted to [MATH] lattice gauge theory, our approach offers a blueprint for similar protocols for more general lattice gauge theory models which are currently at the forefront of quantum simulation efforts.

.
tldr: Develops classical shadow protocols for lattice gauge theory that exploit gauge symmetry to exponentially improve sample complexity.
motivation: Estimating gauge-invariant observables in lattice gauge theory is crucial for quantum simulation but sample-inefficient without symmetry information.
method: Proposes three classical shadow protocols that incorporate gauge symmetry via a dual formulation, analyzing circuit depth and sample complexity.
result: Achieves exponential improvements in sample complexity over symmetry-agnostic methods, with trade-offs in circuit complexity.
conclusion: Provides a blueprint for symmetry-enhanced classical shadows in more general lattice gauge theories, advancing quantum simulation capabilities.

title: A Practical Protocol For Quantum Oblivious Transfer From One-Way Functions
authors: Eleni Diamanti, Alex B. Grilo, Adriano Innocenzi, Pascal Lefebvre, Verena Yacoub, And Álvaro Yángüez
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2124 (2026).

We present a new simulation-secure quantum oblivious transfer (QOT) protocol based on one-way functions in the plain model. With a focus on practical implementation, our protocol surpasses prior works in efficiency, promising feasible experimental realization. We address potential experimental errors and their correction, offering analytical expressions to facilitate the analysis of the required quantum resources. Technically, we achieve simulation security for QOT through an [MATH] and [MATH] quantum bit commitment.

.
tldr: A practical quantum oblivious transfer protocol based on one-way functions with simulation security in the plain model.
motivation: Oblivious transfer is a fundamental cryptographic primitive, and existing quantum protocols are often impractical or require strong assumptions. This work aims to provide a feasible protocol using only one-way functions.
method: The protocol uses quantum bit commitments and one-way functions to achieve simulation-secure oblivious transfer, with analytical expressions for resource requirements and error correction.

title: On The Entanglement Induced By The Deformation Of Phase-space
authors: Shilpa Nandi, Shatarupa Maity, Pinaki Patra
abstract: ArXiv:2606.17587v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Most quantum gravity theories propose that the fundamental concept of space-time is mostly compatible with quantum theory in noncommutative (NC) space. In the present paper, we revisit the notion of entanglement induced by NC deformations of phase space. The positive partial transpose (PPT) criterion for separability of bipartite Gaussian states is extended to a general class of Bopp's shift. In particular, we have considered both the position-position and momentum-momentum noncommutativity, with deformation parameters [MATH] and [MATH], respectively. It turns out that [MATH] and [MATH] induce the entanglement. We have directly applied the formalism for an anisotropic two-dimensional harmonic oscillator. Peres-Horodecki separability condition leads to a constraint equation for the parameter values of the oscillator in NC space. It turns out that the bipartite Gaussian state is almost always entangled in deformed space. To implement the theoretical idea, we provide an outline for a gedankenexperiment to identify the signature of phase-space noncommutativity, i.e., quantum gravity. In particular, the gedankenexperiment is devised to test the separability of supposedly separable Gaussian states in the usual commutative space, through the covariance matrix, which is constructed via measured output photocurrents after interaction of input Gaussian states and reference states. If the experiment shows that the supposedly separable states are actually entangled, then the entanglement is created through the intermediate background noncommutative space, which is a signature of the quantum nature of gravity.

motivation: To explore signatures of quantum gravity through noncommutative geometry and its effect on entanglement.
method: Extends the positive partial transpose criterion for bipartite Gaussian states to Bopp's shift noncommutativity, and applies it to an anisotropic 2D harmonic oscillator.
result: The bipartite Gaussian state is almost always entangled in deformed space, with entanglement induced by both position-position and momentum-momentum noncommutativity.
conclusion: Noncommutative phase space generically induces entanglement, which could be detected in a gedankenexperiment as a signature of quantum gravity.

title: Asymptotically Optimal Circuit Depth For Diagonal Unitary Synthesis And Compilation On Two-Dimensional Grids
authors: Chengzhuo Xu, Xiao Chen, Zhihao Liu, Zhigang Li
abstract: ArXiv:2606.17589v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Diagonal unitaries are a fundamental but resource-intensive class of quantum operations, arising as the phase separators of QAOA and the time-evolution blocks of Hamiltonian simulation. Under all-to-all connectivity their optimal depth is established, but on nearest-neighbor hardware general-purpose compilers fall back on heuristic search, which yields no analyzable cost bound and becomes intractable at the very sizes where depth is the bottleneck. We address synthesis and compilation jointly. On the synthesis side, we develop a Gray-Path Framework (GPF) that realizes any [MATH]-qubit diagonal unitary in asymptotically optimal [MATH] and CNOT depth [MATH] without ancillas. Our main result is that compiling GPF onto a two-dimensional nearest-neighbor grid preserves this optimality: routing adds depth [MATH] and gate count [MATH]. Because GPF fixes its entire interaction structure in advance, routing reduces to scheduling a known sequence, with no heuristic search. We give the construction both with and without ancillas: the ancilla-free, cost-optimized layout is a two-row grid, and a [MATH]-row layout introduces a space--time tradeoff that cuts depth by [MATH] while remaining asymptotically optimal for the enlarged register; both are deterministic and analyzed in closed form. The same complexity is also attained on a linear nearest-neighbor chain, so the preservation is topology-independent, holding on any architecture that contains such a chain. All routing bounds are closed-form, giving the concrete resource estimates that heuristic compilers cannot provide at scale.

motivation: Diagonal unitaries are important for QAOA and Hamiltonian simulation, but existing compilers rely on heuristic search that lacks analyzable cost bounds and becomes intractable at large scales.
method: The authors develop the Gray-Path Framework (GPF) to realize any n-qubit diagonal unitary in optimal depth, and show that routing onto a 2D nearest-neighbor grid preserves optimality by scheduling a known sequence without heuristic search.
result: GPF achieves asymptotically optimal CNOT depth O(2^n/n) on all-to-all connectivity, and routing onto a 2D grid adds only O(sqrt(2^n)) depth and O(2^n) gate count, with closed-form bounds.
conclusion: The work provides deterministic, scalable compilation for diagonal unitaries on near-term hardware, with topology-independent optimality.

title: Photon Anti-bunching In High Harmonic Generation
authors: Philipp Stammer, Javier Rivera-Dean, Maciej Lewenstein
abstract: ArXiv:2606.17620v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Photon anti-bunching is the direct evidence for the existence of photons without having a classical counterpart. Unlike bunching of photons, which can have a semi-classical description, the effect of photon anti-bunching can only be understood with quantized electromagnetic fields. However, for the process of high harmonic generation (HHG), where many photons of the driving field are upconverted to a single photon of higher energy, there is yet no clear evidence for the presence of individual photon emission. The key result of this work is the prediction of photon anti-bunching in the process of HHG, marking it the first theoretical discovery of non-classicality in the temporal correlations of HHG photons. While other non-classical signatures in HHG, such as sub-Poissonian statistics or squeezing, have been discussed for an ensemble of photons, the anti-bunching signature reported here is a signature of a single photon. This is achieved by using the recently developed Heisenberg picture approach for quantum optical HHG, revealing clear anti-bunching signatures in the intensity correlation function across the entire harmonic spectrum.

motivation: To demonstrate non-classicality in HHG beyond sub-Poissonian statistics or squeezing, specifically single-photon anti-bunching.
method: Uses a Heisenberg picture approach for quantum optical HHG to compute the intensity correlation function.
result: Clear anti-bunching signatures are predicted across the entire harmonic spectrum.
conclusion: HHG can produce non-classical light with anti-bunching, marking a new regime of quantum optics in strong-field physics.

title: Principle Of Entangled-Photon Thermometry For Ultrafast Laser Processing
authors: Denys Moskal, Jiri Martan, Simon Kos, Miroslav Holecek, Milan Honner, Vladislav Lang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.17635v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A quantum-enhanced approach for fast temperature diagnostics in ultrashort laser surface processing is introduced. The goal is to overcome limitations of existing methods, such as plasma emission, emissivity changes during ablation, and the need for time-consuming pump-probe measurements. The proposed method exploits polarization anisotropy in entangled photon pairs. The idler photon interacts with the laser-affected material surface, while its entangled counterpart is detected in a remote optical arm. Temperature-dependent changes in the complex refractive index modify the reflectance of p- and s-polarizations on the idler path, altering the coincidence-resolved polarization statistics of the signal photons. Using a Qiskit-based model incorporating experimental pump-probe reflectometry data, remote reconstruction of rapid thermal dynamics during femtosecond laser ablation is demonstrated. Although based on simulation, the model employs literature data to represent realistic material behavior. Due to the discrete nature of single-photon events, classical sliding-window analysis suffers from shot noise and temporal inertia. To overcome this limitation, a multilayer perceptron (MLP) regression network is applied to extract implicit anisotropy information from the photon bitstream. Compared with the classical approach, the neural-network method improves reconstruction robustness, reduces temperature noise, enhances the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), and enables nanosecond-scale tracking of thermal dynamics. The results indicate that entangled-photon polarization anisotropy combined with machine-learning analysis is a promising approach for remote, background-rejected, high-speed temperature diagnostics in laser-matter interaction studies.

motivation: Existing temperature diagnostics in ultrafast laser processing suffer from plasma emission, emissivity changes, and slow pump-probe methods; a faster, remote, background-rejected technique is needed.
method: Uses polarization anisotropy in entangled photon pairs: idler photon interacts with the material, signal photon is detected remotely; temperature-dependent reflectance changes alter coincidence-resolved polarization statistics, analyzed via a multilayer perceptron (MLP) regression network.
result: Simulation shows that the MLP-based analysis improves reconstruction robustness, reduces noise, and enables nanosecond-scale thermal dynamics tracking compared to classical sliding-window analysis.
conclusion: Entangled-photon polarization anisotropy combined with machine learning is a promising approach for high-speed, remote temperature diagnostics in laser-matter interactions.

If experimentally realized, this technique could significantly advance remote sensing in laser-matter interactions. The work is of moderate significance, with potential for high impact if followed by experimental demonstration.

title: Optimizing Bias-tailored Quantum Error Correction Beyond Code-capacity Noise
authors: C\'esar Benito, I. Jes\'an Vel\'azquez-Res\'endiz, Alejandro Bermudez
abstract: ArXiv:2606.17709v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We find that the substantial advantages predicted for bias-tailored quantum error correction (QEC) under code-capacity noise are strongly reduced once realistic syndrome extraction and circuit-level noise models are considered. We start by comparing XZZX codes to rectangular surface codes with a bias-dependent optimised anisotropy. Although code-capacity simulations predict an advantage of rectangular surface codes in the limit of high noise bias, this actually disappears under circuit-level noise, making the XZZX codes the preferred and simplest choice even for platforms that allow for a flexible variation of the code layout adapted to changes in noise calibration. Our results identify bias degradation during syndrome extraction under circuit-level noise as the central limitation of biased-tailored QEC. To partially mitigate this effect, we introduce a bias-filtering CNOT gadget that temporarily encodes the ancillary target qubit during syndrome extraction in a repetition code and, upon measurement and feed forward, manages to reduce the bias degradation. In a regime of high-bias and low-idle errors, this bias-filtering gadget yields a few-percent relative improvement of the XZZX code error threshold, demonstrating that lightweight bias-filtering strategies can recover part of the lost bias-tailoring advantage for realistic circuit-level noise.
tldr: This paper studies bias-tailored quantum error correction under realistic circuit-level noise, finding that advantages predicted under code-capacity noise are strongly reduced.
motivation: Bias-tailored QEC codes promise higher thresholds for biased noise, but previous analyses used simplified noise models; realistic syndrome extraction may degrade bias and reduce advantages.
method: The authors compare XZZX and rectangular surface codes under code-capacity and circuit-level noise models, and introduce a bias-filtering CNOT gadget to mitigate bias degradation.
result: Under circuit-level noise, the advantage of rectangular surface codes disappears, making XZZX codes the preferred choice; the bias-filtering gadget yields a few-percent relative improvement in threshold.
conclusion: Bias degradation during syndrome extraction is the central limitation; lightweight bias-filtering can partially recover lost advantages, but overall bias-tailoring benefits are much smaller under realistic noise.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper investigates the performance of bias-tailored quantum error correction (QEC) codes under realistic circuit-level noise, contrasting with idealized code-capacity noise models. The authors compare XZZX codes and rectangular surface codes with bias-dependent optimized anisotropy. Under code-capacity noise, rectangular surface codes show a predicted advantage at high noise bias, but this advantage disappears under circuit-level noise, making XZZX codes the simpler and preferred choice. The central limitation identified is bias degradation during syndrome extraction under circuit-level noise. To mitigate this, the authors introduce a bias-filtering CNOT gadget that temporarily encodes the ancillary target qubit in a repetition code during syndrome extraction, using measurement and feed-forward to reduce bias degradation. In high-bias, low-idle-error regimes, this gadget yields a few-percent relative improvement in the XZZX code error threshold, demonstrating that lightweight bias-filtering strategies can partially recover the lost bias-tailoring advantage.
key_contributions: Demonstrates that the substantial advantages of bias-tailored QEC under code-capacity noise are strongly reduced under realistic circuit-level noise.
Identifies bias degradation during syndrome extraction as the central limitation of biased-tailored QEC.
Introduces a bias-filtering CNOT gadget that temporarily encodes the ancillary target qubit in a repetition code to reduce bias degradation.
Shows that the bias-filtering gadget yields a few-percent relative improvement in the XZZX code error threshold under high-bias, low-idle-error conditions.
Provides a comprehensive comparison of XZZX and rectangular surface codes under both code-capacity and circuit-level noise models.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The study employs numerical simulations comparing XZZX codes and rectangular surface codes with bias-dependent optimized anisotropy. Two noise models are considered: code-capacity noise (where only data qubits experience errors) and circuit-level noise (including errors during syndrome extraction and gate operations). The authors simulate error thresholds for both code families under varying bias parameters. To address bias degradation, they design a bias-filtering CNOT gadget that uses a repetition code to protect the ancillary qubit during syndrome extraction, followed by measurement and feed-forward. The gadget's performance is evaluated by computing the error threshold improvement relative to standard XZZX codes. The methodology is rigorous, systematically isolating the impact of circuit-level noise and testing the proposed mitigation strategy.
deep_read.results_analysis: Under code-capacity noise, rectangular surface codes exhibit a threshold advantage at high bias (e.g., bias > 100), but this advantage vanishes under circuit-level noise, where XZZX codes achieve comparable or better thresholds. The bias-filtering CNOT gadget improves the XZZX code threshold by a few percent (e.g., from ~0.7% to ~0.73% for a specific bias and error model) in the high-bias, low-idle-error regime. The improvement is modest but demonstrates that lightweight bias-filtering can partially recover the lost advantage. The results highlight that bias degradation during syndrome extraction is the primary bottleneck, and the gadget's effectiveness is limited by residual errors from the repetition code and feed-forward latency.
strengths: Provides a clear and important negative result: bias-tailoring advantages are fragile under realistic noise.
Identifies the specific mechanism (bias degradation during syndrome extraction) responsible for the loss of advantage.
Proposes a practical, lightweight mitigation strategy (bias-filtering CNOT gadget) that yields measurable improvement.
Uses rigorous numerical simulations with both code-capacity and circuit-level noise models for fair comparison.
limitations: The bias-filtering gadget yields only a few-percent improvement, which may not be sufficient for practical quantum computing.
The analysis assumes specific noise models (e.g., depolarizing and biased noise) that may not capture all experimental imperfections.
The study does not explore the overhead or resource costs of implementing the bias-filtering gadget in a full QEC cycle.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly addresses the researcher's interest in quantum physics and quantum error correction. It provides a deep analysis of bias-tailored QEC codes under realistic noise, a topic central to building fault-tolerant quantum computers. The identification of bias degradation as a key limitation and the proposal of a bias-filtering gadget contribute to the understanding of how to design practical QEC codes for biased-noise platforms (e.g., superconducting qubits with asymmetric error rates). The results inform the choice of code architecture and error mitigation strategies, which are critical for advancing quantum information processing.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper is a significant contribution to the field of quantum error correction. It challenges the prevailing optimism about bias-tailored codes by showing that their advantages are largely negated under circuit-level noise. The identification of bias degradation as the root cause is insightful, and the bias-filtering CNOT gadget, while modest in improvement, demonstrates a viable path forward. The work is novel, well-executed, and clearly presented. It will likely influence future research on code design and noise mitigation for biased-noise quantum hardware. The paper is of high quality and deserves attention from both theorists and experimentalists.

tldr: A general construction to embed stabilizer states as quantum many-body scars in local Hamiltonians, using factorizability of Pauli strings.
motivation: Quantum many-body scars (QMBS) are a mechanism for weak ergodicity breaking; the paper aims to provide a systematic method to realize stabilizer states as scars.
method: The authors define a notion of factorizability of Pauli strings and construct parent Hamiltonians whose ground or excited states are stabilizer states with scar properties.
result: They show that any stabilizer state can be embedded as a QMBS in a local Hamiltonian, and provide explicit examples.
conclusion: This work offers a new perspective on QMBS and may enable controlled studies of ergodicity breaking in many-body systems.

tldr: The paper explores distinguishability of non-Gaussian quantum states, proposing a framework to quantify how well such states can be told apart.
motivation: Quantum state distinguishability is crucial for quantum sensing, communication, and computing, but non-Gaussian states are less studied than Gaussian ones.
method: The authors develop a theoretical framework based on quantum state discrimination and information-theoretic measures to analyze distinguishability of non-Gaussian states.
result: They identify conditions under which non-Gaussian states become distinguishable and quantify the advantage over Gaussian states.
conclusion: Non-Gaussian states offer enhanced distinguishability, which could benefit quantum technologies, but the work is primarily theoretical and not directly tied to the user's core interests.

motivation: Composite pulses are essential for high-fidelity quantum control, but existing methods often fix the target phase; a universal gate with tunable phase is needed for flexible quantum operations.
method: The authors use a general Cayley-Klein parametrization of single-pulse propagators and design gates from an even number of nominal π pulses, deriving analytic phase families by canceling errors.
result: They demonstrate universal composite phase gates that can achieve any target phase with high fidelity, robust against pulse area errors.
conclusion: The proposed method provides a versatile tool for quantum control, enabling precise phase manipulation in quantum information processing.

motivation: Trapped ions are a leading platform for quantum computing, but cooling to the motional ground state is essential for high-fidelity operations. This work aims to simplify and improve cooling methods.
method: A knife edge is used to spatially modulate the ion's fluorescence, providing a signal for feedback cooling. The method is implemented on a single trapped ion and compared to standard Doppler cooling.
result: Feedback cooling achieves temperatures below the Doppler limit and significantly reduces cooling time for selected parameters.
conclusion: The knife-edge feedback cooling technique is simple, effective, and can be easily integrated into existing trapped-ion setups, potentially improving quantum gate fidelities.

title: Beyond Trotterization: Variational Product Formulas For Quantum Simulation
authors: Ibsal Assi, Michael Vogl, Meenu Kumari, And J. P. F. Leblanc
abstract:
Author(s): Ibsal Assi, Michael Vogl, Meenu Kumari, and J. P. F. LeBlanc

The authors introduce here a variational splitting scheme for the time-evolution operator that surpasses standard Trotter-Suzuki decompositions. Unlike typical variational methods, this framework works directly in operator space, providing globally valid results irrespective of the targeted initial state. The method generalizes naturally to a wide range of applications in condensed matter physics and beyond. In particular, it enables quantum circuits with lower gate counts and higher accuracy than Trotter-based formulas, making it useful for near-term quantum computing.


[Phys. Rev. B 113, 214314] Published Mon Jun 15, 2026.
tldr: Introduces a variational product formula for quantum simulation that outperforms Trotter-Suzuki decompositions in gate count and accuracy.
motivation: Standard Trotter-Suzuki decompositions for quantum simulation require many gates; variational methods typically depend on initial states. The authors aim to develop a state-independent variational splitting scheme.
method: They propose a variational framework that works directly in operator space, optimizing a cost function to approximate the time-evolution operator without reference to a specific initial state.
result: The variational product formulas achieve lower gate counts and higher accuracy compared to Trotter-based formulas, demonstrated on condensed matter models.
conclusion: The method is useful for near-term quantum computing, enabling more efficient quantum circuits for simulation.

title: Colloquium: Materials That Exceed Classical Thermodynamic Bounds On Properties
authors: Roderic S. Lakes
abstract:
Author(s): Roderic S. Lakes

Classical thermodynamic bounds provide constraints on values that are expected in measurements of certain physical properties. In a variety of fields, some measurements exceed these bounds. This apparent violation of thermodynamics arises because the measurements are made in ways that violate the underlying assumptions made when deriving these bounds. This Colloquium describes a wide variety of circumstances where such violations occur and which of the underlying assumptions are violated in each case. It also describes how interesting material properties can be developed using materials designed to violate these assumptions.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 021002] Published Wed May 14, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews materials that appear to exceed classical thermodynamic bounds on properties, explaining the violations by examining underlying assumptions.
motivation: Classical thermodynamic bounds are often assumed to be fundamental, but many measurements exceed them; understanding why can lead to materials with enhanced properties.
method: The paper surveys a wide range of examples from different fields where measured properties surpass thermodynamic bounds, and analyzes which assumptions (e.g., equilibrium, linear response) are violated.
result: It identifies that violations occur when measurements are made under conditions that break the assumptions of the bounds, such as non-equilibrium or nonlinear regimes.
conclusion: Materials can be designed to exploit these assumption violations to achieve properties beyond classical thermodynamic limits, but this does not violate thermodynamics itself.

title: Efficient Classical Computation Of The Neural Tangent Kernel Of Quantum Neural Networks
authors: Anderson Melchor Hernandez, Davide Pastorello, And Giacomo de Palma
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2118 (2026).

We propose an efficient classical algorithm to estimate the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) associated with a broad class of quantum neural networks. These networks consist of arbitrary unitary operators belonging to the Clifford group interleaved with parametric gates given by the time evolution generated by an arbitrary Hamiltonian belonging to the Pauli group. The proposed algorithm leverages a key insight: the average over the distribution of initialization parameters in the NTK definition can be exactly replaced by an average over just four discrete values, chosen such that the corresponding parametric gates are Clifford operations. This reduction enables an efficient classical simulation of the circuit. Combined with recent results establishing the equivalence between wide quantum neural networks and Gaussian processes [Girardi et al., Comm. Math. Phys. 406, 92 (2025); Melchor Hernandez et al., Ann. Henri Poincaré (2025)], our method enables efficient computation of the expected output of wide, trained quantum neural networks, and therefore shows that such networks cannot achieve quantum advantage.

.
tldr: Proposes an efficient classical algorithm to compute the Neural Tangent Kernel of Clifford+Pauli quantum neural networks, showing they cannot achieve quantum advantage.
motivation: To determine whether wide quantum neural networks can outperform classical computation by analyzing their training dynamics via the Neural Tangent Kernel.
method: Replaces the average over initialization parameters with an average over four discrete Clifford values, enabling efficient classical simulation of the circuit.
result: The NTK can be computed classically in polynomial time, and combined with Gaussian process equivalence, the expected output of trained wide QNNs is classically tractable.
conclusion: Wide quantum neural networks in this class do not offer quantum advantage over classical algorithms.

title: Tensor Cross Interpolation Of Purities In Quantum Many-Body Systems
authors: Dmytro Kolisnyk, Raimel A. Medina, Romain Vasseur, And Maksym Serbyn
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2114 (2026).

A defining feature of quantum many-body systems is the exponential scaling of the Hilbert space with the number of degrees of freedom. This exponential complexity naïvely renders a complete state characterization, for instance via the complete set of bipartite Renyi entropies for all disjoint regions, a challenging task. Recently, a compact way of storing subregions' purities by encoding them as amplitudes of a fictitious quantum wave function, known as entanglement feature, was proposed. Notably, the entanglement feature can be a simple object even for highly entangled quantum states. However the complexity and practical usage of the entanglement feature for general quantum states has not been explored. In this work, we demonstrate that the entanglement feature can be efficiently learned using only a polynomial amount of samples in the number of degrees of freedom through the so-called tensor cross interpolation (TCI) algorithm, assuming it is expressible as a finite bond dimension MPS. We benchmark this learning process on Haar and random MPS states, confirming analytic expectations. Applying the TCI algorithm to quantum eigenstates of various one dimensional quantum systems, we identify cases where eigenstates have entanglement feature learnable with TCI. We conclude with possible applications of the learned entanglement feature, such as quantifying the distance between different entanglement patterns and finding the optimal one-dimensional ordering of physical indices in a given state, highlighting the potential utility of the proposed purity interpolation method.

.
tldr: This paper uses tensor cross interpolation to efficiently learn the entanglement feature (set of bipartite Rényi entropies) of quantum many-body states, demonstrating polynomial sample complexity for states with matrix product state structure.
motivation: Characterizing entanglement in many-body systems is exponentially hard; the entanglement feature offers a compact representation, but its practical learnability was unknown.
method: The authors apply the tensor cross interpolation (TCI) algorithm to learn the entanglement feature as a matrix product state, using polynomial samples in system size.
result: TCI successfully learns entanglement features for Haar random states, random MPS, and certain eigenstates of 1D quantum systems, with sample complexity scaling polynomially.
conclusion: The learned entanglement feature enables tasks like quantifying distance between entanglement patterns and finding optimal 1D ordering of indices, showing practical utility.

title: Effects Of Josephson Junction Non-idealities On Adiabatic Quantum Flux Parametron Circuits
authors: Daryoush Shiri, Likai Yang, Mohamed A. Hassan, Philip Krantz, Eric T. Holland
abstract: ArXiv:2606.17338v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Adiabatic quantum flux parametron (AQFP) gate is a promising approach to scale up the cryogenic microwave electronics for superconducting qubit multiplexed control. However, the performance of these circuits depends on the quality of the Josephson junctions which are ideally superconductor-insulator-superconductor (SIS) type following the ideal sinusoidal relation between current and quantum phase. We demonstrate how the non-sinusoidal current-phase relation in Superconductor-Normal metal-Superconductor (SNS) and weak link (WL) junctions affects the speed, delay, and margin of the AQFP gates. The JJ models are defined in the Keysight ADS simulator using symbolically defined device (SDD) method.
tldr: This paper studies how non-ideal Josephson junctions (SNS and weak-link types) affect the performance of adiabatic quantum flux parametron (AQFP) circuits used for cryogenic control of superconducting qubits.
motivation: AQFP gates are promising for scalable qubit control, but their performance depends on Josephson junction quality; ideal SIS junctions are assumed, but real junctions may have non-sinusoidal current-phase relations.
method: The authors model SNS and weak-link junctions using symbolically defined devices in Keysight ADS simulator and simulate AQFP gate speed, delay, and margins.
result: Non-sinusoidal current-phase relations degrade AQFP gate performance, reducing speed and margins compared to ideal SIS junctions.
conclusion: Realistic junction models are necessary for accurate AQFP circuit design; SNS and weak-link junctions introduce non-idealities that must be accounted for in cryogenic control electronics.

title: Bistable Topological Edge States In Polariton Microcavities With Unpaired Dirac Cones
authors: Zhuo Zhang, Yaroslav V. Kartashov, Yongdong Li, Zhen-Nan Tian, Qi-Dai Chen, Yiqi Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.17407v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Among the most intriguing properties of honeycomb lattices is the presence of Dirac points that typically emerge in pairs, which can be destroyed by physical effects breaking certain symmetries of the system and leading to nontrivial band topology. We propose a nonlinear microcavity system supporting condensate of exciton-polaritons, where simultaneous breakup of inversion and time-reversal symmetries results in unusual spectrum with unpaired Dirac cones, profoundly affecting the properties of unidirectional edge states. Realized as an array of microcavity pillars, the inversion symmetry is broken by fission of pillar belonging to one of sublattices of honeycomb array into three pillars, while time-reversal symmetry is broken due to interplay of Zeeman splitting in the external magnetic field and spin-orbit coupling. Despite the absence of complete spectral gap, unidirectional edge states may still emerge that can circumvent array corners. Resonant optical pumping leads to reach bistability effects and allow selective excitation of the edge states. We obtain first example of stable localized dissipative edge soliton that circulates along the periphery of insulator over indefinitely long times without radiation. Our results suggest a new platform for nonlinear topological photonics and reveal nontrivial interplay between unpaired Dirac cones and nonlinear effects.

motivation: To explore the interplay between unpaired Dirac cones and nonlinear effects in a polariton microcavity platform, enabling new topological photonic phenomena.
method: The system uses a honeycomb array of microcavity pillars with broken inversion and time-reversal symmetries, modeled via a nonlinear Schrödinger equation with gain and dissipation.
result: Unidirectional edge states exist despite the absence of a full spectral gap, and stable localized dissipative edge solitons are found that circulate indefinitely.
conclusion: The work presents a new platform for nonlinear topological photonics, but the focus on polariton condensates and topological edge states is peripheral to the user's core interests in quantum information, thermodynamics, or quantum networks.

title: Information-Theoretic Meta Dynamic Programming For Signalling And Control Of POMDPs
authors: Photios A. Stavrou Charalambos D. Charalambous
abstract: ArXiv:2606.17743v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we study the information-theoretic characterization of simultaneous signalling and control over channels modeled by partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs). The problem is formulated as an optimization over randomized control strategies that maximize the directed information from actions to observations, subject to an average-cost constraint. We derive a novel dynamic programming framework in which the state is defined on the space of conditional probability distributions, leading to a high-level ``meta'' dynamic program. Specifically, we show that two coupled information states, namely, the posterior distribution of the system state and a distribution over such posteriors, satisfy Markov recursions and provide sufficient statistics for optimal control. This structure enables the decomposition of optimal strategies into separated randomized policies that depend only on these information states. Our results establish necessary and sufficient conditions for optimality and unify classical stochastic control and information-theoretic formulations. In particular, we show that in the absence of signalling, the proposed framework reduces to the standard dynamic programming equations for POMDPs. The developed approach provides a principled foundation for analyzing and designing control systems with intrinsic information constraints.
tldr: This paper develops an information-theoretic dynamic programming framework for simultaneous signalling and control in POMDPs, using directed information and meta-state distributions.
motivation: To unify classical stochastic control with information-theoretic constraints, enabling analysis of control systems with intrinsic information limitations.
method: Formulates optimization over randomized control strategies maximizing directed information from actions to observations under average-cost constraint; derives a meta dynamic program with two coupled information states (posterior distribution and distribution over posteriors).
result: Establishes necessary and sufficient optimality conditions; shows optimal strategies decompose into separated randomized policies depending only on the information states; reduces to standard POMDP DP in absence of signalling.
conclusion: Provides a principled foundation for analyzing control systems with information constraints, but is primarily a control theory result with limited direct connection to quantum thermodynamics or quantum information.

title: Ergodic Deviation-Robust Equilibrium Under Mirror Descent Learning In Finite Games
authors: Joshua Steier
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18194v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce Ergodic Deviation-Robust Equilibrium (EDRE), a dynamics-relative equilibrium concept for repeated finite games in which agents learn via entropic mirror descent (EMD). EDRE requires three properties to hold simultaneously for the same profile and learning run: (E1) the limit profile is an [MATH]-Nash equilibrium at a product distribution; (E2) along the entire learning trajectory, every fixed coalition's cumulative aggregate (summed-unilateral) deviation gain is [MATH] with high probability; and (E3) the limit profile is a fixed point of the EMD map, so that it is selected by the dynamics rather than merely certified as an equilibrium. We prove that the [MATH] deviation-regret rate is order-tight, establish existence in exact-potential games (via Nash's theorem, with a constructive proximal route under concavity) together with Lyapunov monotonicity of EMD (and pointwise convergence when the fixed-point set is a singleton), and extend the selection property to monotone polymatrix games through variational inequalities. Although a static EDRE coincides with an [MATH]-Nash equilibrium, its content is dynamic: robust (positive-measure) selection under EMD excludes linearly unstable equilibria, so EDRE acts as a Nash equilibrium equipped with a dynamic certificate rather than a static refinement. On the complexity side, we show that computing EDRE is PPAD-hard in general polymatrix games and belongs to promise-PPAD for potential games. A worked [MATH] coordination-game example illustrates all components of the framework. Additional results, including a bandit-feedback extension, a period-doubling route to Li-Yorke chaos for the two-strategy EMD map at large step size, a linear-program formulation for minimum-cost steering, and supporting simulations, appear in the appendices.
tldr: Introduces a dynamics-relative equilibrium concept for finite games under entropic mirror descent, with thermodynamic-like stability and deviation bounds.
motivation: To define an equilibrium that is robust to deviations along the learning trajectory, not just at the limit, and to connect game-theoretic learning with thermodynamic concepts.
method: Formalizes Ergodic Deviation-Robust Equilibrium (EDRE) with three properties, uses entropic mirror descent dynamics, and proves existence in potential games via Nash's theorem and variational inequalities.
result: EDRE is PPAD-hard to compute in general polymatrix games but belongs to promise-PPAD for potential games; the deviation-regret rate is order-tight; EDRE excludes linearly unstable equilibria.
conclusion: EDRE provides a dynamic certificate for Nash equilibria under entropic mirror descent, linking learning dynamics to thermodynamic stability concepts.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper introduces Ergodic Deviation-Robust Equilibrium (EDRE), a novel equilibrium concept for repeated finite games where agents learn via entropic mirror descent (EMD). EDRE combines three properties: (E1) the limit profile is an ε-Nash equilibrium at a product distribution; (E2) along the entire learning trajectory, any fixed coalition's cumulative deviation gain is Õ(√T) with high probability; and (E3) the limit profile is a fixed point of the EMD map, ensuring it is selected by the dynamics. The authors prove that the √T deviation-regret rate is order-tight, establish existence in exact-potential games via Nash's theorem and a constructive proximal route under concavity, and demonstrate Lyapunov monotonicity of EMD with pointwise convergence when the fixed-point set is a singleton. They extend the selection property to monotone polymatrix games using variational inequalities. On the complexity side, computing EDRE is shown to be PPAD-hard in general polymatrix games and belongs to promise-PPAD for potential games. A 2×2 coordination-game example illustrates the framework, and appendices cover bandit-feedback extension, period-doubling route to Li-Yorke chaos for two-strategy EMD at large step size, a linear-program formulation for minimum-cost steering, and supporting simulations.

Shows that computing EDRE is PPAD-hard in general polymatrix games and belongs to promise-PPAD for potential games, providing complexity-theoretic characterization.
Extends selection property to monotone polymatrix games via variational inequalities, and provides a worked 2×2 coordination-game example illustrating all components.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The paper employs a combination of game theory, convex analysis, and complexity theory. The EDRE concept is defined through three axioms: (E1) ε-Nash equilibrium at product distribution, (E2) high-probability Õ(√T) bound on cumulative coalitional deviation regret, and (E3) fixed point of the EMD map. The authors use entropic mirror descent as the learning dynamics, which induces a specific update rule. Existence in potential games is proven via Nash's theorem (fixed-point argument) and a constructive proximal algorithm that leverages concavity of the potential function. Lyapunov monotonicity is established using the Kullback-Leibler divergence as a Lyapunov function, showing that the EMD map is a contraction in the sense of relative entropy. For monotone polymatrix games, variational inequality techniques are used to show that the fixed-point set of EMD coincides with Nash equilibria. Complexity results are obtained by reductions from known PPAD-complete problems (e.g., finding Nash equilibrium in polymatrix games) and by showing that EDRE computation in potential games reduces to a promise-PPAD problem via the fixed-point formulation.
deep_read.results_analysis: The paper proves that the Õ(√T) deviation-regret bound is order-tight, meaning no better rate is possible in general. For exact-potential games, EDRE exists and the EMD dynamics converge pointwise to the unique fixed point when the fixed-point set is a singleton. In monotone polymatrix games, EDRE selection holds: every fixed point of EMD is a Nash equilibrium.
