We examine the hydrogen atom through a regularized de Broglie--Bohm representation, in which stationary amplitude current constraints generate separable Sturm--Liouville branches. In this formulation, the radial, orbital, and magnetic sectors acquire canonical Langer-like inverse square corrections. The modified boundary value problems allow analytical solutions and produce a hydrogen-like spectrum with regularized radial and angular indices. Consequently, radial Coulomb quantization acquires an orbital dependent shift, lifting the Coulomb degeneracy and producing a spectral ordering that follows the Aufbau/Madelung sequence. On this basis, we construct the ordering of the regularized de Broglie--Bohm states and show that the spectral structure retains the standard degenerate Rydberg sequence in the l=0 sector. The separated amplitudes are represented by generalized special function branches, including the associated Laguerre, Legendre, and Bessel functions with non-integral parameters arising from regularized separation. Therefore, the treatment is intended as an analytical examination of spectral ordering in a regularized one center Coulomb problem rather than as a replacement for the many electron atomic structure theory. Keywords: de Broglie--Bohm representation; Coulomb spectrum; canonical regularization; Langer correction; Sturm--Liouville equations; Aufbau principle; Madelung ordering; associated Legendre functions; associated Laguerre functions; Bessel functions.
tldr: This paper uses a de Broglie-Bohm representation with canonical regularization to lift Coulomb degeneracy in hydrogen, producing an Aufbau-like spectral ordering.
motivation: The hydrogen atom exhibits Coulomb degeneracy across orbital levels, while the empirical Aufbau/Madelung ordering applies to many-electron atoms. The authors aim to derive a similar ordering from a regularized single-particle model.
method: They apply a de Broglie-Bohm representation with stationary amplitude current constraints, leading to separable Sturm-Liouville branches. Canonical Langer-like inverse square corrections are introduced, modifying the boundary value problems.
result: The regularization lifts Coulomb degeneracy by introducing orbital-dependent shifts in radial quantization, yielding a spectral ordering that follows the Aufbau/Madelung sequence. The l=0 sector retains the standard degenerate Rydberg sequence.
conclusion: The treatment provides an analytical examination of spectral ordering in a regularized one-center Coulomb problem, but is not intended as a replacement for many-electron atomic structure theory.

title: Homogeneous Boltzmann-type Equations On Dense Graphs
authors: Andrea Tosin Gabriele Taricco
abstract: ArXiv:2606.17638v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In kinetic theory, interactions between particles are typically assumed to be "all-to-all", meaning that any pair of randomly selected particles may, in principle, interact. This assumption originates from the theory of colliding gas molecules; however, it may be less appropriate for describing other forms of interaction, such as social interactions. These are more naturally characterised as "some-to-some", reflecting the existence of preferential connections between agents. In this paper, we consider homogeneous Boltzmann-type equations on finite graphs that model such networks of preferential interactions, and we rigorously derive their dense graph limit as the number of agents tends to infinity. We also investigate the long-time behaviour of the limiting equation in the case of linear pairwise interactions, characterising the emergent equilibrium distributions and relating them to their counterparts in the classical "all-to-all" setting.
tldr: This paper studies homogeneous Boltzmann-type equations on finite graphs and derives their dense graph limit, focusing on social interaction networks rather than quantum or thermodynamic systems.
motivation: Classical kinetic theory assumes all-to-all interactions, which is inappropriate for social networks where interactions are preferential. The authors aim to model such 'some-to-some' interactions using graph-based Boltzmann equations.
method: They consider homogeneous Boltzmann-type equations on finite graphs, then rigorously derive the dense graph limit as the number of agents tends to infinity. For linear pairwise interactions, they analyze long-time behavior and characterize equilibrium distributions.
result: The dense graph limit is obtained, and for linear interactions, emergent equilibrium distributions are characterized and related to those in the classical all-to-all setting.
conclusion: The work provides a mathematical framework for kinetic equations on networks, but it is purely classical and unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, or quantum hardware.

title: First-order Phase Transitions In The Three-dimensional Blume-Capel Ferromagnet
authors: D. Mataragkas, A. Vasilopoulos, Z. D. Vatansever, Y. Kim, D. -H. Kim, N. G Fytas
abstract: ArXiv:2606.17691v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate first-order phase transitions in the three-dimensional Blume-Capel ferromagnet on the simple cubic lattice by combining multicanonical simulations with two-parameter Wang-Landau sampling. The generalized-ensemble approach enables a detailed characterization of the coexistence region over a broad range of temperatures and crystal-field couplings, extending from the vicinity of the tricritical point deep into the first-order regime. We analyze the finite-size scaling behavior of thermodynamic observables, with particular emphasis on the energy probability density function, free-energy barriers, and interfacial properties. The evolution of the double-peaked energy distributions reveals a gradual crossover from weak to strong first-order behavior as the temperature is lowered. From the scaling of the free-energy barrier we determine the interface tension along the coexistence line and characterize its approach to the tricritical region through its vanishing behavior. In parallel, a field-mixing analysis based on the joint density of states obtained from two-parameter Wang-Landau simulations is employed to locate first-order transition points and probe tricritical behavior. While this approach has been highly successful in two-dimensional realizations of the Blume-Capel model, we find that in three dimensions its practical implementation becomes increasingly sensitive in the vicinity of the tricritical region, where the shallow structure of the relevant scaling variable distribution limits the ability to resolve coexistence conditions for the system sizes currently accessible. These results delineate the range of applicability of the method in three dimensions and provide a consistent picture of the first-order regime of the model.
tldr: This paper studies first-order phase transitions in the 3D Blume-Capel ferromagnet using multicanonical and Wang-Landau simulations.
motivation: To characterize the first-order regime and tricritical behavior of a classical spin model, which is a standard problem in statistical mechanics.
method: Combines multicanonical simulations with two-parameter Wang-Landau sampling to compute joint densities of states and analyze finite-size scaling of energy distributions and free-energy barriers.
result: Reveals a gradual crossover from weak to strong first-order behavior as temperature decreases, and determines interface tension along the coexistence line; field-mixing analysis works less well in 3D near the tricritical point.
conclusion: Provides a consistent picture of the first-order regime of the 3D Blume-Capel model and delineates the applicability of the field-mixing method in three dimensions.

title: Hybrid Digital-Analog Approximate Inverse Preconditioning For Krylov Methods
authors: Shikhar Shah, Rui Peng Li, Tayfun Gokmen, Vassilis Kalantzis, Lior Horesh, Yuanzhe Xi
abstract: ArXiv:2606.17227v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Analog in-memory computing enables highly parallel matrix-vector multiplications with reduced data movement, but the resulting operations are noisy, quantized, and affected by device- and circuit-level non-idealities. This paper studies approximate inverse preconditioning for Krylov subspace methods in a hybrid digital-analog setting. The digital host performs sparse products with the coefficient matrix and the precision-sensitive Krylov operations, while preconditioner applications are performed through analog crossbar matrix-vector multiplications. Since the realized preconditioner is inexact and application-dependent, the outer iteration is formulated as the flexible GMRES method. We show that analog execution changes the usual preconditioner design problem in the sense that a stronger digital preconditioner may be less effective after analog scaling, write noise, input/output perturbations, quantization, and clipping are taken into account. We compare various block Jacobi preconditioning schemes including exact block inverses, sparse approximate inverses, Monte Carlo approximate inverses (MCAI), damping, and nested block Jacobi schemes. Numerical experiments with realistic analog matrix-vector simulations show that analog-aware choices of block size, damping, MCAI construction accuracy, and nesting are important for robust convergence.
tldr: This paper studies hybrid digital-analog preconditioning for Krylov methods using analog in-memory computing, focusing on numerical linear algebra rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: Analog in-memory computing offers efficient matrix-vector multiplications but introduces noise and quantization, motivating the need for robust preconditioning in iterative solvers.
method: The authors propose a flexible GMRES framework where the digital host handles sparse products and Krylov operations, while preconditioner applications are performed via analog crossbar arrays. They compare block Jacobi, sparse approximate inverses, Monte Carlo approximate inverses, damping, and nested schemes.
result: Analog-aware choices of block size, damping, and construction accuracy are critical for convergence; a stronger digital preconditioner may become less effective after analog non-idealities.
conclusion: Hybrid digital-analog preconditioning can be effective if designed with analog constraints in mind, but the approach is specific to classical computing hardware.

title: Accelerated Convex Optimization Via Hamiltonian Dynamics With Deterministic Integration Time
authors: Xiuyuan Wang, Vishwak Srinivasan, Qiang Fu, Siddharth Mitra, Ashia Wilson, Andre Wibisono
abstract: ArXiv:2606.17260v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop Hamiltonian dynamics-based algorithms for smooth convex optimization that achieve accelerated rates of convergence. By exploiting contraction of averaged Hamiltonian flow trajectories rather than requiring contraction at trajectory endpoints, we show that Hamiltonian dynamics-based optimization methods admit deterministic and accelerated convergence guarantees, extending prior work that is limited to quadratic objectives or holds only in expectation. We analyze an idealized continuous-time algorithm and derive practical discrete-time implementations with optimal first-order complexity, thereby establishing Hamiltonian dynamics as a useful algorithmic primitive for deterministic accelerated convex optimization.
tldr: This paper develops Hamiltonian dynamics-based algorithms for deterministic accelerated convex optimization, unrelated to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: To achieve accelerated convergence rates in smooth convex optimization using Hamiltonian dynamics with deterministic guarantees.
method: Exploits contraction of averaged Hamiltonian flow trajectories and derives discrete-time implementations with optimal first-order complexity.
result: Establishes Hamiltonian dynamics as a useful algorithmic primitive for deterministic accelerated convex optimization.
conclusion: The proposed methods achieve accelerated rates without relying on stochasticity or quadratic objectives.

title: Construction Of Codes Over A Commutative Non-unital Ring From Simplicial Complexes And Their Applications
authors: Vidya Sagar, Shikha Patel, Sanjay Kumar Singh
abstract: ArXiv:2606.17300v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this article, we investigate the construction of linear codes over a finite ring [MATH], where [MATH] is taken to be an extension of a commutative non-unital ring [MATH] of order [MATH]. Our approach is based on the defining set method. The defining sets considered in this work are derived from general simplicial complexes that may contain multiple maximal elements. We determine the parameters of these codes over [MATH] and study their Gray images. We also study the corresponding subfield-like codes. We show that these Gray image codes and subfield-like codes produce several families of divisible codes. Furthermore, we establish sufficient conditions under which these codes are minimal, optimal, and self-orthogonal. As applications of our results, we obtain several families of projective few-weight codes, and locally recoverable codes with small locality. We also study the minimal access structures of secret-sharing schemes associated with the duals of these minimal codes. Moreover, we construct several families of strongly regular graphs from projective two-weight codes and determine their parameters explicitly.
tldr: This paper constructs linear codes over a commutative non-unital ring using simplicial complexes, and studies their properties and applications to secret sharing and strongly regular graphs.
motivation: To explore code constructions over non-standard algebraic structures and derive families of codes with desirable properties like minimality, optimality, and self-orthogonality.
method: The defining set method is used, where defining sets are derived from general simplicial complexes. Parameters of the codes over the ring are determined, and Gray images and subfield-like codes are studied.
result: Several families of divisible codes, projective few-weight codes, and locally recoverable codes are obtained. Conditions for minimal, optimal, and self-orthogonal codes are established. Strongly regular graphs are constructed from projective two-weight codes.
conclusion: The work provides new code families with applications in secret sharing and graph theory, but is primarily algebraic coding theory with no direct connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: Beyond IGO-Flow: Toward Convergence Analysis Of Igo In Continuous Spaces
authors: Youhei Akimoto Ryosuke Kimura
abstract: ArXiv:2606.17523v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Information-Geometric Optimization (IGO) provides a unified framework for black-box optimization by interpreting the adaptation of a search distribution as a natural gradient update. Despite its conceptual importance, the convergence theory of IGO remains limited: most existing results concern continuous-time idealizations such as the IGO flow, rather than discrete-time updates with non-infinitesimal learning rates. In this paper, we study discrete-time IGO in continuous spaces, formulated as natural gradient updates in the expectation-parameter coordinates of an exponential family. In particular, we analyze IGO over the multivariate Gaussian family on strongly convex quadratic objective functions. Our analysis covers a setting that simultaneously incorporates full covariance adaptation, a fixed positive learning rate, and quantile-based weights. In this setting, we prove that the covariance matrix converges to the zero matrix. We further show that the mean vector converges to the global optimum, provided that the condition number of the appropriately scaled covariance matrix is bounded at sufficiently frequent iterations. These results advance the convergence theory of IGO and help bridge the gap between the mathematical theory of IGO and practical covariance-adaptive search methods such as CMA-ES.
tldr: This paper analyzes the convergence of discrete-time Information-Geometric Optimization (IGO) in continuous spaces, focusing on multivariate Gaussian families and quadratic objectives.
motivation: Existing convergence theory for IGO is limited to continuous-time idealizations; this work aims to bridge the gap to practical discrete-time algorithms with fixed learning rates.
method: The authors formulate IGO as natural gradient updates in expectation-parameter coordinates of an exponential family and analyze its dynamics on strongly convex quadratic functions with full covariance adaptation and quantile-based weights.
result: They prove that the covariance matrix converges to zero and that the mean vector converges to the global optimum under a bounded condition number condition.
conclusion: The results advance the convergence theory of IGO, providing a foundation for understanding practical covariance-adaptive search methods like CMA-ES.

title: Non-asymptotic Tail Bounds For The Kostlan--Shub--Smale Field: Tensor Pca And Spherical $k$-Spin Complexity
authors: Jean-Marc Aza\"is (IMT), Federico Dalmao (UDELAR), Yohann de Castro
abstract: ArXiv:2606.17665v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper builds a hierarchy of explicit, non-asymptotic tail bounds for the supremum of the Kostlan--Shub--Smale (KSS) random field on the sphere, and applies it to two problems: Spiked Tensor PCA and the landscape of the spherical [MATH]-spin model. For Tensor PCA, we study the non-asymptotic statistical limits of estimating a rank-[MATH] symmetric signal tensor of order~[MATH] and dimension~[MATH] from a single Gaussian observation at signal-to-noise ratio~[MATH], through the , the MLE restricted to normalized rank-[MATH] tensors of coherence at least~[MATH]. Our analysis uses a single reduction: a deterministic geometric inequality (the Tube Method) and a rank-reduction step bound the estimation error by the supremum of the canonical KSS field, which the Kac--Rice formula turns into a Gaussian integral against the expected absolute characteristic polynomial of a shifted Gaussian Orthogonal Ensemble, controlled in turn by the four explicit tail bounds of our hierarchy (three from a Mehta--Fyodorov representation, one from a Ben Arous--Dembo--Guionnet large deviation). The same reduction yields two results, each with explicit constants. For estimation, a finite-[MATH] error bound recovers the asymptotically optimal rate~[MATH] of Perry, Wein and Bandeira, with explicit dependence on the rank~[MATH] and the coherence~[MATH]. For the landscape, a two-sided non-asymptotic bracketing of the annealed complexity of the spherical [MATH]-spin Hamiltonian recovers the Auffinger--Ben Arous--ern\'y complexity function in the high-dimensional limit.
tldr: The paper derives non-asymptotic tail bounds for the Kostlan-Shub-Smale random field and applies them to spiked tensor PCA and spherical spin glass complexity.
motivation: To obtain explicit finite-sample error bounds for tensor PCA and to characterize the landscape complexity of spherical spin glasses.
method: Uses the tube method, Kac-Rice formula, and Mehta-Fyodorov/Ben Arous-Dembo-Guionnet representations to bound the supremum of the KSS field.
result: Recovers the optimal asymptotic rate for tensor PCA with explicit constants and provides non-asymptotic bracketing of the annealed complexity for the spherical p-spin model.
conclusion: The hierarchy of tail bounds yields tight finite-sample guarantees for high-dimensional statistical and spin glass problems.

title: When Rough Data Helps: A Phase Transition In Convergence Rates For Kernel Recovery In Integral Operators
authors: Jihong Wang, Fei Lu, Yue Yu
abstract: ArXiv:2606.17672v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Learning kernels in operators from data is a fundamental task that arises in nonlocal continuum mechanics, operator learning, and interacting particle systems. A central question is how the roughness of input data impacts the accuracy of kernel recovery. We quantify the roughness of the input data via its spectral decay exponent and analyze how it determines the degree of ill-posedness of the inverse problem and, consequently, the convergence rates of the Tikhonov-regularized estimator in the small-noise limit. Within this framework, we identify a phase transition between an under-rough regime, in which rougher data improves recovery, and an over-rough regime, in which further roughening leads to slower rates. These theoretical findings are supported by numerical experiments ranging from idealized settings to more realistic configurations, with quantitative agreement in the former and broad consistency of the main trends in the latter.
tldr: This paper studies how the roughness of input data affects convergence rates in kernel recovery for integral operators, identifying a phase transition in the ill-posedness of the inverse problem.
motivation: Understanding the impact of data roughness on kernel recovery is important for applications in nonlocal continuum mechanics, operator learning, and interacting particle systems.
method: The authors quantify data roughness via spectral decay exponent and analyze the convergence rates of Tikhonov-regularized estimators in the small-noise limit.
result: They identify a phase transition: in the under-rough regime, rougher data improves recovery, while in the over-rough regime, further roughening slows rates.
conclusion: The theoretical findings are supported by numerical experiments, showing quantitative agreement in idealized settings and broad consistency in realistic configurations.

title: A Hypothesis-Testing Analysis Of Blind Recognition For Polar Codes
authors: Changwei Tu, Cheng Yang, Xianzhao Feng, Kai Niu
abstract: ArXiv:2606.17705v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Blind recognition of polar-coded transmissions is an important task in non-cooperative wireless forensics and security-oriented signal analysis. When the code length is known or has been estimated, recovering the frozen/information bit-position pattern is a key step in identifying the underlying polar-code structure and enabling subsequent information recovery from intercepted observations. In this paper, blind recognition of polar codes is investigated from a hypothesis-testing perspective under the successive cancellation (SC)-based synthetic bit-channel representation. First, under an ideal SC-consistent condition, we formulate position-wise recognition as a binary hypothesis test between frozen-position and information-position models, which provides a theoretical benchmark for analyzing their intrinsic distinguishability. Second, we show that the adopted soft recognition metric admits an exact shifted log-likelihood-ratio interpretation. This justifies ln 2 as the neutral threshold under equal priors and costs, while unequal priors or costs lead to the corresponding Bayesian threshold shift. Third, under the ideal SC-consistent model and this neutral setting, we derive upper and lower bounds on the position-wise and sequence-level recognition error probabilities with multiple independent observations. The resulting overlap coefficient is further related to the classical Bhattacharyya parameter, establishing an interpretable link between blind-recognition difficulty and polar synthetic-channel reliability. Simulation results show that the derived bounds characterize the recognition performance under the ideal SC-consistent model and capture the effects of code length, the number of intercepted observations, and SNR. Further paired comparisons in the tested settings indicate that the SC-consistent recursion provides a good sequence-level match to the realistic SC-recursive procedure.
tldr: This paper presents a hypothesis-testing framework for blind recognition of polar codes, focusing on distinguishing frozen from information bit positions.
motivation: Blind recognition of polar codes is needed for non-cooperative wireless forensics and security-oriented signal analysis when the code structure is unknown.
method: The authors formulate position-wise recognition as a binary hypothesis test under an ideal successive cancellation (SC) model, derive bounds on error probabilities, and relate the overlap coefficient to the Bhattacharyya parameter.
result: Bounds on recognition error probabilities are derived and validated via simulations, showing the effects of code length, number of observations, and SNR.
conclusion: The SC-consistent model provides a good match to realistic SC decoding for blind recognition, and the derived bounds characterize performance effectively.

title: The 2026 Algorithmic Information Theory Data Compression Challenge
authors: Andr\'e Ribeiro, R\'uben Garrido, Violeta Ramos, Ant\'onio Alberto, Diogo Fernandes, Jo\~ao Varela, Eduardo Lopes, Rodrigo Abreu, Hugo Ribeiro, Tom\'as Br\'as, David Pelicano, Afonso Ferreira, Sebasti\~ao Teixeira, Maria Linhares, Martim Santos, Rui Machado, Duarte Santos, Gabriel Silva, Guilherme Rosa, Jo\~ao Rold\~ao, Henrique Teixeira, Cl\'audia Seabra, Ricardo Fonseca, Richard Miranda, Hugo Castro, \^angela Ribeiro, Fouad Bellili, Lu\'is Diogo, Andr\'e Cardoso, Armando J. Pinho, Diogo Pratas
abstract: ArXiv:2606.17712v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Lossless data compression remains central to computer science, with direct impact on storage, communication bandwidth, computational cost, and energy consumption. It is also closely related to Algorithmic Information Theory, where compressibility provides an operational measure of structure and non-randomness. This paper presents the 2026 Algorithmic Information Theory Data Compression Challenge, a benchmark for evaluating general-purpose lossless compressors under realistic constraints. Submissions were encouraged to use arithmetic or range coding, limited to at most 8 GB of memory, and required to include a decompressor no larger than 1 MB. The benchmark comprised sixteen heterogeneous files, split into public training and hidden testing datasets. In total, 117 valid submitted compressors were evaluated alongside established reference compressors using compression ratio, compression and decompression time, Weissman score, and Pareto-frontier analysis. The results show that performance depends strongly on the optimization criterion: fast compressors achieved the best speed-oriented scores, whereas modelling-intensive compressors produced smaller outputs at higher computational cost. A Normalized Compression Distance analysis further revealed clusters of related submissions and distinguished incremental variants from more independent implementations. Selected submissions were described for their methodological novelty or competitive performance and further tested on four large external datasets, where several achieved competitive or superior results relative to established compressors. Overall, the challenge confirms the importance of probabilistic modelling, hidden testing, and external datasets for assessing compression performance and generalization. Benchmark resources, leaderboard data, binaries, and selected source code are publicly available at [URL].
tldr: A benchmark challenge for lossless data compression, evaluating compressors on ratio, speed, and memory, with ties to algorithmic information theory.
motivation: Lossless compression is crucial for storage and communication; the challenge aims to advance general-purpose compressors under realistic constraints.
method: 117 compressors were tested on 16 heterogeneous files using metrics like compression ratio, time, Weissman score, and Pareto-frontier analysis, with hidden test sets and external validation.
result: Performance varied by optimization criterion; modeling-intensive compressors achieved better ratios but slower speeds; NCD analysis revealed clusters of related submissions.
conclusion: Probabilistic modeling, hidden testing, and external datasets are important for fair compression benchmarking; the challenge provides public resources for future work.

title: A Symmetric Mechanism For Symmetry-breaking In Oscillator Networks With Strong Nonlinear Coupling
authors: Yangyang Wang Theodore Vo
abstract: ArXiv:2606.17780v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this article, we describe and analyse a novel mechanism for symmetry-breaking in minimal symmetrically coupled identical slow/fast oscillator networks with strong nonlinear mutually inhibitory coupling. We show that the symmetry-breaking, surprisingly, originates from the canard dynamics of a folded node that lies on the axis of symmetry. By applying geometric singular perturbation theory and the blow-up technique to a normal form, we determine the geometric mechanisms by which the {\em symmetric folded node} induces symmetry-breaking. More specifically, we show that (i) the fold curve of the coupled system is orthogonal to the axis of symmetry at the symmetric folded node; (ii) there is only one primary maximal canard (either strong or weak, depending on parameters), which always lies on the axis of symmetry and is the axis of rotation for the twisting of solutions; and (iii) the number of rotations is the key local diagnostic feature that breaks the symmetry. Our work is closely related to that of Kristiansen and Pedersen [SIAM J. Appl. Dyn. Syst., {\bf 22} (2023)] on symmetrically coupled FitzHugh-Nagumo oscillators with strong linear inhibitory gap junctional coupling, however, we consider nonlinear coupling and we identify and study multiple sub-types of their `cusped singularities'. We demonstrate our theoretical results by applying them to a model of the eukaryotic cell cycle in which the symmetric folded node plays a key role in rhythmogenesis. More specifically, we study periodic and quasi-periodic symmetry-breaking mixed-mode oscillatory attractors of the cell cycle model. We show that the local twisting induced by the symmetric folded node is the local mechanism that both breaks the symmetry and generates the small-amplitude oscillations in the mixed-mode dynamics.
tldr: This paper studies symmetry-breaking in oscillator networks with strong nonlinear coupling using geometric singular perturbation theory and blow-up techniques, focusing on canard dynamics and folded nodes.
motivation: Understanding symmetry-breaking mechanisms in coupled oscillator networks is important for modeling biological rhythms and other complex systems.
method: The authors apply geometric singular perturbation theory and the blow-up technique to a normal form of symmetrically coupled slow/fast oscillators with nonlinear inhibitory coupling.
result: They show that symmetry-breaking originates from a symmetric folded node on the axis of symmetry, with the number of rotations of canards serving as the key diagnostic feature.
conclusion: The mechanism is demonstrated in a eukaryotic cell cycle model, where the symmetric folded node generates periodic and quasi-periodic symmetry-breaking mixed-mode oscillations.

title: From Ergodic Theory And Probability To Fractal Geometry And Dynamics: Themes In The Work Of Manfred Denker
authors: Suzanne Boyd, Herold Dehling, Martin Schmoll, Manuel Stadlbauer, Christian Wolf
abstract: ArXiv:2606.17857v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This article surveys the mathematical contributions of Manfred Denker, with a focus on themes that connect ergodic theory, probability theory, dynamical systems, fractal geometry, and statistics. Denker's highly influential work includes a systematic study of the statistical properties of dynamical systems, the development of limit theorems for dependent processes, and the use of thermodynamic formalism to relate geometric and measure-theoretic properties. Particular emphasis is placed on the emergence of probabilistic behavior in deterministic systems, including central limit theorems, invariance principles or local limit theorems, under weak dependence assumptions or in infinite measure. Further topics include equilibrium states and transfer operator methods, the role of conformal measures in fractal geometry, and the asymptotic theory of statistical procedures for dependent data, such as rank statistics and U-statistics. In addition to these theoretical developments, the survey highlights contributions connecting rigorous analysis with computational and statistical methods. Taken together, these works illustrate a unifying perspective in which ergodic, probabilistic, geometric, and statistical methods interact in the study of dynamical systems.
tldr: A survey of Manfred Denker's contributions to ergodic theory, probability, dynamical systems, and fractal geometry, with no direct connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: To review the mathematical work of Manfred Denker, highlighting themes that connect ergodic theory, probability, dynamical systems, and fractal geometry.
method: Survey of Denker's research, covering statistical properties of dynamical systems, limit theorems, thermodynamic formalism, equilibrium states, transfer operators, and conformal measures.
result: The survey illustrates a unifying perspective where ergodic, probabilistic, geometric, and statistical methods interact in dynamical systems.
conclusion: Denker's work is foundational in mathematics but does not address quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Auto-correlation Function Keying
authors: Weijiang Zhao, Yifeng Xiong, Fan Liu, Shuangyang Li, Jianhua Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.17970v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Communication-centric ISAC is a promising paradigm for future 6G networks, in which data payload signals are expected to be reused for sensing to enhance time-frequency resource efficiency. For random payload signals, existing studies have mainly characterized the expected sidelobe level (ESL) of the periodic auto-correlation function (P-ACF). However, ESL only captures the average sidelobe behavior and does not control large spurious sidelobe peaks in individual payload realizations, which may deteriorate weak-target detection performance. This motivates the design of information-bearing signals whose random P-ACF satisfies stringent peak sidelobe level (PSL) constraints. In this paper, we formulate a mutual information maximization problem under PSL constraints and a power budget. For quasi-static frequency-flat channels, we show that a continuous auto-correlation function (ACF)-domain uniform construction provides an asymptotically optimal high-SNR design principle. Motivated by this principle, we propose auto-correlation function keying (ACFK), a finite-constellation modulation architecture that embeds data symbols directly onto the ACF-domain sidelobes. ACFK enables exact control of the nominal P-ACF, which coincides with the actual P-ACF when a spectral non-negativity constraint is met. When this is not the case, we quantify the non-negativity violation probability and bound the resulting peak sidelobe level ratio (PSLR) degradation. We further provide a reference ISAC transceiver design for ACFK over quasi-static multipath channels, together with high-SNR approximate BER analysis. Numerical results validate the theoretical analysis and show that, compared with a generalized probabilistic amplitude shaping (PAS) baseline, ACFK provides substantially stronger PSLR control and improved weak-target detection performance under comparable sensing and communication settings.
tldr: This paper proposes a modulation scheme for integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) that embeds data into the auto-correlation function sidelobes to control peak sidelobe level.
motivation: Random payload signals in ISAC can cause large spurious sidelobe peaks that degrade weak-target detection; existing average-based metrics do not control worst-case behavior.
method: The authors formulate a mutual information maximization problem under peak sidelobe level constraints, derive an asymptotically optimal design principle, and propose auto-correlation function keying (ACFK) as a finite-constellation modulation that directly controls the nominal periodic auto-correlation function.
result: ACFK provides exact control of the nominal P-ACF when a spectral non-negativity constraint is met; otherwise, the violation probability and PSLR degradation are quantified. Numerical results show stronger PSLR control and improved weak-target detection compared to probabilistic amplitude shaping.
conclusion: ACFK is an effective modulation for ISAC that balances communication and sensing performance by embedding data in the ACF domain.

tldr: This paper studies the Sommerfeld coefficient enhancement and magnetic short-range order in a hyperkagome 3d electron system, focusing on material-specific properties.
motivation: To understand the origin of the large Sommerfeld coefficient in Mn-based hyperkagome systems, which is attributed to fluctuating magnetic moments but lacks systematic study.
method: Experimental measurements including specific heat, magnetic susceptibility, and neutron scattering on hyperkagome materials.
result: Observation of enhanced Sommerfeld coefficient and evidence of magnetic short-range order.
conclusion: The large Sommerfeld coefficient is linked to magnetic fluctuations and short-range order, providing insight into correlated electron systems.

title: Low-energy Excitations In $A$-site Ordered ${\mathrm{SmBaMn}}_{2}{\mathrm{O}}_{6}$
authors: Mirian Garcia Fernandez, Abhishek Nag, Stefano Agrestini, Sahil Tippireddy, Dirk Backes, Xiaoyang Chen, Urs Staub, Taka-Hisa Arima, And Kejin Zhou

tldr: This paper studies low-energy excitations in A-site ordered SmBaMn2O6, focusing on spin, charge, and orbital degrees of freedom in a condensed matter system.

method: Resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS) at the Mn L-edge and O K-edge, combined with theoretical modeling.
result: Observation of dispersive spin excitations (magnons) and orbital excitations (orbitons), with evidence of coupling between them.
conclusion: The material exhibits rich low-energy physics with coupled spin-orbital excitations, relevant for understanding multiferroic and strongly correlated systems.

title: Pressure-induced $b1$ To $b2$ Phase Transition In CeN Studied By $ab Initio$ Correlation Matrix Renormalization Theory Calculations
authors: Jun Liu, Jianhua Zhang, Yongxin Yao, Kai-Ming Ho, And Cai-Zhuang Wang

motivation: To understand the structural and electronic properties of CeN under pressure, particularly the b1 to b2 phase transition.
method: Ab initio correlation matrix renormalization theory (CMRT) calculations.
result: CMRT reproduces the ambient pressure equation of state and predicts the phase transition pressure and electronic density of states.
conclusion: CMRT is effective for studying correlated materials like CeN under pressure, providing insights into its phase transition.

title: Tuning Terahertz Optomechanics Of ${\mathrm{MoS}}_{2}$ Bilayers With Homogeneous In-plane Strain
authors: S. Patel, Jose D. Mella, S. Puri, Salvador Barraza-Lopez, And H. Nakamura

result: Biaxial tensile strain contracts the interlayer van der Waals gap, hardening the breathing modes and leading to a large Grüneisen parameter.
conclusion: Strain engineering can tune THz optomechanics in MoS2 bilayers, enabling nonlinear mechanical control.

tldr: This paper uses polarized Raman spectroscopy to study atomic displacements in TbMnO3, a multiferroic material, but does not connect to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: The microscopic origin of ferroelectricity in type-II multiferroics like TbMnO3 is unresolved; understanding this could advance condensed matter physics.
method: Polarized Raman spectroscopy is used to isolate individual Raman tensors and detect femtometer-scale atomic displacements.
result: Direct evidence of anionic displacement driving multiferroicity is provided.
conclusion: The study resolves the microscopic mechanism of multiferroicity in TbMnO3.

title: Hall Anomaly In The Mixed State Of type-II Superconductors: Evidence For Vacancies Within Vortex Lattice Domains
authors: Ruonan Guo, Yong-Cong Chen, Da Jiang, And Ping Ao

Despite numerous recent studies on the Hall anomaly following the discovery of cuprate superconductivity, its origin remains contentious. We demonstrate—without invoking adjustable parameters—that a previously proposed mechanism, in which vacancies form within vortex lattice domains, provides a comp…


[Phys. Rev. B 113, 214513] Published Fri Jun 12, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes a vacancy mechanism within vortex lattice domains to explain the Hall anomaly in type-II superconductors, without invoking adjustable parameters.
motivation: The Hall anomaly in mixed-state type-II superconductors, especially cuprates, remains controversial; the authors aim to validate a previously proposed mechanism.
method: The authors demonstrate through calculations that vacancies forming within vortex lattice domains can account for the Hall anomaly, using no adjustable parameters.
result: The vacancy mechanism provides a consistent explanation for the Hall anomaly in the mixed state.
conclusion: The study supports the vacancy model as a viable explanation for the Hall anomaly, contributing to the understanding of vortex dynamics in superconductors.

title: Revisiting The Symmetry And Optical Phonons Of Altermagnetic $α$-MnTe
authors: Ece Uykur, Marcos V. Gonçalves-Faria, Sahana Rößler, Victoria A. Ginga, Marcus Schmidt, Stephan Winnerl, Manfred Helm, And Alexander A. Tsirlin

We show that mechanical stress applied to crystals of this material causes a drastic broadening of Bragg peaks that conceals signatures of addi…


[Phys. Rev. B 113, 224107] Published Fri Jun 12, 2026.
tldr: This paper investigates the symmetry and optical phonons of altermagnetic α-MnTe using infrared and Raman spectroscopies and high-resolution x-ray diffraction.
motivation: To resolve controversies regarding the crystal structure and phonon modes of α-MnTe, which is an altermagnetic material.
method: Combined infrared and Raman spectroscopies with high-resolution x-ray diffraction, including analysis of mechanical stress effects on Bragg peaks.
result: Mechanical stress broadens Bragg peaks, obscuring additional structural signatures; the study clarifies the symmetry and phonon behavior.
conclusion: The findings resolve ambiguities in the structural and vibrational properties of α-MnTe, contributing to the understanding of altermagnetic materials.

By identifying the poles and residues of the Laplace tra…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 064133] Published Tue Jun 16, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies the asymptotic decay of spatial correlations in one-dimensional hard-rod fluids using Laplace transform pole analysis.
motivation: Understanding the decay of correlations in confined hard-core fluids is important for statistical mechanics of classical fluids.
method: The authors use Laplace transform techniques and pole analysis to derive the asymptotic behavior of the radial distribution function at high packing fractions.
result: They show that spatial correlations decay algebraically in strictly 1D systems and exponentially in quasi-1D confined geometries.
conclusion: The work provides a theoretical framework for correlation decay in hard-core fluids, but has no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Resource And Population Dynamics In An Agent-environment Interaction Model
authors: Gaston Briozzo, Gustavo J. Sibona, And Fernando Peruani
abstract:

In any ecosystem, the conditions of the environment and the characteristics of the species that inhabit it are entangled, coevolving in space and time. We introduce a model that couples active agents with a dynamic environment, interpreted as a nutrient source. Agents are persistent random walkers t…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 064406] Published Mon Jun 15, 2026.
tldr: This paper models the coevolution of active agents and a dynamic nutrient environment, focusing on population dynamics and resource consumption.
motivation: To understand how species characteristics and environmental conditions coevolve in ecosystems, using a minimal model of active agents and a diffusing resource.
method: The authors introduce a model where agents perform persistent random walks and consume a diffusing nutrient field, with the environment evolving via diffusion and regeneration.
result: The model exhibits complex spatiotemporal patterns and population dynamics, including extinction, coexistence, and oscillations depending on agent density and resource regeneration rate.
conclusion: The coupling between agent behavior and environment dynamics is crucial for ecosystem stability, and the model provides a framework for studying such coevolution.

title: Chromatic Percolation In Two-dimensional Multitype Particle Systems With Extended-range Homotypic Repulsion
authors: Tingting Yin, Yan Sui, Xueying Yuan, And Xian Kong

Cells in many tissues repel like neighbors over extended ranges, yet standard jamming models ignore this diversity. [Phys. Rev. E 113, 065412] Published Fri Jun 12, 2026.
tldr: This paper introduces chromatic percolation in multitype particle systems with extended-range homotypic repulsion, linking percolation to mechanical jamming.
motivation: Standard jamming models ignore diversity in cell repulsion ranges; the authors aim to understand how homotypic repulsion drives percolation and jamming in multitype assemblies.
method: They define chromatic percolation as percolation of like-type particles under extended-range homotypic repulsion and map it to mechanical jamming using computational models.
result: The study reveals a relationship between chromatic percolation and jamming transitions in two-dimensional multitype systems.
conclusion: Chromatic percolation provides a framework to connect percolation theory with jamming in biological tissues and soft matter.

title: Supratransmission In Lattices With Purely Nonlinear Coupling
authors: Defri Ahmad, Tae-Yeon Kim, Andreas Schiffer, Jinkyu Yang, And Hadi Susanto

tldr: This paper studies supratransmission in nonlinear lattices with purely nonlinear coupling, where energy propagation occurs without a linear passband.
motivation: To extend the phenomenon of supratransmission to systems lacking linear spectrum, which is relevant for understanding energy transport in nonlinear media.
method: The authors analyze a lattice model with purely nonlinear coupling using analytical and numerical methods to study energy transmission thresholds.
result: They find that supratransmission can occur even without linear modes, with energy propagation driven by nonlinearity alone.
conclusion: The work demonstrates a new regime of supratransmission in purely nonlinear lattices, broadening the scope of nonlinear wave phenomena.

Discrete Ricci curvature serves as a fundamental geometric tool for quantifying the structural characteristics of complex networks, effectively capturing the richness of their connection patterns. Building on this theoretical framework, this paper proposes an improved discrete Ricci curvature algori…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 064304] Published Tue Jun 09, 2026.
tldr: This paper applies discrete Ricci flow and information entropy optimization to community detection in complex networks.
motivation: Community detection is important for understanding network structure, and discrete Ricci curvature provides a geometric tool to capture connection patterns.
method: The authors propose an improved discrete Ricci curvature algorithm and combine it with normalized Ricci flow and information entropy optimization to detect communities.
result: The method effectively identifies community structures in complex networks, as demonstrated on benchmark datasets.
conclusion: The proposed approach offers a novel geometric perspective for community detection, but it is not directly related to quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

authors: Hugo Le Roy And Paolo de Los Rios

[Phys. Rev. E 113, 064405] Published Tue Jun 09, 2026.
tldr: This paper models biomolecular condensates as sticker-spacer networks and shows that entropic clustering of stickers leads to aging behavior.
motivation: Biomolecular condensates exhibit viscoelasticity and aging, which are not fully understood from a physical perspective.
method: The authors develop a theoretical model based on stickers and spacers, using statistical mechanics to study the network structure and dynamics.
result: Entropic effects cause stickers to cluster over time, leading to an aging response in the condensate's mechanical properties.
conclusion: The aging of biocondensates can be explained by entropic clustering without invoking specific biochemical interactions.

motivation: Understanding dissipation in polymer chains is important for soft matter physics and biophysics, but the work does not connect to quantum information or thermodynamics.
method: The authors simulate a sequence of spring-dashpots tethered at one end and pulled by a harmonic trap using linear and symmetric protocols, computing the work dissipated.
result: The variation of dissipation with chain length and pulling protocol is characterized numerically.
conclusion: The study provides insights into dissipative response in classical polymer models, but has no relevance to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

motivation: Understanding the role of higher-order interactions in contagion dynamics from the perspective of critical phenomena.
method: The authors develop a mesoscopic model for higher-order contagion and analyze it using renormalization group techniques near the upper critical dimension.
result: They find that higher-order interactions modify the critical exponents and scaling behavior compared to standard contagion models.
conclusion: Higher-order interactions lead to new universality classes in contagion processes, with implications for modeling complex social and biological systems.

title: Current-induced Successive Structural Phase Transitions Beyond Thermal Equilibrium In Single-crystal ${\mathrm{VO}}_{2}$

conclusion: Current can induce structural phase transitions beyond thermal equilibrium, offering a pathway to access hidden phases in correlated materials.

method: They included correlated atom vibrations in HR-TEM image simulations to model the effect of phonon edge modes.
result: The simulations account for the observed enhanced vibrations, confirming the presence of localized phonon edge states.
conclusion: Phonon edge modes are responsible for the enhanced atomic vibrations seen at edges of MoS2 in HR-TEM.

method: The authors analyze recurrent neural networks with asymmetric interactions, incorporating self-couplings or sparse excitatory intermodule connections, and study the resulting manifold of stable configurations.
result: They demonstrate that such networks can develop a densely connected manifold of dynamically accessible stable configurations, enabling learning.
conclusion: Asymmetric recurrent neural networks with appropriate couplings can support rich dynamical learning, with implications for neural computation.

motivation: Understanding the complex dynamics of liquid water, especially in deeply supercooled regimes, is important for fundamental physics and applications.
method: Classical molecular dynamics simulations of TIP4P water across a wide temperature range.
result: Characterization of dielectric relaxation and nonlinear shear rheology responses.
conclusion: The study provides insights into water's dynamic properties but does not connect to quantum information or thermodynamics.

authors: Xiangyu Luo, Ludovica Zullo, Sahaj Patel, Dongjin Oh, Willa Mihalyi-Koch, Emma Lian, Jiaruo Li, Qian Song, Asish K. Kundu, Anil Rajapitamahuni, Elio Vescovo, Natalia Olszowska, Rafał Kurleto, Dawid Wutke, Xavier Roy, Giorgio Sangiovanni, And Riccardo Comin

Angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy of layered transition-metal oxyhalides reveals intrinsic flat bands that remain stable at room temperature, providing a tunable platform for investigating strongly correlated electron states.

method: The authors synthesize layered transition-metal oxyhalides and use angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) to measure the electronic band structure, revealing flat bands that are robust against temperature.
result: They observe intrinsic flat bands that remain stable up to room temperature, with orbital selectivity and tunability via material composition.
conclusion: These materials provide a promising platform for studying strongly correlated electron physics and potentially for applications in quantum simulation or devices, though no direct connection to quantum information or thermodynamics is made.

authors: Beini Gao, Mahdi Ghafariasl, Mahmoud Jalali Mehrabad, Tsung-Sheng Huang, Lifu Zhang, Deric Session, Pranshoo Upadhyay, Rundong Ma, Ghadah Alshalan, Daniel Suarez, Supratik Sarkar, Suji Park, Houk Jang, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Ming Xie, You Zhou, And Mohammad Hafezi

Magneto-optical spectroscopy of twisted WSe

motivation: To investigate the quantum anomalous Hall phase in twisted bilayer WSe2 and understand the interplay between topology and magnetism in moiré materials.
method: Magneto-optical spectroscopy, specifically attractive polaron spectroscopy, is used to probe the electronic structure and magnetic ordering of twisted bilayer WSe2 under applied electric fields.
result: The study reveals a spontaneous quantum anomalous Hall phase and demonstrates electric-field control over transitions between ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic orders.
conclusion: Twisted bilayer WSe2 is a promising platform for exploring topological phases and magnetic order, with potential for future quantum devices.

title: Elastic And Structural Anisotropy In Silica Thin Films For Gravitational-Wave Detectors
authors: Brenda Bracco, Michele Magnozzi, Stefano Colace, Maurizio Canepa, Giulio Favaro, Marco Bazzan, Massimo Granata, David Hofman, Alessandro Di Michele, Laura Silenzi, Gianpietro Cagnoli, Giovanni Carlotti, Paola Sassi, And Silvia Corezzi

method: The authors characterize the elastic and structural properties of silica thin films using experimental techniques to detect hidden anisotropy and test the effects of heat treatment.
result: They find that silica films exhibit hidden anisotropy that resists standard heat treatment, which has implications for coating design and postprocessing.
conclusion: The discovery informs strategies for coating deposition and postprocessing to reduce thermal noise in gravitational-wave detectors.
