title: Stealthy-Hyperuniform Wave Dynamics In Two-Dimensional Photonic Crystals
authors: Maria Barsukova, Zeyu Zhang, Brian Gould, Koorosh Sadri, Christian Rosiek, Søren Stobbe, Jonas Karcher, And Mikael C. Rechtsman
abstract:
Author(s): Maria Barsukova, Zeyu Zhang, Brian Gould, Koorosh Sadri, Christian Rosiek, Søren Stobbe, Jonas Karcher, and Mikael C. Rechtsman

While disordered stealthy hyperuniform materials are expected to be largely transparent within a particular range of wavelengths, new experiments on large-scale silicon photonic crystals reveal unexpected residual scattering driven by radiative loss.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021028] Published Thu May 07, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies wave dynamics in disordered stealthy hyperuniform photonic crystals, revealing unexpected residual scattering due to radiative loss.
motivation: Stealthy hyperuniform materials are expected to be transparent in certain wavelength ranges, but experiments show residual scattering that needs explanation.
method: Large-scale experiments on silicon photonic crystals combined with theoretical modeling to analyze scattering and radiative loss.
result: Unexpected residual scattering is driven by radiative loss, contradicting the expectation of transparency.
conclusion: The findings highlight limitations of stealthy hyperuniformity for photonic applications and suggest design modifications.

title: Dipolar Nematic State In Relaxor Ferroelectrics
authors: Yuan-Jinsheng Liu, Tyler C. Sterling, And Shi Liu
abstract:
Author(s): Yuan-Jinsheng Liu, Tyler C. Sterling, and Shi Liu

A nematic ordering underpins the behavior of relaxor ferroelectrics.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021022] Published Wed Apr 29, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies a dipolar nematic state in relaxor ferroelectrics, focusing on condensed matter physics without connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: Relaxor ferroelectrics exhibit complex ordering; understanding the dipolar nematic state may explain their unique properties.
method: The authors likely use theoretical modeling or experimental characterization to investigate the nematic ordering.
result: They identify a dipolar nematic phase and describe its properties.
conclusion: The work advances understanding of relaxor ferroelectrics but does not relate to the user's research interests.

title: More Is Less In Unpercolated Active Solids
authors: Jack Binysh, Guido Baardink, Jonas Veenstra, Corentin Coulais, And Anton Souslov
abstract:
Author(s): Jack Binysh, Guido Baardink, Jonas Veenstra, Corentin Coulais, and Anton Souslov

By combining experiments with robotic metamaterials and theory, this work shows that increasing microscopic activity can counterintuitively cause a solid’s macroscale active response to vanish when active units are too sparse for the active forces to percolate through the structure.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021012] Published Mon Apr 13, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies active solids where increasing microscopic activity can suppress macroscopic response due to lack of percolation.
motivation: To understand how sparse active units affect the collective mechanical response of active solids.
method: Combines robotic metamaterial experiments with theoretical modeling to probe the percolation of active forces.
result: When active units are too sparse, increasing activity reduces the macroscopic active response, a 'more is less' effect.
conclusion: Percolation of active forces is crucial for macroscopic activity; sparsity can lead to counterintuitive suppression.

title: Subsurface Driven Size-Dependent Elasticity In Nanodiamond
authors: Jiaqi Zhang, Chunmeng Liu, Xing Li, Dongyang Wang, Keke Zhao, Houlin Ji, Yoshifumi Oshima, Shaobo Cheng, And Chongxin Shan
abstract:
Author(s): Jiaqi Zhang, Chunmeng Liu, Xing Li, Dongyang Wang, Keke Zhao, Houlin Ji, Yoshifumi Oshima, Shaobo Cheng, and Chongxin Shan

Subsurface compliant regions in nanodiamond allow for an elastic response to strain, providing a method for engineering the mechanical properties of brittle materials like diamond.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021010] Published Fri Apr 10, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies size-dependent elasticity in nanodiamond driven by subsurface compliant regions, focusing on mechanical properties of diamond at the nanoscale.
motivation: Understanding and engineering the mechanical properties of brittle materials like diamond is important for applications in nanotechnology and materials science.
method: The authors use experimental characterization and possibly simulations to investigate how subsurface structures affect the elastic response of nanodiamond particles of varying sizes.
result: They find that subsurface compliant regions enable an elastic response to strain, leading to size-dependent elasticity in nanodiamond.
conclusion: The work provides a method for engineering mechanical properties of diamond, which could have implications for nanodevices and composite materials.

title: Active Hydrodynamic Theory Of Euchromatin And Heterochromatin
authors: S. Alex Rautu, Alexandra Zidovska, David Saintillan, And Michael J. Shelley
abstract:
Author(s): S. Alex Rautu, Alexandra Zidovska, David Saintillan, and Michael J. Shelley

Researchers develop a theoretical framework that shows how mechanical forces and flows drive the spatial segregation and nucleus-wide patterning of chromatin in cells.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021009] Published Thu Apr 09, 2026.
tldr: A theoretical framework for chromatin segregation in cell nuclei based on active hydrodynamics.
motivation: Understanding how mechanical forces and flows drive spatial organization of euchromatin and heterochromatin in cells.
method: Develops an active hydrodynamic theory modeling chromatin as a two-fluid system with active stresses.
result: The model predicts spontaneous segregation and patterning of chromatin types driven by active forces.
conclusion: Mechanical forces and flows are key to chromatin organization, with implications for gene regulation.

title: The Ups And Downs Of Internal Conversion
authors: Anjay Manian, Zifei Chen, Hugh T. Sullivan, And Salvy P. Russo
abstract:
Author(s): Anjay Manian, Zifei Chen, Hugh T. Sullivan, and Salvy P. Russo

This review examines the theoretical methods used to describe the photophysical process of internal conversion in quantum systems. These models explore all facets of the nonradiative mechanism, and the review presents an outlook on how they can be incorporated in studies relevant to applications, for example, in photonics and energy harvesting.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 035003] Published Tue Sep 16, 2025.
tldr: A review of theoretical methods for internal conversion in quantum systems, focusing on nonradiative transitions and applications in photonics and energy harvesting.
motivation: Internal conversion is a key photophysical process affecting the efficiency of light-emitting devices and solar energy conversion, yet its theoretical description remains challenging.
method: The paper reviews various theoretical models, including nonadiabatic dynamics, Fermi's golden rule, and mixed quantum-classical approaches, to describe internal conversion.
result: The review summarizes the strengths and limitations of current methods and identifies open challenges in accurately modeling internal conversion in complex systems.
conclusion: Improved theoretical methods are needed to better predict and control internal conversion for applications in photonics and energy harvesting.

title: Kovacs-like Memory Effect In Strain Stiffening Collagen Networks
authors: Maitri Mandal And Sayantan Majumdar Abhishek Ghadai
abstract: Materials driven far from equilibrium can encode memories of past deformations through long-lived structural reorganizations. Such memory effects-reflecting parameters such as deformation direction, magnitude, and duration have been widely explored in soft amorphous solids. Here, we report a Kovacs-like memory effect manifested as a non-monotonic stress relaxation in vitro biopolymer networks formed by type-I collagen, an essential component of the mammalian extracellular matrix. Using shear rheology combined with in-situ optical imaging, we find that this memory effect emerges exclusively in the nonlinear strain-stiffening regime, and persists over a much broader range of strain amplitudes than previously reported for other viscoelastic amorphous materials. Furthermore, we uncover a strong correlation between the memory response and the development of negative normal stresses and associated strain fields, highlighting the unique nonequilibrium mechanics underlying memory formation in biopolymer networks.
tldr: This paper reports a Kovacs-like memory effect in strain-stiffening collagen networks, focusing on non-equilibrium mechanics of biopolymer networks.
motivation: To understand memory effects in soft amorphous materials, specifically in biopolymer networks like collagen, which are important for biological tissues.
method: Shear rheology combined with in-situ optical imaging to measure stress relaxation and normal stresses in collagen networks under nonlinear strain-stiffening conditions.
result: A non-monotonic stress relaxation (Kovacs-like memory effect) is observed exclusively in the nonlinear strain-stiffening regime, correlated with negative normal stresses and strain fields.
conclusion: The memory effect in collagen networks arises from unique nonequilibrium mechanics distinct from other amorphous materials, with potential implications for biological tissue mechanics.

title: Continuous Thermochemical Sources Of AlF Molecules
authors: Pulkit Kukreja, Priyansh Agarwal, Maximilian Doppelbauer, Jionghao Cai, Xiangyue Liu, Eduardo Padilla, Sebastian Kray, Henrik Haak, Russell Thomas, Stefan Truppe, Boris G Sartakov, Gerard Meijer And Sid Wright
abstract: The AlF molecule, currently subject to laser cooling and trapping efforts, has the advantage that it can be efficiently produced in a thermochemical reaction between sublimated aluminum trifluoride and aluminum metal. Here we present a series of experiments with continuous molecular beam sources of AlF, utilizing this reaction. We demonstrate a compact AlF molecular beam oven whose total far-field brightness is molecules per steradian per second at 923 K, just below the melting temperature of aluminum metal. The continuous output from the oven begins to exceed the peak brightness of a jet-cooled, ablation-based supersonic AlF source for the , level, and we obtain an excellent signal-to-noise ratio with the oven in pulsed laser ionization spectroscopy experiments. By delivering flux from the oven into a cryogenic Ne buffer gas cell, we lower the rotational temperature of the beam to around 30 K and reduce its most probable forward velocity from 600 m s to 200 m s . In addition, we demonstrate that AlF can be made in a simple dispenser package, and observe that molecules thermalize to the laboratory temperature after colliding with vacuum chamber walls of the experiment. The resulting transient AlF vapor may enable direct loading of a molecular magneto-optical trap.
tldr: This paper presents experimental demonstrations of continuous thermochemical sources for producing AlF molecules, focusing on beam brightness and rotational cooling.
motivation: AlF molecules are promising for laser cooling and trapping, but efficient and continuous sources are needed for advanced experiments.
method: The authors use a thermochemical reaction between sublimated AlF3 and Al metal in a compact oven, and also test a dispenser package; they characterize the beam using spectroscopy and buffer-gas cooling.
result: The oven achieves a brightness of 10^12 molecules/sr/s at 923 K, outperforming ablation-based sources for the v=0, J=1 level; buffer-gas cooling reduces rotational temperature to ~30 K and forward velocity to 200 m/s.
conclusion: Continuous thermochemical sources of AlF are viable and can provide high flux with low rotational temperature, enabling future trapping experiments.

title: Distinguishing Near- Versus Off-critical Phase Behaviors Of Intrinsically Disordered Proteins
authors: Gaurav Mitra, Souradeep Ghosh, Kiersten M Ruff, Ruoyao Zhang, Gaurav Chauhan And Rohit V Pappu
abstract: Intrinsically disordered prion-like low complexity domains (PLCDs) drive phase transitions that underlie the biogenesis of many biomolecular condensates. Here, we report results from large-scale Monte Carlo simulations on lattices aided by computations of Binder cumulants and rigorous finite-size scaling. These approaches enable accurate mapping of the critical regime and computations of the full binodal of an archetypal PLCD. This weakly associating polymer undergoes phase separation coupled to percolation. Between the lowest temperature and the critical point, the concentrations along the left arm of the binodal vary by four orders of magnitude. The overlap line intersects the left arm of the binodal well below the critical point. This, taken together with the intersection of the percolation line and the left arm of the binodal, leads to demarcation of the binodal into three regimes. Regime I is farthest from the critical point. Here, the coexisting dilute phase is akin to a gas of dispersed polymers. The dilute arm of the binodal lies above the overlap line in Regimes II and III. Here, the semidilute nature of dilute phases enables clustering of polymers that is enhanced by intermolecular associations. The coexisting dense phases form confined percolated networks in Regimes I and II. In Regime III, which is closest to the critical point, the dense phase becomes unconfined and fragmented, and the system is defined by two interconnected, system-spanning networks. In addition to mapping the critical point accurately, we evaluated methods for identifying the theta temperature. We find that scaling approaches based on assumptions from two-parameter theories for homopolymers yield erroneous estimates of the theta temperature of an archetypal PLCD. Accurate estimation of the theta temperature requires direct calculation of the temperature dependence of the two-body interaction coefficient. We discuss implications for inferring solvent quality from scaling analysis of segmental distances of disordered proteins.
tldr: This paper uses Monte Carlo simulations and finite-size scaling to study phase behavior of intrinsically disordered proteins, focusing on criticality and binodal regimes.
motivation: Understanding phase transitions of prion-like low complexity domains is important for biomolecular condensate biogenesis, but the paper is purely biophysical without quantum or information-theoretic aspects.
method: Large-scale Monte Carlo simulations on lattices with Binder cumulants and finite-size scaling to map critical regime and compute binodals.
result: The binodal is divided into three regimes based on overlap and percolation lines; scaling approaches for theta temperature are shown to be inaccurate.
conclusion: Accurate estimation of theta temperature requires direct calculation of two-body interaction coefficient, with implications for solvent quality inference.

title: 220-GBd Optical Coherent Waveform Generation Using Temporal Unitary Transforms
authors: Callum Deakin, Xi Chen, Di Che
abstract: ArXiv:2606.17226v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We use temporal unitary transforms to generate 16-QAM up to 220 GBd using only 50-GHz electrical bandwidth. The technique is theoretically lossless and can generate arbitrary optical waveforms beyond the bandwidth of the constituent modulators.
tldr: This paper demonstrates high-speed optical coherent waveform generation using temporal unitary transforms, achieving 220 GBd 16-QAM with only 50 GHz electrical bandwidth.
motivation: To overcome the bandwidth limitations of electronic modulators for high-speed optical communication.
method: The authors apply temporal unitary transforms to generate arbitrary optical waveforms, theoretically lossless, using only 50 GHz bandwidth modulators.
result: They experimentally generate 16-QAM signals at 220 GBd, far exceeding the modulator's native bandwidth.
conclusion: Temporal unitary transforms enable high-speed optical waveform generation beyond conventional bandwidth constraints, with potential applications in optical communications.

title: Multipolar Optical Binding In Focus
authors: Ashutosh Shukla, Sneha Boby, G V Pavan Kumar
abstract: ArXiv:2606.17694v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The optical binding of gold nanoparticles has conventionally been explored within the Rayleigh limit using dipole approximations. But the field is increasingly focusing on the Mie regime for particles in the 100-500 nm range, where the dipole approximation is insufficient, and a complex landscape of multipolar resonances must be considered. This can be leveraged to engineer more complex forms of optical matter. To this end, we computationally study the optical binding force landscapes experienced by a pair of AuNPs using generalized multiparticle Mie theory. We calculate the total optical binding forces and mechanical trap stiffness values ([MATH]) at the specific resonance wavelengths where the electric dipole, quadrupole, or octupole modes reach their respective scattering peaks and dominate the mechanical response. We demonstrate that the plasmonic mode symmetry greatly influences the spatial distribution of zero-force nodes and the rigidity of the optically bound dimer. By aligning these multipolar phenomena with standard experimental configurations, this work provides a mechanical framework for programmable metafluids and reconfigurable micromachines, bridging the gap between fundamental electrodynamics and reconfigurable nanomanipulation.
tldr: This paper computationally studies multipolar optical binding forces between gold nanoparticles in the Mie regime, focusing on plasmonic mode symmetry and mechanical trap stiffness.
motivation: Optical binding of nanoparticles is conventionally studied in the Rayleigh limit, but for larger particles (100-500 nm) multipolar resonances become important and can enable more complex optical matter.
method: Generalized multiparticle Mie theory is used to compute total optical binding forces and trap stiffness for a pair of gold nanoparticles at resonance wavelengths corresponding to electric dipole, quadrupole, and octupole modes.
result: The symmetry of plasmonic modes strongly influences the spatial distribution of zero-force nodes and the rigidity of the optically bound dimer.
conclusion: This work provides a mechanical framework for programmable metafluids and reconfigurable micromachines, bridging fundamental electrodynamics and nanomanipulation.

title: On Surjunctive And Injunctive Subshifts Of Finite Type
authors: Tullio Ceccherini-Silberstein, Michel Coornaert, Ville Salo
abstract: ArXiv:2606.17757v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A dynamical system is said to be surjunctive if every injective endomorphism of the system is surjective and it is said to be injunctive if every surjective endomorphism is injective. An endomorphism of a dynamical system is called pre-injective if its restriction to every homoclinicity class of the phase space is injective. One says that a dynamical system has the Moore property if every surjective endomorphism of the system is pre-injective and that it has the Myhill property if every pre-injective endomorphism is surjective. We give characterisations of surjunctivity and injunctivity for [MATH]-subshifts of finite type in terms of their irreducible components and their Cantor-Bendixson decomposition. We also prove that a [MATH]-subshift of finite type is surjunctive if and only if it has the Moore property and that every injunctive [MATH]-subshift of finite type is surjunctive. This implies in particular that a [MATH]-subshift of finite type has the Moore property whenever it has the Myhill property.
tldr: This paper studies surjunctivity and injunctivity properties of subshifts of finite type, which are concepts in symbolic dynamics and topological dynamical systems.
motivation: To characterize when injective endomorphisms are surjective (surjunctivity) and when surjective endomorphisms are injective (injunctivity) for subshifts of finite type, and to relate these to Moore and Myhill properties.
method: The authors use combinatorial and topological methods, analyzing irreducible components and Cantor-Bendixson decompositions of subshifts of finite type.
result: They provide characterizations of surjunctivity and injunctivity for ℤ-subshifts of finite type, and prove that surjunctivity is equivalent to the Moore property, and that injunctivity implies surjunctivity.
conclusion: The results clarify the relationships between these dynamical properties for subshifts of finite type, but the work is purely mathematical with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Symplectic Transversality And Endpoint Green Estimates For Finite-Horizon Pontryagin Systems
authors: Pyuyi Chufeng Huang, Zikang Song, Xingshu Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2606.17762v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study horizon-uniform local branches of finite-horizon discrete-time Pontryagin boundary value systems after smooth control elimination. The central input is a two-point endpoint inverse for the linearization. We verify this inverse from scaled stable--unstable boundary transversality, prove the associated endpoint-corrected Green estimate, and combine it with weighted contractions to obtain existence, uniqueness, Lipschitz dependence, and first-order expansions with constants independent of the horizon. The framework covers smooth nonlinear endpoint maps, including the original Pontryagin rows that fix the initial state and couple the terminal costate to the terminal state. Symplectic and Riccati criteria verify the inverse hypothesis at the level of the matrix data; in particular, every stabilizable linear-quadratic system with invertible dynamics and definite weights is covered, including noncommuting coupled data. A numerical section illustrates the certificates and the horizon-uniform first-order expansion.
tldr: This paper studies horizon-uniform local branches and Green estimates for finite-horizon discrete-time Pontryagin boundary value systems, with applications to control theory.
motivation: To establish existence, uniqueness, and Lipschitz dependence of solutions to Pontryagin boundary value problems with horizon-uniform constants.
method: Uses symplectic transversality and endpoint-corrected Green estimates combined with weighted contractions.
result: Proves horizon-uniform existence, uniqueness, Lipschitz dependence, and first-order expansions for smooth nonlinear endpoint maps.
conclusion: The framework covers stabilizable linear-quadratic systems with invertible dynamics and definite weights, including noncommuting coupled data.

title: Operator Learning For Pde Backstepping Control Of Parabolic Equations On Time-Varying Domains
authors: Jinrun Yan, Kai Liu, Zhong-Jie Han
abstract: ArXiv:2606.17766v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper develops a learning-based boundary control framework for stabilizing a parabolic equation defined on time-varying spatial domain. Although the partial differential equation (PDE) backstepping method provides a systematic theoretical framework for such moving-boundary systems, its real-time implementation is hindered by the need to repeatedly solve time-varying kernel PDEs on evolving domains. To overcome this limitation, we first formulate the time-varying backstepping design as an operator that maps the moving-boundary trajectory to the corresponding backstepping kernel. By mapping the time-varying domain of the backstepping kernel equation onto a fixed reference domain, we establish the continuous dependence of the kernel on the moving-boundary trajectory, which provides the theoretical basis for approximating the backstepping design operator by a neural operator. Based on the approximate kernel operator, we construct the corresponding boundary feedback controller to stabilize the system. It is shown that the closed-loop system admits an exponential decay estimate on any prescribed finite time interval. For numerical implementation, DeepONet is employed to learn the time-varying kernel operator from offline-generated numerical kernel solutions and is subsequently deployed online to generate the required time-varying kernels without repeatedly solving the kernel PDE. Numerical benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed neural-operator-based implementation bypasses repeated online solution of the time-varying kernel PDE, achieves a significant acceleration of close to three orders of magnitude compared with conventional numerical kernel solvers, and thus enables real-time stabilization of the system on time-varying spatial domain.
tldr: This paper uses neural operators to learn the backstepping kernel for boundary control of parabolic PDEs on time-varying domains, achieving real-time stabilization.
motivation: Real-time implementation of PDE backstepping control for moving-boundary systems is hindered by the need to repeatedly solve time-varying kernel PDEs.
method: The backstepping design is formulated as an operator mapping the moving-boundary trajectory to the kernel, and a DeepONet is trained to approximate this operator from offline data.
result: The neural-operator-based controller achieves exponential stability on finite time intervals and accelerates computation by nearly three orders of magnitude compared to conventional solvers.
conclusion: The proposed learning-based framework enables real-time stabilization of parabolic equations on time-varying domains, bypassing repeated online kernel PDE solutions.

title: Optimizing The Principal Coefficient Of Elliptic Equations Using $L^p$-regularity, $p < \infty$
authors: Ala' Alalabi, Lorena Bociu, Paul Manns
abstract: ArXiv:2606.17788v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study coefficient identification problems for elliptic partial differential equations with total variation regularization and control constraints. Existing related literature relies on continuity and differentiability properties of the control-to-state operator with respect to the [MATH]-norm. While this is sufficient for deriving optimality conditions, it is not well-suited for numerical algorithms, as it neglects the spatial extent of perturbations and leads to a qualitative discrepancy compared to [MATH]-norms with [MATH]. In this work, we address this gap by exploiting [MATH]-regularity results to establish differentiability properties of the control-to-state operator with respect to [MATH]-norms for finite [MATH]. Based on this framework, we derive first- and second-order differentiability results for the reduced objective functional and establish first-order optimality conditions involving a restricted subdifferential characterization of the total variation seminorm and corresponding regularity of the associated multipliers. Building on this, we analyze a nonsmooth trust-region method based on an [MATH]-trust region for [MATH] and prove its convergence to first-order stationary points.
tldr: This paper studies coefficient identification for elliptic PDEs with total variation regularization using Lp-regularity for p<∞.
motivation: Existing methods rely on L∞-norm differentiability, which is not well-suited for numerical algorithms due to neglect of spatial extent of perturbations.
method: The authors exploit Lp-regularity results to establish differentiability of the control-to-state operator in Lp-norms, derive optimality conditions, and analyze a nonsmooth trust-region method.
result: They prove convergence of the trust-region method to first-order stationary points under the Lp framework.
conclusion: The Lp-based approach bridges the gap between theory and numerics for PDE-constrained optimization with total variation regularization.

title: Cross-connections Of The Normed Algebra Of Finite Rank Bounded Operators On A Hilbert Space
authors: P. G. Romeo A. Anju
abstract: ArXiv:2606.17796v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this article we examine the cross-connections of the normal category of finite dimensional subspaces of a Hilbert space and it's dual space. Further, we describe the cross-connection semigroup of cones, which is a normed algebra isomrphic to the normed algebra of finite rank bounded operators on a Hilbert space. We also characterize compact operators and their spectrum by the normal cones in the normal category of proper subspaces of a Hilbert space.
tldr: This paper studies cross-connections in the normed algebra of finite rank bounded operators on a Hilbert space, focusing on categorical and algebraic structures rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: To understand the algebraic and categorical structure of finite rank operators and compact operators on Hilbert spaces via cross-connections.
method: Uses category theory and normed algebra to analyze normal cones and cross-connection semigroups.
result: Describes a normed algebra isomorphic to the algebra of finite rank bounded operators and characterizes compact operators via normal cones.
conclusion: The cross-connection approach provides an algebraic framework for studying operator algebras, but has no direct application to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Kalman Structure And Observability For Transport Systems
authors: Yacouba Simpore
abstract: ArXiv:2606.17814v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study observability and controllability for constant-coefficient first-order hyperbolic systems on the real line when only part of the state is observed or controlled. Even when the Kalman rank condition holds, the usual \(L^2(\mathbb R)^N\)-observability estimate may fail because some components are detected only through the dynamics. We show that the Kalman structure determines the appropriate observability estimate. A component that becomes visible after \(k\) algebraic steps is measured at low Fourier frequencies with a weight of order \(|\xi|^{2k}\) in the Fourier variable. This yields a natural Kalman-adapted observation space for the system. We also prove localized observability for diagonalizable systems on observation sets with uniformly bounded gaps and, separately, extend the whole-line construction to systems with real spectrum and Jordan blocks.
tldr: This paper studies observability and controllability for constant-coefficient first-order hyperbolic systems on the real line, focusing on the Kalman structure and its effect on observability estimates.
motivation: To understand how partial observation or control affects observability estimates for hyperbolic systems, especially when the Kalman rank condition holds but standard estimates fail.
method: The authors analyze the Kalman structure of the system to derive weighted Fourier estimates for components that become visible after algebraic steps, and prove localized observability for diagonalizable systems.
result: They show that the Kalman structure determines the appropriate observability estimate, with components visible after k steps measured at low Fourier frequencies with weight |ξ|^{2k}, and extend results to systems with real spectrum and Jordan blocks.
conclusion: The Kalman structure provides a natural adapted observation space, and localized observability holds for diagonalizable systems on observation sets with uniformly bounded gaps.

title: On Injectivity Of Phase Retrieval
authors: Zhangsong Li
abstract: ArXiv:2606.17922v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this short note, we prove that if [MATH] with [MATH] has i.i.d.\ standard complex Gaussian entries, then the probability that the phase retrieval map generated by [MATH] is not injective is positive. This proves Part (1) of a conjecture of Cynthia Vinzant, which was later restated by Afonso S. Bandeira in . The main result of this paper was obtained using generative AI, in particular the Rethlas system.
tldr: Proves that phase retrieval maps with i.i.d. standard complex Gaussian matrices are not injective with positive probability.
motivation: To resolve a conjecture about injectivity of phase retrieval maps, which is a problem in signal processing and applied mathematics.
method: Uses probabilistic arguments and properties of Gaussian random matrices to show non-injectivity.
result: Shows that the probability of non-injectivity is positive for such matrices.
conclusion: Part (1) of the conjecture is proven; the result is obtained with the aid of generative AI.

title: A Stone-Cech Collecting Semantics For Residual Process Behaviour
authors: Mike Stannett
abstract: ArXiv:2606.17228v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper develops a compact collecting semantics for the residual behaviour left by nonterminating computation. For sequential time this is the tail-cluster set of the stream in the Stone-Cech compactification of the observation space. It gives a common semantics to ordinary recurrence, mixed recurrent behaviour, and escape through noncompact parts of the observation space. The basic theory establishes tail invariance, functoriality under continuous observations, and a temporal reading for clopen observations: containment in the corresponding clopen region of beta-X is eventual truth, while nonempty intersection is recurrence. Progress and fairness assumptions are represented by strengthening the time filter. Relational meanings are obtained by compactifying products, so correlations between observations made along the same asymptotic view of time are retained. The main application is to residual behaviour in CCS. Infinite executions are read as streams of residual processes modulo structural congruence. The resulting semantics distinguishes stable divergence, finite recurrent divergence, mixed recurrence with escape, and escape through unbounded residual growth. It validates residual-tail laws for prefixing, guarded unfolding, finite choice, and finite prefix-choice forms, while also identifying the boundary of those laws under parallel composition and synchronisation. Finite observational quotients provide the computational interface to the compact semantics: abstract meanings become recurrent states and strongly connected component calculations, and resource observations detect unbounded escape without requiring individual points of the Stone-Cech remainder to be inspected.
tldr: Develops a compact semantics for residual process behavior using Stone-Cech compactification, applied to CCS.
motivation: To provide a unified semantic framework for nonterminating computation, including recurrence and divergence.
method: Uses Stone-Cech compactification of observation space to define tail-cluster sets and tail invariance.
result: Distinguishes stable divergence, finite recurrent divergence, mixed recurrence with escape, and unbounded residual growth.
conclusion: The semantics validates residual-tail laws for process algebra constructs and identifies boundaries under parallel composition.

title: Syntactic Systems Cannot See Semantic Invariants
authors: Fabio F. G. Buono
abstract: ArXiv:2606.17275v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We start from a small open question, where Hetzl and Vierling asked whether two theories of induction, open induction and clause set cycles, are incomparable. They proved one direction and left the other open. Here we close it, and the proof is almost embarrassingly short, because the rules for addition can only fire when the first argument is [MATH] or a successor, a Skolem constant is neither, so the terms [MATH] and [MATH] can never be touched, and a machine that can never touch them can never prove they are equal. The thing that separates the two theories is the order of two constants, and that order is a fact about numbers, not about symbols. We extract from this proof a small general principle, the Syntactic Invariance Principle, that names the shape of such arguments. We then close with a few speculative remarks on how this same shape appears, informally, in the known barriers to settling [MATH] versus [MATH], where each barrier seems to point to a level of description that the techniques in the barrier cannot reach. We raise this as a suggestion rather than a theorem, since the analogy is real but we do not push it past the point where we can defend it. Along the way we raise an open question that the analogy suggests but does not settle, on whether a fast algorithm for [MATH], were it to exist, would always be exhibitable as a machine you can write down or whether it could be found, in some cases, only as a function on the numbers.
tldr: The paper discusses a syntactic invariance principle in proof theory and its speculative analogy to barriers in complexity theory, with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.
motivation: To resolve an open question about the incomparability of two induction theories and to extract a general principle about syntactic versus semantic reasoning.
method: The author provides a short proof that clause set cycles cannot prove the equality of two Skolem constants, then generalizes this to the Syntactic Invariance Principle, and draws informal analogies to P vs NP barriers.
result: The open question is closed with a simple proof, and a principle is formulated that highlights limitations of syntactic systems in capturing semantic invariants.
conclusion: The syntactic invariance principle may offer a new perspective on known barriers in complexity theory, but this remains speculative.

title: Sa-ra-jscc: SNR-Adaptive And Semantic-Rate-Aware Joint Source-Channel Coding
authors: Shitong Zhang, Yaping Sun, Hao Chen, Xiaoyi Li, Bo Gu, Xiaodong Xu, Nan Ma
abstract: ArXiv:2606.17940v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In joint source-channel coding (JSCC)-based semantic communication systems, achieving stable and reliable image semantic transmission under channel constraints remains a key challenge. In most channel adaptation modules, the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) is often injected into each layer of a channel-adaptation model in an independent and layer-wise manner, which undermines global coordination across layers. Therefore, consistent noise-robust representations may fail to be learned throughout the model. To address this problem, we propose SA-RA-JSCC, a novel channel-adaptive JSCC model. SA-RA-JSCC maps SNR into a unified semantic vector in the feature space and then applies a one-shot global reweighting to the encoded features, thereby enabling globally consistent and learnable channel adaptation. Moreover, in order to further enhance the anti-channel capability of semantic information, a semantic-rate-aware module is introduced, enabling the adaptive policy to respond simultaneously to fluctuations in channel quality and changes in semantic-rate constraints, thereby enhancing global network coordination and channel adaptivity. Extensive experiment results across multiple channels and datasets demonstrate that SA-RA-JSCC significantly outperforms existing semantic communication models in terms of reconstruction metrics such as PSNR and MS-SSIM, exhibiting stronger robustness across a broad range of SNR regimes.
tldr: A joint source-channel coding scheme for semantic communication that adapts to SNR and semantic rate.
motivation: Existing JSCC models lack global coordination across layers when adapting to channel SNR, leading to suboptimal noise-robust representations.
method: Proposes SA-RA-JSCC which maps SNR into a unified semantic vector for global reweighting of encoded features, and adds a semantic-rate-aware module for joint adaptation.
result: Outperforms existing semantic communication models in PSNR and MS-SSIM across various channels and SNR regimes.
conclusion: The proposed method achieves more robust and adaptive image transmission under channel constraints.

title: An Empirical Analysis Of Ai Slop In Music Streaming
authors: Stanley Wu, Josephine Passananti, Viresh Mittal, Wenxin Ding, Haitao Zheng, Ben Y. Zhao
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18052v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generative AI models lower the bar for content creation, making it easy for any user to create professional-looking images, text and music with minimal effort. This has enabled a new cottage industry around creation of "AI slop" mass quantities of mediocre content produced to generate revenue, often through misrepresentation as human-authored content, or scams involving automated scripts and fake consumption. While there are obvious parallels between the AI-slop industry and "traditional" email spam networks, it might be too early to determine if AI slop generation can grow into a similar self-sustaining industry. In this paper, we look specifically at the music industry, and explore the question: Can we prevent AI music slop from growing into a self-sustaining shadow industry? To answer this question, we characterize the current state of AI slop in music, and its pipeline from generation, distribution, and consumption by users on streaming platforms. By examining growth and engagement on Spotify, we confirm that AI music exhibits AI slop characteristics: the overwhelming majority (93%) of AI music receive few, if any listener plays, and are rarely recommended. AI musicians "spray and pray," releasing large volumes of music across multiple genres in hopes of generating a hit. We also explore the AI slop pipeline by generating and publishing our own AI tracks onto streaming through 11 indie music distributors. We find distributors have inconsistent and largely unenforced policies on AI music, making it surprisingly easy to publish mass produced AI songs. Finally, we consider AI music detection, and find that current methods lack accuracy or robustness. As generation costs decrease, we believe slop generation in music will become self-sustainable, unless concrete steps are taken by the music industry. We consider and discuss potential mitigation methods based on our findings.
tldr: This paper analyzes the phenomenon of AI-generated music slop on streaming platforms, its distribution, and potential mitigation strategies.
motivation: To determine whether AI music slop can become a self-sustaining industry and to characterize its current state.
method: The authors analyze Spotify data, publish their own AI-generated tracks through distributors, and evaluate AI music detection methods.
result: 93% of AI music receives few plays, distributors have inconsistent policies, and current detection methods are inaccurate.
conclusion: Without industry action, AI slop in music will become self-sustaining as generation costs decrease.

title: Learning Red Agent Policy From Observations For Neurosymbolic Autonomous Cyber Agents
authors: Ankita Samaddar, Sandeep Neema, Daniel Balasubramanian, Xenofon Koutsoukos
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18223v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: With sophisticated cyber-attacks becoming increasingly prevalent, modern networks require intelligent autonomous cyber-defense agents trained via Reinforcement Learning (RL). These agents employ neurosymbolic approaches such as behavior trees with learning-enabled components (LECs) to learn, reason, adapt, and implement security rules while maintaining critical operations. However, these autonomous networks are partially observable systems, i.e., the cyber-attacker's (red agent's) actions are not observable, making it difficult for the defender to predict red actions, learn red policies, or assess the attacker's intrusion levels. To address this, we propose a Policy Learning Technique using imitation learning to learn policies for partially observable RL agents with discrete states and discrete actions. We apply this technique in an autonomous cyber environment to predict red agent's actions from network observations and defender actions. Integrated with a neurosymbolic cyber-defense agent, our method effectively handles different red policies and achieves high prediction accuracy across diverse simulated scenarios.
tldr: This paper uses imitation learning to predict attacker actions in autonomous cyber defense, with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: Autonomous cyber-defense agents need to predict attacker actions in partially observable environments to improve security.
method: The authors propose a policy learning technique based on imitation learning to infer the red agent's policy from network observations and defender actions.
result: The method achieves high prediction accuracy across diverse simulated cyber scenarios.
conclusion: Imitation learning can effectively predict attacker policies in autonomous cyber environments, enhancing neurosymbolic defense agents.

Using particle-in-cell simulations to study nonrelativistic laser pulse propagation in an under-critical plasma, we identify a novel mechanism that occurs during the growth of turbulent magnetic loops: electron penetration heating. The loops have an electromagnetic left-hand chirality distinct from …


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 065205] Published Mon Jun 08, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies electron penetration heating in turbulent magnetic loops driven by nonrelativistic laser-plasma interaction using particle-in-cell simulations.
motivation: To understand a novel heating mechanism in laser-plasma interactions relevant to laboratory astrophysics and inertial confinement fusion.
method: Particle-in-cell simulations of nonrelativistic laser pulse propagation in under-critical plasma.
result: Identified electron penetration heating during growth of turbulent magnetic loops with left-hand chirality.
conclusion: The mechanism may impact energy transport in magnetized plasmas.

title: When Surface Dynamics Fakes Symmetry: Oxygen On Rh(100) Revisited
authors: Lutz Hammer, Tilman Kißlinger, Margareta Wagner, Reinhard B. Neder, Michael Schmid, Ulrike Diebold, And M. Alexander Schneider
abstract:
Author(s): Lutz Hammer, Tilman Kißlinger, Margareta Wagner, Reinhard B. Neder, Michael Schmid, Ulrike Diebold, and M. Alexander Schneider

Heating a long-range ordered adsorbate phase beyond its stability temperature does not necessarily result in a disordered phase; it can also break up into heavily fluctuating ordered domains. Temporal and/or spatial averaging over these fluctuations may give the impression of both a wrong periodicit…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023296] Published Mon Jun 15, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies oxygen adsorption on Rh(100) surface, revealing that fluctuating ordered domains can mimic a wrong surface symmetry under averaging.
motivation: Understanding the behavior of adsorbate phases on metal surfaces is important for surface science, but the paper does not connect to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
method: The authors use scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) and low-energy electron diffraction (LEED) to observe the surface structure and dynamics, combined with density functional theory (DFT) calculations.
result: They find that above the stability temperature, the ordered phase breaks into fluctuating domains that, when averaged, appear to have a different periodicity, leading to a misinterpretation of the surface symmetry.
conclusion: Care must be taken in interpreting averaged surface measurements, as dynamic fluctuations can create false symmetry signals.

title: Revealing Charge Anisotropies In Metal Compounds Via High-purity X-ray Polarimetry
authors: Lena Scherthan, Juliusz A. Wolny, Isabelle Faus, Olaf Leupold, Kai S. Schulze, Sebastian Höfer, Robert Loetzsch, Berit Marx-Glowna, Christopher E. Anson, Annie K. Powell, Ingo Uschmann, Hans-Christian Wille, Gerhard G. Paulus, Volker Schünemann, And Ralf Röhlsberger

Linear polarization analysis of hard x-rays is employed to probe electronic anisotropies in metal-containing complexes with high selectivity. We use polarization-resolved nuclear forward scattering (PR-NFS) of synchrotron radiation at the 14.4 keV nuclear resonance of [MATH] to determine…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023297] Published Mon Jun 15, 2026.
tldr: This paper uses high-purity X-ray polarimetry to probe charge anisotropies in metal compounds via nuclear forward scattering.
motivation: Understanding electronic anisotropies in metal complexes is important for materials science, but the paper does not connect to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
method: The authors employ polarization-resolved nuclear forward scattering (PR-NFS) of synchrotron radiation at the 14.4 keV nuclear resonance of 57Fe to measure linear polarization of hard X-rays.
result: The technique reveals charge anisotropies in metal-containing complexes with high selectivity.
conclusion: High-purity X-ray polarimetry is a powerful tool for probing electronic structure, but the work is purely in condensed matter characterization without quantum information or thermodynamics relevance.

title: Commissioning And Full Realization Of A Collinear Resonance Ionization Spectroscopy Setup At Beijing Radioactive Ion-beam Facility
authors: W. C. Mei et Al.
abstract:
Author(s): W. C. Mei et al.

A PLASEN (Precision LAser Spectroscopy for Exotic Nuclei) system, consisting of a compact radio-frequency quadrupole cooler buncher (RFQ-cb) and a collinear resonance ionization spectroscopy setup, has now been fully commissioned with radioactive ion beams at the Beijing Radioactive Ion-beam Facilit…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023286] Published Fri Jun 12, 2026.
tldr: This paper describes the commissioning of a collinear resonance ionization spectroscopy setup for exotic nuclei at a radioactive ion-beam facility.
motivation: To enable precision laser spectroscopy of short-lived isotopes for nuclear structure studies.
method: A PLASEN system combining a radio-frequency quadrupole cooler buncher with collinear resonance ionization spectroscopy was installed and tested with radioactive beams.
result: The setup was successfully commissioned, demonstrating its capability for high-resolution spectroscopy of exotic nuclei.
conclusion: The system is now operational and will be used for nuclear physics experiments.

title: Excitation Of Confined Bulk Plasmons In Metallic Nanoparticles By Penetrating Electron Beams Within A Nonlocal Analytical Approach
authors: Mattin Urbieta, Eduardo Ogando, Alberto Rivacoba, Javier Aizpurua, And Nerea Zabala
abstract:
Author(s): Mattin Urbieta, Eduardo Ogando, Alberto Rivacoba, Javier Aizpurua, and Nerea Zabala

Using a linear hydrodynamic model, we theoretically investigate the interaction between penetrating electron beams and sub-5-nm metallic spherical nanoparticles. We derive an analytical expression of the electron energy loss probability that includes nonlocal effects in the response of the confined …


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023279] Published Thu Jun 11, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies electron energy loss in metallic nanoparticles using a nonlocal hydrodynamic model, focusing on plasmon excitation.
motivation: To understand nonlocal effects in the optical response of sub-5-nm metallic nanoparticles when probed by penetrating electron beams.
method: A linear hydrodynamic model is used to derive an analytical expression for the electron energy loss probability, incorporating nonlocal dielectric response.
result: The analytical expression reveals how nonlocal effects modify the energy loss spectrum compared to local approximations.
conclusion: Nonlocal effects are significant for small nanoparticles and must be included for accurate interpretation of electron energy loss spectroscopy.

title: Membrane-associated Self-assembly For Cellular Decision-making
authors: Samuel L. Foley And Margaret E. Johnson
abstract:
Author(s): Samuel L. Foley and Margaret E. Johnson

Cellular decision-making based on information received from the external environment is frequently initiated by transmembrane receptors. These receptors are known to propagate such information by triggering a series of irreversible, energy-consuming reactions. While this active mechanism ensures swi…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023280] Published Thu Jun 11, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies membrane-associated self-assembly for cellular decision-making, a topic in biophysics and systems biology.
motivation: Understanding how cells process external signals to make decisions is fundamental to biology and medicine.
method: The authors use computational modeling and simulations to study self-assembly of membrane-bound proteins.
result: They show that self-assembly can act as a switch for cellular decisions, with timescales and thresholds tunable by parameters.
conclusion: Membrane self-assembly provides a robust mechanism for cellular decision-making without active energy consumption.

title: Visualizing Bulk Band Structure In ${\mathrm{Fe}}_{4}\mathrm{N}$ Thin Films By Spin- And Angle-resolved Photoelectron Spectroscopy
authors: Karen Nakanishi, Masaaki Kakoki, Kiyotaka Ohwada, Kenta Kuroda, Kazuki Sumida, Hitoshi Sato, Koji Miyamoto, Taichi Okuda, Shinji Isogami, Keisuke Masuda, Yuya Sakuraba, And Akio Kimura
abstract:
Author(s): Karen Nakanishi, Masaaki Kakoki, Kiyotaka Ohwada, Kenta Kuroda, Kazuki Sumida, Hitoshi Sato, Koji Miyamoto, Taichi Okuda, Shinji Isogami, Keisuke Masuda, Yuya Sakuraba, and Akio Kimura

The bulk band structure of an in situ prepared ferromagnetic [MATH] thin film has been investigated using spin- and angle-resolved photoelectron spectroscopy with synchrotron radiation. It was observed that most of the bands near the Fermi level are of minority spin. The exper…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023257] Published Mon Jun 08, 2026.
tldr: This paper uses spin- and angle-resolved photoelectron spectroscopy to visualize the bulk band structure of ferromagnetic Fe4N thin films.
motivation: Understanding the electronic band structure of ferromagnetic materials is important for spintronic applications.
method: Spin- and angle-resolved photoelectron spectroscopy with synchrotron radiation was performed on in situ prepared Fe4N thin films.
result: Most bands near the Fermi level are of minority spin, and the experimental band structure agrees well with first-principles calculations.
conclusion: The study provides detailed insight into the spin-dependent electronic structure of Fe4N, relevant for spintronics.

title: Tracking Ultrafast Ion Diffusion Dynamics In ${\mathrm{AgCrSe}}_{2}$ Superionic Conductor
authors: Jianmin Yang, Lin Xie, Mingyuan Hu, Yingpeng Qi, Jun Li, Baohai Jia, Jianghe Feng, Zijing Chen, Michel Bosman, Dao Xiang, And Jiaqing He

Direct spatial and temporal characterization of ion diffusion in superionic conductors provides a better link to macroscopic properties and high-performance material design.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021024] Published Fri May 01, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies ultrafast ion diffusion dynamics in a superionic conductor using experimental techniques.
motivation: Understanding ion diffusion in superionic conductors is important for designing high-performance materials.
method: The authors use direct spatial and temporal characterization methods to track ion motion.
result: They provide detailed dynamics of ion diffusion in AgCrSe2.

title: Effect Of Glass Stability On The Low Frequency Vibrations Of Vapor Deposited Glasses
authors: I. Festi, E. Alfinelli, D. Bessas, F. Caporaletti, A. I. Chumakov, M. Moratalla, M. A. Ramos, M. Rodríguez-López, C. Rodríguez-Tinoco, J. Rodríguez-Viejo, And G. Baldi
abstract:
Author(s): I. Festi, E. Alfinelli, D. Bessas, F. Caporaletti, A. I. Chumakov, M. Moratalla, M. A. Ramos, M. Rodríguez-López, C. Rodríguez-Tinoco, J. Rodríguez-Viejo, and G. Baldi

An improved inelastic x-ray scattering technique helps clarify the connections between complex vibrations and the properties of glasses.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021021] Published Tue Apr 28, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies low-frequency vibrations in vapor-deposited glasses using inelastic x-ray scattering, focusing on the effect of glass stability.
motivation: Understanding the vibrational properties of glasses is important for their mechanical and thermal behavior, but the connection between stability and low-frequency vibrations is not well understood.
method: The authors use an improved inelastic x-ray scattering technique to measure the vibrational density of states in vapor-deposited glasses with varying stability.
result: They find that more stable glasses exhibit suppressed low-frequency vibrational modes, indicating a correlation between stability and the boson peak.
conclusion: The results provide insight into the microscopic origin of the boson peak and the role of glass stability in determining vibrational properties.

title: Fundamentals Of Vacuum Breakdown In High-gradient Accelerator Structures
authors: Walter Wuensch, Sergio Calatroni, Flyura Djurabekova, Andreas Kyritsakis, And Yinon Ashkenazy
abstract:
Author(s): Walter Wuensch, Sergio Calatroni, Flyura Djurabekova, Andreas Kyritsakis, and Yinon Ashkenazy

Vacuum breakdown or arcing happens when a very strong electric field causes a metal surface in a vacuum to suddenly form plasma, allowing large electrical currents to flow. Breakdown can damage particle accelerators, fusion reactors, satellites, and x-ray devices, though it is useful in technologies like plasma thrusters. Scientists have studied this unpredictable and fast phenomenon for over a century. Recent advances in experiments and computer simulations now provide a coherent mechanistic picture: tiny surface defects, electrical stress, heat, and emitted particles interact in complex ways to trigger breakdowns. These insights could improve high-power technologies and make advanced accelerators more reliable and efficient.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025004] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews the physics of vacuum breakdown in high-gradient accelerator structures, focusing on surface defects, electric fields, and plasma formation.
motivation: Vacuum breakdown limits the performance of particle accelerators and other high-voltage devices; understanding its mechanism is crucial for improving reliability.
method: The authors synthesize experimental observations and computer simulations to build a coherent mechanistic picture of the breakdown process.
result: A multi-step model involving surface defects, electrical stress, heating, and particle emission explains the onset of vacuum arcs.
conclusion: Insights from this work can help design more robust accelerator structures and other high-power technologies.

title: Radiation Forces And Torques In Optics And Acoustics
authors: Ivan Toftul, Sebastian Golat, Francisco J. Rodríguez-Fortuño, Franco Nori, Yuri Kivshar, And Konstantin Y. Bliokh
abstract:
Author(s): Ivan Toftul, Sebastian Golat, Francisco J. Rodríguez-Fortuño, Franco Nori, Yuri Kivshar, and Konstantin Y. Bliokh

This review presents a unified perspective of how local energy, momentum, and spin densities in optical and acoustic wave fields induce forces and torques on particles—a topic that has captivated researchers for centuries. Applications discussed include trapping and manipulation of atoms and nanoparticles by light, sorting of biological cells by the combination of acoustics and microfluidics, and pulling forces that draw particles against the direction of wave propagation.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025002] Published Thu Apr 30, 2026.
tldr: A review of radiation forces and torques in optics and acoustics, focusing on classical wave-matter interactions.
motivation: To provide a unified perspective on how local energy, momentum, and spin densities in wave fields induce forces and torques on particles.
method: Review of theoretical and experimental work on optical and acoustic radiation forces, including trapping, sorting, and pulling effects.
result: Summarizes key mechanisms and applications of radiation forces and torques in both optics and acoustics.
conclusion: The field has broad applications in particle manipulation, but the paper does not connect to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Pressure Effects On Metals, Alloys, And Compounds Of Transplutonium Elements
authors: Tyler W. Hines, Nicholas B. Beck, Kacy N. Mendoza, Joseph M. Sperling, And Thomas E. Albrecht
abstract:
Author(s): Tyler W. Hines, Nicholas B. Beck, Kacy N. Mendoza, Joseph M. Sperling, and Thomas E. Albrecht

Materials containing transplutonium elements (the actinides Am–Cm that come after Pu in the periodic table) are important for nuclear power, nuclear waste management, and long-term storage. They also have fascinating properties, with 5
[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 015004] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: A review of the physics and chemistry of transplutonium elements under high pressure, focusing on their electronic properties and applications in nuclear energy.
motivation: Transplutonium materials are important for nuclear power and waste management, and their 5f electrons exhibit unique behavior at the boundary of localization and itinerancy.
method: The paper reviews experimental and theoretical studies of metals, alloys, compounds, and coordination complexes under high pressure, addressing challenges due to radioactivity and complex electronic structure.
result: The review summarizes the current understanding of pressure-induced changes in electronic structure, bonding, and phase transitions in transplutonium materials.
conclusion: The work expands knowledge of heavy-element behavior under extreme conditions, but does not directly connect to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Colloquium: Multimessenger Astronomy With Continuous Gravitational Waves And Future Detectors
authors: Benjamin J. Owen
abstract:
Author(s): Benjamin J. Owen

The search for continuous gravitational waves from rotating neutron stars represents a key frontier of gravitational-wave astrophysics, with strong connections to electromagnetic astronomy, nuclear astrophysics, and condensed matter physics. This Colloquium discusses the detection prospects for these long-lived yet elusive signals in the upcoming generation of gravitational-wave detectors, emphasizing the importance of simultaneous electromagnetic observations. It also surveys the potential implications of such multimessenger observations for our understanding of the physical and astrophysical processes taking place in the extremely dense environments of their sources.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011002] Published Tue Mar 10, 2026.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews the prospects for detecting continuous gravitational waves from rotating neutron stars and their multimessenger connections.
motivation: Continuous gravitational waves are a key frontier in gravitational-wave astrophysics, with implications for nuclear astrophysics and condensed matter physics.
method: The paper surveys detection prospects for upcoming gravitational-wave detectors and discusses simultaneous electromagnetic observations.
result: It highlights the potential of multimessenger observations to understand dense environments in neutron stars.
conclusion: Multimessenger astronomy with continuous gravitational waves will provide new insights into neutron star physics.

title: Neutron Stars And The Dense Matter Equation Of State
authors: Katerina Chatziioannou, H. Thankful Cromartie, Stefano Gandolfi, Ingo Tews, David Radice, Andrew W. Steiner, And Anna L. Watts
abstract:
Author(s): Katerina Chatziioannou, H. Thankful Cromartie, Stefano Gandolfi, Ingo Tews, David Radice, Andrew W. Steiner, and Anna L. Watts

Neutron stars, the remnants of supernova explosions, are the densest objects in the Universe. A typical neutron star has a mass between one and two solar masses, and a radius of around 12 km. The density at the center of the star is higher than that in atomic nuclei. As a result, the properties of neutron stars provide important information about the behavior of ordinary matter under extreme compression. In recent years, new information about neutron stars has emerged from two sources. The first is the observation of the gravitational-wave signal from the final inspiral of a coalescing binary neutron star. The second is a careful measurement of the x-ray pulse profile of a spinning neutron star. This review discusses these measurements and summarizes how they constrain masses, radii, and central densities. The results are compared to predictions based on calculations of the nuclear equation of state at densities comparable to that in atomic nuclei, which are then extrapolated to higher density. The review ends with an outlook on future observational opportunities.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045007] Published Wed Dec 24, 2025.
tldr: A review of neutron star observations and the dense matter equation of state, focusing on gravitational waves and X-ray pulse profiles.
motivation: Neutron stars are the densest objects in the universe, and their properties provide crucial tests of nuclear physics under extreme conditions.
method: The paper reviews recent observational results from gravitational-wave signals (binary neutron star mergers) and X-ray pulse profile measurements, comparing them to theoretical predictions of the nuclear equation of state.
result: The measurements constrain neutron star masses, radii, and central densities, and are compared to extrapolations of nuclear equation of state models.
conclusion: Future observations will further refine our understanding of dense matter, but the paper does not directly address quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Nobel Lecture: Physics Is A Point Of View
authors: John J. Hopfield
abstract:
Author(s): John J. Hopfield

The 2024 Nobel Prize for Physics was shared by John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton. This paper is the text of the address given in conjunction with the award.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 030501] Published Mon Aug 25, 2025.
tldr: Nobel lecture by John Hopfield reflecting on his career and the interdisciplinary nature of physics.
motivation: To share personal insights and perspectives on physics as a field of study.
method: Narrative and reflective lecture.
result: No new scientific results; a retrospective on the development of neural networks and physics.
conclusion: Physics is a way of thinking that can inspire discoveries across disciplines.

title: Nobel Lecture: Boltzmann Machines
authors: Geoffrey Hinton
abstract:
Author(s): Geoffrey Hinton

The 2024 Nobel Prize for Physics was shared by John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton. This paper is the text of the address given in conjunction with the award.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 030502] Published Mon Aug 25, 2025.
tldr: This is the Nobel lecture by Geoffrey Hinton on Boltzmann machines, a foundational concept in machine learning.
motivation: To present the development and significance of Boltzmann machines in the context of artificial neural networks and their impact on physics and computer science.
method: The lecture reviews the history, theory, and applications of Boltzmann machines, including their connection to statistical physics.
result: Boltzmann machines are a class of stochastic neural networks that can learn complex probability distributions, serving as a precursor to modern deep learning.
conclusion: Boltzmann machines have had a profound influence on machine learning and illustrate the cross-fertilization between physics and computer science.

title: Order And Disorder At The Atomic Scale: Microscopy Applied To Semiconductors
authors: Enrico Di Russo, Tom Verstijnen, Paul Koenraad, Konstantinos Pantzas, Gilles Patriarche, And Lorenzo Rigutti
abstract:
Author(s): Enrico Di Russo, Tom Verstijnen, Paul Koenraad, Konstantinos Pantzas, Gilles Patriarche, and Lorenzo Rigutti

Atomic-scale details, especially those of disorder, are important for material properties, especially in semiconductors, but they are also extremely difficult to measure. Real-space methods can give direct access to this information, but typically, that access is limited. This review reports the application of three real-space techniques for measuring disorder to compound semiconductor materials: scanning tunneling microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and atom-probe microscopy. Where possible, it emphasizes cases in which the probes have been combined to achieve a more complete picture of the defects.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025006] Published Thu Jun 26, 2025.
tldr: A review of real-space microscopy techniques for measuring atomic-scale disorder in semiconductors.
motivation: Atomic-scale disorder critically affects semiconductor properties but is difficult to measure; the paper reviews three real-space techniques to address this challenge.
method: The authors review scanning tunneling microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and atom-probe microscopy, emphasizing combined use for a complete defect picture.
result: The review highlights capabilities and limitations of each technique and cases where combining them yields more comprehensive disorder characterization.
conclusion: Real-space microscopy techniques, especially when combined, provide direct access to atomic-scale disorder in semiconductors, which is essential for understanding material properties.

title: Quantum Physics Of Stars
authors: M. Wiescher, C. A. Bertulani, C. R. Brune, R. J. Deboer, A. Diaz-Torres, L. R. Gasques, K. Langanke, P. Navrátil, W. Nazarewicz, J. Okołowicz, D. R. Phillips, M. Płoszajczak, S. Quaglioni, And A. Tumino
abstract:
Author(s): M. Wiescher, C. A. Bertulani, C. R. Brune, R. J. deBoer, A. Diaz-Torres, L. R. Gasques, K. Langanke, P. Navrátil, W. Nazarewicz, J. Okołowicz, D. R. Phillips, M. Płoszajczak, S. Quaglioni, and A. Tumino

There are many nuclear reactions that are of central importance for stellar burning and element formation. In typical stars, these reactions take place at very low energy, and many of them have very small rates, making it difficult to measure them directly in the laboratory. On the theoretical side, the low-energy regime is governed by quantum-mechanical phenomena like tunneling, near-threshold resonances, and interference effects. This review summarizes the state of the art in the theory of low-energy nuclear reactions in stars and describes new ideas for studying these reactions on Earth.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025003] Published Tue May 27, 2025.
tldr: A review of low-energy nuclear reactions in stars, focusing on quantum tunneling and resonance phenomena.
motivation: Understanding nuclear reactions in stars is crucial for stellar burning and element formation, but many reactions are difficult to measure directly due to low rates.
method: The paper reviews theoretical approaches including quantum tunneling, near-threshold resonances, and interference effects, and discusses experimental techniques for studying these reactions on Earth.
result: Summarizes the state of the art in low-energy nuclear reaction theory and outlines new ideas for laboratory measurements.
conclusion: Quantum mechanical effects dominate low-energy stellar reactions, and continued theoretical and experimental efforts are needed to improve our understanding.

title: Codata Recommended Values Of The Fundamental Physical Constants: 2022
authors: Peter J. Mohr, David B. Newell, Barry N. Taylor, And Eite Tiesinga
abstract:
Author(s): Peter J. Mohr, David B. Newell, Barry N. Taylor, and Eite Tiesinga

This review contains the 2022 self-consistent set of values of the constants and conversion factors of physics and chemistry recommended by the Committee on Data for Science and Technology (CODATA). The CODATA values are based on a least-squares adjustment that takes into account all data available up to the end of 2022. Details of the data selection and methodology are described.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025002] Published Wed Apr 30, 2025.
tldr: This paper presents the 2022 CODATA recommended values of fundamental physical constants.
motivation: Accurate and consistent values of fundamental constants are essential for science and technology.
method: A least-squares adjustment of all available experimental and theoretical data up to the end of 2022.
result: A self-consistent set of values and conversion factors for physics and chemistry.
conclusion: The CODATA 2022 values provide the most accurate and reliable set of fundamental constants to date.

title: The Need For Optoacoustic Microscopy
authors: Ludwig Englert, Dominik Jüstel, And Vasilis Ntziachristos
abstract:
Author(s): Ludwig Englert, Dominik Jüstel, and Vasilis Ntziachristos

Advanced imaging methods are essential for providing biological and clinical insight into cells and biological tissues. Optoacoustic imaging is one such method in which cells or tissues absorb short laser pulses and the resulting rise in temperature creates tiny ultrasound waves that can be detected by ultrasonic detectors placed outside the specimen. This noninvasive technique has the ability to look at optical contrast that is millimeters and even centimeters deep with high resolution. This review discusses the basic physics, how the method impacts biological and clinical research, and the latest developments in multimodal microscopy and imaging combining optical and optoacoustic techniques.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015005] Published Tue Mar 04, 2025.
tldr: This review discusses optoacoustic microscopy, a biomedical imaging technique that uses laser-induced ultrasound to image deep tissues with optical contrast.
motivation: Advanced imaging methods are needed to provide biological and clinical insight into cells and tissues, and optoacoustic imaging offers noninvasive deep-tissue imaging with high resolution.
method: The paper reviews the basic physics of optoacoustic imaging, where short laser pulses are absorbed by tissues, causing a temperature rise that generates ultrasound waves detected by external sensors.
result: The technique enables imaging of optical contrast at depths of millimeters to centimeters with high resolution, and recent developments combine optical and optoacoustic methods for multimodal microscopy.
conclusion: Optoacoustic microscopy is a valuable tool for biological and clinical research, but it is unrelated to the user's research interests in quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Wannier-function Software Ecosystem For Materials Simulations
authors: Antimo Marrazzo, Sophie Beck, Elena R. Margine, Nicola Marzari, Arash A. Mostofi, Junfeng Qiao, Ivo Souza, Stepan S. Tsirkin, Jonathan R. Yates, And Giovanni Pizzi
abstract:
Author(s): Antimo Marrazzo, Sophie Beck, Elena R. Margine, Nicola Marzari, Arash A. Mostofi, Junfeng Qiao, Ivo Souza, Stepan S. Tsirkin, Jonathan R. Yates, and Giovanni Pizzi

The description of the electronic structure in terms of extended Bloch states has made it possible to understand and calculate many properties in condensed-matter physics. However, understanding and insight often require a local description, and Wannier functions provide an exact and insightful map of extended reciprocal-space Bloch states into localized real-space orbitals. Applications range far and wide, from ultra-accurate integrations to topological invariants, and their widespread uptake by the electronic-structure community has resulted in a growing and interoperable ecosystem of methods and associated software tools. This review provides a description of this ecosystem that has now become a major instrument for the electronic-structure community in its pursuit of understanding, discovering, and designing materials.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 96, 045008] Published Mon Dec 23, 2024.
tldr: A review of the Wannier-function software ecosystem for materials simulations.
motivation: To provide a comprehensive overview of the methods and tools based on Wannier functions for electronic structure calculations.
method: The paper surveys various software packages and their interoperability, focusing on the generation and use of maximally localized Wannier functions.
result: It describes the ecosystem's capabilities for computing band structures, topological invariants, and other properties.
conclusion: The Wannier-function ecosystem is a major instrument for the electronic-structure community, enabling accurate and insightful materials simulations.

title: Kinetic Solitary Electrostatic Structures In Collisionless Plasma: Phase-space Holes
authors: I. H. Hutchinson
abstract:
Author(s): I. H. Hutchinson

Plasma is usually taught to be a quasineutral gas of charged and neutral particles that exhibits collective behavior. However, satellites regularly observe solitary potential structures in space plasmas that are isolated positive or negative potential humps, called electron or ion holes. In the 1970s, laboratory observations were made of electron holes. This review presents an overview of the observation of these electrostatic structures and presents their origin and their stability, using analytic theory and simulations. The role of kinetically unstable velocity distributions is identified as a key driver.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 96, 045007] Published Tue Dec 10, 2024.
tldr: A review of kinetic solitary electrostatic structures (phase-space holes) in collisionless plasma, covering observations, theory, and simulations.
motivation: To understand the origin, stability, and dynamics of isolated potential structures observed in space plasmas.
method: Review of satellite observations, analytic theory, and particle-in-cell simulations.
result: Phase-space holes arise from kinetically unstable velocity distributions and are stable over long times.
conclusion: These structures are ubiquitous in space plasmas and play a key role in plasma turbulence and transport.

title: Electron Spin Drift In Long-distance Plasma Wakefield Acceleration
authors: Ming Zeng And Dazhang Li Yilan Guo
abstract: Plasma based wakefield acceleration of polarized electron beams has recently attracted considerable research interest. Previous works have found the forced spin oscillation of electrons due to two-dimensional betatron oscillation in particle trajectory and discovered longitudinal depolarization mechanism in plasma wakefield. In this work, we present a three-dimensional analytical model for the electron spin dynamics and derive the evolution of polarization during long-distance plasma wakefield acceleration. Our analysis reveals several phenomena including a transverse rotational spin drift leading to depolarization, a reversal of the drift frequency, and a consequent recovery of polarization. This work can offer guidance on future plasma-based accelerators for polarized electron beams.
tldr: This paper presents a three-dimensional analytical model for electron spin dynamics in plasma wakefield acceleration, focusing on spin drift and depolarization.
motivation: Polarized electron beams are important for high-energy physics, but spin dynamics in plasma accelerators are not well understood, especially over long distances.
method: The authors develop a 3D analytical model for spin evolution, incorporating betatron oscillations and wakefield effects, and derive equations for polarization dynamics.
result: They find a transverse rotational spin drift that causes depolarization, a reversal of drift frequency, and a subsequent recovery of polarization.
conclusion: The work provides guidance for designing plasma-based accelerators that preserve electron beam polarization.

title: Mean Field Game Model Of The Impact Of Reductions In Support On Faculty Research Activity
authors: Robert A. Brownahttps://ror.org/05qwgg493faculty Of Computing & Data Sciences, Boston University, Boston, MA 02215
